GuardDuty is a threat detection service and does not inspect an image's package vulnerabilities. Checking only at build time misses CVEs disclosed afterward. The conditions that the deployment pipeline cannot be modified and that there is no capacity to build a scan schedule eliminate scan on push and the build-stage scan.

exam-dop-c02-17.prompt: A fintech company wants to track, per service, a latency objective of "99% of requests within 300 ms" and the error budget burn rate for 30 microservices running on Amazon EKS, and wants to receive alarms when the burn rate is high. The service teams use a mix of Java, Python, and Node.js and have different deployment schedules, so code changes cannot be coordinated at the same time. Changes to service code must be minimized, and the company also wants to avoid managing formulas that calculate objective attainment by hand. The objectives must be managed at the service and operation level, and metrics and traces are already collected in Amazon CloudWatch and AWS X-Ray. The SRE team has only 2 people. Calls between services use a mix of gRPC and HTTP, and the EKS cluster already collects metrics with Container Insights. The company wants to view the error budget burn rate over two windows, 1 hour and 6 hours, and executives receive a quarterly per-service report on a monthly 99.9% availability objective. Introducing a service mesh or sidecars is not on this quarter's roadmap, and the current configuration must be kept as is. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use CloudWatch Application Signals to automatically instrument the services on Amazon EKS, create latency SLOs per service and operation, and then set burn rate alarms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a TargetResponseTime p99 alarm on the ALB target group for each service, and calculate the error budget burn rate yourself with dashboard metric math.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add PutMetricData calls to each service's code to publish latency yourself, calculate attainment and budget burn with metric math, and set alarms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raise AWS X-Ray sampling to 100% and turn on X-Ray Insights notifications to track latency SLO violations and error budget burn.

exam-dop-c02-17.explanation: Application Signals SLOs are the correct answer. Application Signals automatically collects Latency and Availability metrics for services and operations and lets you create SLOs and set alarms on attainment and error budget burn rate (burn rate), so code changes and formula management are small. An ALB response time alarm has no objectives or budget concept at the level of operations inside a service, so you would have to write the formulas yourself. Adding PutMetricData to the code would require modifying 30 services. X-Ray Insights is anomaly detection and does not define target values or an error budget, and 100% sampling only increases cost. The requirement for objectives and burn rate at the service and operation level cannot be met by ALB metrics or X-Ray alone.

exam-dop-c02-18.prompt: The web tier of a video streaming company needs 6 instances during peak hours. At peak, one instance handles one-sixth of the total load and has no spare CPU headroom. The service must run without a capacity shortage during peak hours even if one entire Availability Zone in the Seoul Region fails, and when one zone disappears, the remaining instances must handle the entire peak load. Normal-time cost must be as low as possible. The Auto Scaling group distributes instances evenly across multiple Availability Zones, and the instance type and size are fixed. A design that assumes new capacity can be obtained in time after a failure occurs is not allowed. The service runs On-Demand, and reserved capacity contracts are outside the scope of this review. All instances are stateless servers built from the same AMI, subnets exist in all three AZs, and the Application Load Balancer also spans three AZs. This question asks for the minimum capacity during peak hours, and a failure of one AZ is assumed to be a situation in which all instances in that AZ disappear at the same time. The instance type of the Auto Scaling group is fixed, subnet capacity in each AZ is sufficient, and instances are not concentrated in a single AZ. Which configuration meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Keep 6 instances in each of 2 Availability Zones, for a total of 12 instances, as the minimum capacity during peak hours.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep 3 instances in each of 3 Availability Zones, for a total of 9 instances, as the minimum capacity during peak hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keep 2 instances in each of 3 Availability Zones, for a total of 6 instances, and accept that CPU utilization of the remaining 4 instances rises when one zone disappears.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keep 3 instances in each of 2 Availability Zones, for a total of 6 instances, and leave it to Auto Scaling to fill the capacity in the remaining zone when a failure occurs.

exam-dop-c02-18.explanation: The correct answer is 3 instances in each of 3 Availability Zones, for a total of 9. Even if one zone disappears, 6 instances remain in the other two zones, which satisfies the peak capacity, and for static stability the design does not depend on obtaining new capacity during a failure. A configuration with 6 instances in each of 2 zones, 12 in total, also satisfies the requirement but has 3 more instances and is less cost-effective. Keeping 3 instances in each of 2 zones, 6 in total, and leaving it to Auto Scaling after a failure drops capacity to 3 instances right after the failure, and scaling is a control plane operation that depends on obtaining new capacity, which violates the constraint. With 2 instances in each of 3 zones, 6 in total, only 4 instances remain when one zone disappears, which does not satisfy the peak capacity of 6. Under the condition that reserved capacity contracts are not under review, the configuration that increases the number of AZs to reduce the total number of instances is the cheapest.

exam-dop-c02-19.prompt: In a SaaS organization, 5 to 10 new accounts are created every week. The security team wants to automate, without human intervention, enabling Amazon GuardDuty and deploying an IAM role for auditing in each new account. It wants to use a delegated administrator and AWS CloudFormation for the service settings. A new account must have the same security baseline within minutes of creation, and the product teams that create accounts have no permission to configure security settings. The organization has all features enabled, and the accounts are spread across 3 OUs. Currently two security team members configure accounts manually by following a checklist, and omissions keep recurring. Both settings are for the Seoul Region, and new accounts are created with the Organizations CreateAccount API rather than AWS Control Tower. The IAM role for auditing is defined in a single template, and the security team has already designated a delegated administrator account. The platform team is responsible for creating new accounts, but afterward the security settings must be aligned automatically according to the security team's policy. Which TWO configurations meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an AWS Config aggregator at the organization level, and GuardDuty and the audit role are automatically installed in new accounts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the GuardDuty delegated administrator account, turn on the organization's auto-enable setting so that GuardDuty is automatically enabled in new member accounts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When a new account is created, have the responsible person log in to the account, turn on GuardDuty, and deploy the stack directly by following the checklist.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Target the organization OUs with service-managed StackSets and turn on automatic deployment so that the audit role stack is automatically deployed to new accounts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the SCP allows the guardduty:CreateDetector action, GuardDuty is automatically turned on in new accounts and the role is also created.

exam-dop-c02-19.explanation: The correct answers are the GuardDuty organization auto-enable setting and StackSets automatic deployment. The auto-enable setting of the delegated administrator turns on GuardDuty for new member accounts, and automatic deployment of service-managed StackSets deploys the role stack to new accounts that join the OU. An SCP does not grant permissions or turn on services and only sets a ceiling. A Config aggregator is a feature that collects configuration and compliance data and does not install other services. Manual work following a checklist requires human intervention, which conflicts with the automation requirement and with minimizing operational overhead. The conditions that the product teams have no permission to configure security settings and that the work must be handled without human intervention eliminate the checklist approach.

exam-dop-c02-20.prompt: On a payment platform, when a database failure occurs, more than 20 alarms for application server error rate, response latency, and queue backlog go into ALARM at the same time, and dozens of Amazon SNS text messages are sent to the on-call engineer. The cause is the same, and separate database alarms that watch the DB instance CPU and connection count already exist; the engineer wants to be paged only once when the database is actually abnormal. The individual alarm metrics must be kept as they are, and detection latency must not increase. The on-call rotation must page only one person at a time, and the alarm history must continue to be retained per individual metric for post-incident analysis. The configuration must stay simple even when new services are added, and the company does not want to operate separate code for deduplicating notifications. The 20 or so alarms are owned by different teams and each has its own SNS topic, but on-call receives pages only through one topic connected to the paging service. The composite alarm rule must be able to express a combination of the database alarm and multiple service alarms. The on-call engineer wants to know immediately from a single alarm which component is the cause, and the database abnormality is already defined by two alarms. Which solution meets the requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the evaluation period and the number of data points of all alarms so that transient alarms are not mixed in, reducing the number of alarms that fire at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply a filter policy to the SNS subscription so that only the first of the messages arriving in the same time window is delivered to the on-call engineer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set the composite alarm rule to fire when both the database alarm and the application error rate alarm are in ALARM, and remove the SNS actions from the child alarms so that only the composite alarm pages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receive alarm state change events through Amazon EventBridge, have a Lambda function record them in Amazon DynamoDB to deduplicate, and then publish only one message to Amazon SNS.

exam-dop-c02-20.explanation: A composite alarm is the correct answer. A composite alarm evaluates the states of other alarms with AND and OR, so the individual metrics and evaluation settings can stay as they are while paging comes from only one place, the composite alarm. Increasing the evaluation period conflicts with the constraint on detection latency and still leaves the problem of many alarms firing. An SNS filter policy is a message attribute matching feature and cannot deduplicate by time window or by cause. Implementing your own deduplication with EventBridge, Lambda, and DynamoDB requires maintaining code and a state store, so it has the highest operational overhead. The condition that the individual alarm metrics and evaluation settings are kept and detection latency must not increase eliminates extending the evaluation period.

exam-dop-c02-21.prompt: The security team of a retail group wants to centrally close, in one operation, security group rules that open inbound port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0 across 3 OUs (45 accounts) and 3 Regions of the organization. Applying the change to all accounts at once carries a risk of outage, so the number of account and Region locations running at the same time must be limited, and the run must stop if errors exceed 10%. The company wants to take the list of target accounts from the organization and does not want to edit the list by hand when accounts are added. The execution history must be viewable centrally in one place, and access must use only temporary credentials without creating long-term credentials in each account. The security team has 4 people and cannot spend time developing one-off scripts. The execution roles that Automation will assume have already been deployed to the 45 target accounts with StackSets, and the only rules to remove are those with port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0, regardless of tags. The work is carried out outside business hours, and some accounts with restricted access may fail. The results are included in an organization-wide audit report, so success and failure per account and Region must remain in the execution history. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Share the runbook with each account administrator, have them run it themselves in each account on a set date, and collect completion status in a spreadsheet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run a script that iterates over 45 account profiles using long-term IAM user access keys from the management account and removes the rules with the AWS CLI.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run the revoke-security-group-ingress command on each EC2 instance with Run Command, and add security group modification permissions to the instance profiles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: From the delegated administrator account, run SSM Automation across multiple accounts and Regions targeting the OUs, and set concurrency and an error threshold.

exam-dop-c02-21.explanation: Multi-account and multi-Region Automation is the correct answer. If you target the OUs from the central account, the account list is expanded from the organization, and location concurrency and the error threshold control the rollout speed and stop conditions (deploying the execution roles in the target accounts with StackSets is the recommended method). Manual execution per account has no controllable concurrency or error threshold and requires people to handle 45 accounts. A long-term access key script carries a key exposure risk and requires building concurrency control code yourself. A security group is an account and Region level resource, not something inside an instance, so Run Command does not fit and only needlessly broadens the instance profile permissions. The execution roles are already deployed, so the prerequisite for multi-account Automation is met, and running manually per account does not satisfy the concurrency and error threshold requirements.

exam-dop-c02-22.prompt: The order service of a global SaaS stores order data in Amazon Aurora MySQL and session data in an Amazon DynamoDB table in the Seoul Region. The company wants to use the Osaka Region as disaster recovery (DR) in case the entire Seoul Region fails. The requirements are to limit data loss to a few seconds, to make the DR Region writable within minutes during a failure, and to have no recovery step that takes long, such as restoring from a snapshot. The Osaka Region normally receives no write load, and the company also wants to automate the recovery procedure and run regular DR drills. The order database is about 2 TB and there are 2 DBAs, so managed features are preferred over building and monitoring replication setups by hand. The Aurora cluster in Seoul already has a read replica in the same Region, and the Osaka Region has a VPC and application AMIs ready, so only the connection endpoint needs to change during recovery. DR failover automation is handled as a separate task. Recovery drills are held every six months, and drills must not affect the service in the Seoul Region. Which TWO components meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an Aurora read replica in another Availability Zone in the Seoul Region, and when a failure occurs, promote this replica so that the application in the Osaka Region connects to it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure the session table as a DynamoDB global table, add a replica in the Osaka Region, and have the Osaka replica receive reads and writes as is when a failure occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure the Aurora database as an Aurora global database, add a secondary cluster in Osaka, and promote and use the secondary cluster when a failure occurs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on continuous backups for the DynamoDB table, and when a failure occurs, run a point-in-time restore in the Osaka Region to create a new table and have the application use that table.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Copy Aurora cluster snapshots to the Osaka Region every hour with AWS Backup, and when a failure occurs, restore a new cluster from a snapshot to resume the service.

exam-dop-c02-22.explanation: The correct answers are an Aurora global database and a DynamoDB global table. An Aurora global database uses dedicated storage-level infrastructure to replicate to the secondary Region, typically with latency under 1 second, and the secondary cluster can be promoted during a failure, which satisfies data loss of a few seconds and a fast writable state. A DynamoDB global table replicates continuously across Regions, so the Osaka replica can receive reads and writes right away. Copying snapshots and restoring takes a long time to restore and has a data loss window measured in hours, which violates the requirements. A point-in-time restore also takes time to create a new table. A read replica in the same Region does not help with a failure of the entire Region. The background that a read replica already exists in the same Region does not protect against a Regional failure, so it does not change the judgment of the correct answer.

exam-dop-c02-23.prompt: An AWS CodePipeline pipeline in the shared services account of a game company stores build artifacts in the pipeline artifact bucket and deploys them to an AWS CodeDeploy application in the production account. The pipeline must be operated in only one place, the shared services account (so that approval history and audit logs can be viewed in one place). The artifact bucket is currently encrypted with the default AWS managed key (aws/s3), and the deploy action in the production account fails because it cannot read the artifacts. The artifacts may include production configuration files, so approaches that open the bucket to the outside or weaken encryption will not pass the security review. The production account must not access resources in the shared services account other than the CodeDeploy permissions that the deployment will exercise. Builds run in AWS CodeBuild in the Seoul Region, and the CodeDeploy deployment group in the production account is already prepared. Production account administrators must not be able to change the pipeline configuration in the shared services account, and deployments happen three or four times a day. The pipeline's approval stages and deployment history are retained in one place, the shared services account, for audit purposes. Which actions are needed to meet this requirement in a safe way that grants only the permissions needed in the production account? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create in the production account a cross-account role that the pipeline service role can assume, grant it CodeDeploy permissions and access to the artifact bucket and the KMS key, and specify it as the roleArn of the deploy action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a statement that allows the production account root to the key policy of the aws/s3 AWS managed key so that the production account can decrypt the artifacts with the same managed key, and leave the bucket policy and the cross-account role unchanged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a separate CodePipeline in the production account that subscribes to the source repository in the shared services account, replace the artifact bucket with a new bucket owned by the production account, run the pipelines in both accounts in parallel, and manage deployment history separately per account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Disable encryption on the artifact bucket and allow s3:GetObject to the entire production account in the bucket policy so that anyone in the production account can read the artifact objects without key permissions, and do not create a separate role.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replace the artifact store encryption key with a customer managed KMS key in the shared services account, grant usage permissions to the service role and the production account, and allow the production account role to read through the bucket policy.

exam-dop-c02-23.explanation: The correct answers are to have the production account read the artifacts by using a customer managed KMS key and a bucket policy, and to create a cross-account role in the production account that the pipeline service role assumes. An AWS managed key has a key policy that cannot be changed, so it cannot be shared with another account, which means a customer managed key is required, and cross-account access works only when both the key policy and the bucket policy allow the other account. The deploy action assumes the production account role to call CodeDeploy and access the bucket and the key. Adding the production account to the managed key policy does not work because the policy cannot be modified. Turning off encryption and opening read access to the entire account is excessive permission that breaks the principle of least privilege. Putting a separate pipeline in the production account violates the constraint that the pipeline is operated in only one account. The condition that production account administrators must not be able to change the pipeline also supports keeping the pipeline in the single shared services account.

exam-dop-c02-24.prompt: An e-commerce company remediates, with an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook, RDS instances that an AWS Config rule detects as publicly accessible. Instances tagged Env=prod may have connection drops during remediation, so remediation must run only after one of two approvers approves, while other environments must be remediated automatically right away. The solution runs in a single account, and the company wants to minimize custom code. The approval request must be delivered to the responsible people through Amazon SNS, instances that are not prod must be remediated immediately without waiting for approval, and the approval wait time must not exceed one day. The operations team has 3 people and cannot develop a new approval system, and the Config automatic remediation configuration is already in use in the development environment. The remediation runbook changes the PubliclyAccessible attribute of an RDS instance to false, and prod instances experience a brief connection drop. The two approvers are specified as IAM roles, and there are many non-prod instances, so approval requests piling up would be a problem. The runbook is already written as an SSM document, and the only parts to be changed are the approval step and the branching setup. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exclude prod instances from Config automatic remediation, have the responsible person who receives the noncompliance notification through Amazon SNS turn off public access manually in the console, and configure automatic remediation only for the other non-prod environments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Develop your own approval system in which a remediation Lambda function puts an approval request message into Amazon SQS and polls for the responder's reply, call it from Config remediation, and handle the response deadline and the verification of the number of approvers in code.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use an IAM policy condition to deny the modify action of the remediation role on resources tagged prod so that remediation does not run without approval, and after approval have the responsible person lift the policy separately.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use aws:branch so that only when the Env tag is prod it goes through aws:approve (2 approvers, minimum 1 approval, timeout 86400 seconds), and attach this runbook to Config automatic remediation.

exam-dop-c02-24.explanation: A runbook that uses aws:branch and aws:approve is the correct answer. aws:approve pauses Automation until a designated approver approves and announces the request through Amazon SNS, and because the default timeout is 7 days, the one-day limit is met by setting the timeout to 86400 seconds. If the branch applies the approval only to prod, other environments are remediated immediately without waiting for approval, which meets the requirements without code. Excluding prod from automatic remediation and handling it manually removes the flow in which remediation runs automatically after approval and increases the responsible person's work. An SQS approval system requires custom development and maintenance. An IAM deny condition only makes remediation fail and provides no path to run it after approval. The condition that there are many non-prod instances and approval waits cannot be applied to them puts the approach of requiring approval for all remediation at a disadvantage.

exam-dop-c02-25.prompt: The website of an e-commerce company runs on 24 Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. During in-place deployments, some instances served a mix of the old and new versions, which repeatedly caused problems. The company wants to prepare the new version fully on separate instances and then switch over at once at the ALB, and during the hour after deployment it must be possible to immediately roll back to the old-version instances if a problem is found. After 1 hour, the previous instances must be cleaned up to save cost. During the Black Friday period, a failed deployment means lost revenue, so rollback must not take longer than a few minutes. The team already uses AWS CodeDeploy as its deployment tool and has no staff to maintain separate deployment scripts. Target groups can be used on the ALB for blue and green, the deployment artifacts are in Amazon S3, and the CodeDeploy agent is installed on all instances. New instances created by scale-out during the deployment must also receive the same version. The pre-deployment check is already implemented with a CodeDeploy hook and does not need to be built again. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a CodeDeploy EC2 blue/green deployment to copy the Auto Scaling group and create a replacement environment, reroute traffic all at once, and specify in the deployment group settings that the original instances are terminated after waiting 60 minutes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use a CodeDeploy in-place deployment with the HalfAtATime configuration, perform a manual rollback that redeploys the previous revision if a problem is found, and keep using the instances without replacing them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a new Auto Scaling group and target group with AWS CloudFormation for every deployment, write a script that changes the ALB listener rule, and add a scheduled Lambda function that deletes the previous group after 1 hour.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the launch template version of the existing Auto Scaling group to the new AMI, run an instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage of 100%, and use instance refresh rollback if there is a problem, even after completion.

exam-dop-c02-25.explanation: CodeDeploy EC2 blue/green deployment is the correct answer. The entire replacement environment is prepared first and switched over at once, so versions are not mixed, and specifying that the original instances terminate after waiting 60 minutes allows an immediate rollback to the old environment during that time and automatic cleanup afterward. An in-place deployment replaces instances sequentially, so the version mixing problem remains and rollback requires a redeployment. Building it yourself with CloudFormation and Lambda is possible but requires maintaining scripts and cleanup tasks yourself. An instance refresh can be rolled back only while it is in progress and cannot be rolled back after completion, and versions are also mixed during replacement. The condition that there is no staff to maintain separate deployment scripts eliminates the self-built stack replacement approach.

exam-dop-c02-26.prompt: At a consumer lending company, multiple teams create hundreds of log groups, and some logs contain data in the form of card numbers and Korean resident registration numbers. The company must mask this data at ingestion time in all log groups, including those created in the future, and allow viewing of the original data only for the security audit role. Development teams can create log groups freely, and ordinary developers who read the logs must not be allowed access to the original data. The masking results are used for compliance reporting, so there must be no per-team configuration omissions. The log ingestion paths (agents, Lambda, containers) differ by team, so the ingestion-side code cannot be modified. The log groups exist only in the Seoul Region, and each team has a different retention period and encryption key. The security team wants to manage, in one place, the policy that defines which data types to mask. The security audit role is attached to only a few security staff, and viewing of the original data is allowed only at the time of an audit. Card numbers appear in the logs in a 16-digit format, and Korean resident registration numbers appear in a format that includes a hyphen. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Build a script that attaches a data protection policy to each log group, run it with Amazon EventBridge when a new log group is created to add the policy, and have the responsible team reattach the policy on log groups where the run failed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply a subscription filter to all log groups so that a Lambda function writes a copy with sensitive values masked to a new log group, set a short retention period on the original log groups so that they are deleted automatically, and let ordinary developers read only the copies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify in an account-level data protection policy a managed data identifier for card numbers and a custom data identifier that defines the Korean resident registration number format with a regular expression, and grant the logs:Unmask permission only to the security audit role.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Encrypt the log groups with a customer managed KMS key, allow only the security audit role to decrypt with the key policy so that ordinary users cannot see the original data, and configure every new log group to be associated with the same key.

exam-dop-c02-26.explanation: An account-level data protection policy is the correct answer. An account policy applies to both existing log groups and log groups created in the future, card numbers are matched by a managed data identifier, and Korean resident registration numbers, which are not in the managed list, are defined with a regular-expression-based custom data identifier and masked together. Masked data is hidden at ingestion time, and only principals with the logs:Unmask permission can see the original. A per-log-group script leaves a gap between the creation of a new group and the attachment of the policy, and the code must also be maintained. A subscription filter with a Lambda copy stores the original data in the source log group and requires operating a pipeline yourself. KMS encryption protects data at rest and cannot mask at the field level. The condition that the ingestion paths differ by team so code cannot be modified and the condition that log groups created in the future must be included support the account-level policy.

exam-dop-c02-27.prompt: An order processing company uses a local sampling rule JSON file of the AWS X-Ray SDK for its order service running on 120 Amazon EC2 instances. Each instance samples independently, so the total amount recorded is larger than expected and trace storage costs have grown. The /checkout path must be kept at a high rate for incident analysis and all other paths at a low rate, and the company does not want to redeploy code every time the rules change. The trace storage volume must be reduced to one-third or less of the current volume, and /checkout requests must be traced without exception during incident analysis. Instances scale in and out frequently, and the company does not want a procedure that separately deploys a rule file whenever a new instance starts. The service is written in Java, and the X-Ray SDK and daemon are installed on all instances. The current local rule is a fixed rate of 5%, and high-volume paths such as the search API are recorded at the same rate, so most traces have low value. The payments team wants all /checkout calls to be recorded. Trace storage cost is increasing noticeably on the monthly bill, and the finance team has asked for a reduction plan by next quarter. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a /checkout entry to the local JSON rule and redeploy it to all 120 instances, and afterward repeat the redeployment and restart in the same way every time the rate changes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an X-Ray group and include only /checkout requests in the filter expression, so that traces not belonging to the group are not recorded and cost is reduced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Record all traces but shorten the X-Ray data retention period to lower storage cost, and query only /checkout when needed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Define sampling rules in the X-Ray service (with a high priority for the /checkout rule) and configure remote sampling so that the library reads the service's rules.

exam-dop-c02-27.explanation: Service-side sampling rules with remote sampling are the correct answer. When rules are placed in X-Ray, the service distributes the reservoir to instances as per-instance quotas, so the combined recorded volume does not balloon, a higher-priority /checkout rule can set its own rate, and changes do not require redeployment. A local JSON file samples independently per instance, so the reservoirs add up and changes require redeployment. A group is a feature for filtering stored traces and does not change the amount recorded. Recording everything increases cost, and the X-Ray retention period is not an item that users can shorten to save cost. The condition that the company does not want to deploy a rule file separately to new instances eliminates the local JSON approach.

exam-dop-c02-28.prompt: A real estate platform runs a manually created Amazon S3 bucket and Amazon DynamoDB table in production, and data has already accumulated (tens of TB in the bucket, hundreds of millions of items in the table). These two resources must be brought under the management of a new AWS CloudFormation stack without deletion or re-creation. The template defines properties that match the current configuration of both resources. The service must not be interrupted during the import, and no resource replacement must occur if the template is changed right after the import. The infrastructure team wants to change these resources only through code from now on, and has neither the time nor the budget to copy data. Both resources are in the Seoul Region and do not belong to any other CloudFormation stack. Properties such as encryption and versioning are defined in the template with the same values as the current ones, and the work will be done in a weekend maintenance window, but applications that read and write both resources must keep running. After the work, the names and ARNs of the two resources must not change because other teams already reference these ARNs in their configuration. Which actions are needed to import them safely so that no data is lost? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copy the data of the existing bucket and table to new resources created from the template, then delete the originals and reuse the names so that the new resources take the place of the originals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a change set of the import type for the stack, specify each resource's identifier value (bucket name, table name), and run the change set to associate the existing resources with the logical IDs in the template.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify the DeletionPolicy attribute in the definition of both resources to be imported. Each resource to be imported must have this attribute for the import to succeed, and specifying Retain is safe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on termination protection for the stack so that the stack is not deleted even if the import fails partway, and the existing resources are automatically attached to the stack while termination protection is on.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Set a stack policy on both resources that denies all update actions until the import is finished, and release the policy after the import is complete to allow template changes.

exam-dop-c02-28.explanation: The correct answers are specifying DeletionPolicy on the resources to be imported, and specifying the resource identifiers in an import change set and running it. A resource import succeeds only when each resource to be imported has a DeletionPolicy attribute, maps the existing resources to the logical IDs in the template by using the identifier properties and actual values, and incorporates the existing resources into the stack as they are, without creating or deleting any resources. A stack policy is a means of protecting against updates and is not a condition required for import. Copying data and deleting the originals violates the requirement to import without deletion or re-creation. Termination protection only prevents stack deletion and has no function for attaching existing resources. The condition that there is no time or budget to copy tens of TB of data eliminates the copy-and-replace approach.

exam-dop-c02-29.prompt: A financial services team stores more than 1,200 container images in an Amazon ECR private registry. Currently only basic scanning on push is enabled, so a CVE disclosed after an image is pushed is not discovered until the next build. Vulnerabilities in Java and Python libraries must also be detected, and an automatic notification must go to the security team's SNS topic when a new critical vulnerability appears. The security team wants to see the vulnerability status of the entire registry in one place during the monthly audit. The number of images to scan keeps growing, and many of them are stored for months without being newly pushed or run. Build pipelines differ by team, so modifications must be minimized. The images are spread across 40 repositories in the Seoul Region, and Java (Maven) and Python (pip) services are mixed. The security team wants to be notified the same day when new CRITICAL and HIGH vulnerabilities appear, and the build pipelines differ by team so they are hard to modify. The security team exports vulnerability results as a PDF report at the monthly audit, so it is important that the results are collected in one place. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an open-source image scanner to the AWS CodeBuild stage of all build pipelines to check for vulnerabilities at build time, fail the build if there are critical findings, and notify through Amazon SNS.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set a lifecycle policy on each repository to delete images older than 30 days so that old vulnerable images do not remain in the registry, and notify of delete events through Amazon SNS.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the registry scanning configuration to enhanced scanning (Amazon Inspector integration) with continuous scanning and set the rescan duration based on the push date to Lifetime, and deliver high-severity Inspector finding events to the SNS topic with an EventBridge rule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keep basic scanning, have an EventBridge scheduled rule run a Lambda function every day that calls StartImageScan on all images, and receive scan completion events through EventBridge to forward them to Amazon SNS, where the Lambda function builds the list of images to scan by querying the repositories each time.

exam-dop-c02-29.explanation: The correct answer is to turn on continuous scanning with enhanced scanning and set the rescan duration based on the push date to Lifetime. Enhanced scanning integrates with Amazon Inspector to check both operating system and programming language package vulnerabilities, updates the findings when a new CVE is disclosed, and emits EventBridge events. The default monitoring period is 7 days for newly enabled registries, so images that are stored for a long time without being touched would fall out of the rescan scope, and the Lifetime setting is therefore required. Basic scanning scans only operating system vulnerabilities, so it does not meet the Java and Python library requirement. A build-stage scanner misses CVEs disclosed after the push and also requires large pipeline changes. Deleting old images is image lifecycle management, not a means of detecting vulnerabilities. The condition that many images are stored for a long time without being touched makes it necessary to set the rescan duration to Lifetime.

exam-dop-c02-30.prompt: The security team of a fintech organization wants to restrict scheduling of deletion of customer managed KMS keys (ScheduleKeyDeletion) so that only the security administration role can perform it, and to be notified within minutes when a key deletion is attempted. Administrators of the 20 member accounts can change IAM policies in their own accounts, so this restriction must not be bypassable by them. A key scheduled for deletion must be cancellable by the security team during the waiting period, but unauthorized scheduling attempts must be blocked in the first place. This requirement arose after an incident in which a former employee scheduled key deletion and it was only discovered later. The organization already uses SCPs, and an organization CloudTrail trail is turned on in all accounts. The waiting period after scheduling deletion is already standardized at 30 days. The security administration role is a single SecurityAdmin role in the security account, and the application roles in member accounts only use the keys. This measure must be maintained without manual work by the security team even as the number of accounts grows. The deletion-scheduling notification should be delivered to both the security team's chat channel and email. Which combination is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deploy a deny statement for kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion to the IAM policies of each account with StackSets, and replace notifications with a monthly CloudTrail log review.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the key policy to deny deletion scheduling, and receive notifications by viewing AWS Config rule evaluation results after the key goes into a pending deletion state.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apply an SCP that denies deletion scheduling to principals other than the security administration role, and receive CloudTrail events through Amazon EventBridge and send notifications through Amazon SNS.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Set the deletion waiting period for all keys to the shortest, 7 days, and have the responsible person cancel it in the console within 7 days if deletion is scheduled.

exam-dop-c02-30.explanation: The combination of an SCP deny and an EventBridge notification is the correct answer. An SCP is a ceiling that member account administrators cannot change, so it prevents deletion scheduling by anything other than the security administration role, and receiving the ScheduleKeyDeletion call recorded in CloudTrail through EventBridge delivers a notification within minutes. Account IAM policies can be modified by account administrators, and a monthly log review has too much notification delay. A key policy change can be reverted by the account's key administrators, and Config evaluation is after-the-fact detection with delay. The waiting period is a value specified at scheduling time and is not a preventive measure, and leaving the cancellation to a person is a structure that is easy to miss. The condition that member account administrators can change IAM policies makes an SCP the only preventive measure that cannot be bypassed.

exam-dop-c02-31.prompt: The SRE team at a food delivery app company wants to handle assignment of owners, status tracking, and linking of related resources and runbooks in one place when an Amazon CloudWatch alarm goes into ALARM. There are dozens of alarms per day, there is no dedicated development staff, and the company must use only AWS services without adopting an external ticketing system. Each incident must retain its action history and owner, and when an alarm occurs, ticket creation must happen automatically without human handling. Currently the team manages alarms with email notifications and a shared spreadsheet, and owners have often been missed. The team already uses AWS Systems Manager for instance management. The OpsItem must record the owner, priority, and related resources, and the post-incident retrospective reconstructs the timeline from them. The team operates in a single account in the Seoul Region. At night one person is on call, so when an alarm fires, the responder must be able to open the OpsItem on a mobile device as well. The OpsItem title must show the alarm name and severity so that the responder can set priorities. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead, given that development and maintenance must be minimal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an OpsCenter OpsItem creation action to the alarm actions, link the related resources and runbooks to the OpsItem, and have the owner update the status.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Send an Amazon SNS email as the alarm action and set a procedure in which the owner manually records the incident status and owner in a shared spreadsheet.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invoke a Lambda function from the alarm to create your own ticket table in Amazon DynamoDB, and develop a web screen yourself for assigning owners and updating status.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place an alarm status widget on a CloudWatch dashboard and operate by having the shift worker watch the screen and assign the owner verbally.

exam-dop-c02-31.explanation: An OpsCenter OpsItem is the correct answer. When a Systems Manager action is added to the alarm actions, an OpsItem is created automatically on ALARM, and the OpsItem manages the owner, status, related resources, and runbook links in one place, so no additional development is needed. Email and a spreadsheet make status tracking manual and prone to omissions and duplicates. A DynamoDB ticket system and a web screen must be developed and maintained by yourself, which has the highest operational overhead. Dashboard watching and verbal assignment leave no record and require staff to keep watching the screen. The conditions that a ticket is created automatically when an alarm occurs and that no external SaaS is used eliminate the email and spreadsheet approach.

exam-dop-c02-32.prompt: A securities company wants to protect its Amazon RDS and Amazon EBS backups against ransomware and insider threats. The requirements are that backups must not be deleted even if the production account is compromised, and that no one, including the root user, can delete a backup or change the retention policy before the retention period (minimum 35 days). All accounts belong to the same AWS Organizations organization, and the scenario in which administrator permissions of the production account are stolen must be assumed. A copy of each recovery point must also exist in a separate account that production account administrators cannot access. Backups are already performed once a day with AWS Backup, and the company does not want to change the backup tool. The backup targets are 30 RDS instances and 200 EBS volumes, and the backup plan is deployed through an Organizations backup policy. A dedicated backup account has already been created in the organization, and recovery drills are performed every six months from this account's recovery points. The additional cost of creating copies of recovery points has already been approved in the security budget. A restore test of the recovery points is performed once every six months to verify that they are usable. Which configuration is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set up cross-account copy to a vault in a separate dedicated backup account, apply a vault lock in governance mode to that vault, and grant the permission to change the retention period only to the security team's IAM role.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set up cross-account copy to a vault in a separate dedicated backup account, and apply a vault lock in compliance mode (grace time of 3 days or more, minimum retention of 35 days) to that vault.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Export the backups to an Amazon S3 bucket, store them in a bucket in a separate account, and turn on S3 Object Lock in governance mode and MFA Delete so that objects cannot be deleted for 35 days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apply a vault lock in compliance mode to the same vault in the production account, deny backup deletion for all principals with the vault access policy, and specify a retention period of 35 days or more.

exam-dop-c02-32.explanation: The correct answer is a configuration that copies across accounts to a dedicated backup account and applies a compliance mode vault lock. In compliance mode, once the grace time ends, the lock and the vault can no longer be changed or deleted, so neither the root user nor AWS can delete a backup before the retention period, and because a copy exists in a separate account it survives a compromise of the production account. The grace time must be at least 3 days. Governance mode allows a user with sufficient permissions to remove the lock, which violates the requirement that no one can delete. Keeping backups only in the same account does not protect against a compromise of the production account. S3 Object Lock in governance mode can also be bypassed by a privileged user. The scenario in which the production account administrator permissions are stolen and the requirement that even the root user cannot delete eliminate governance mode and same-account storage.

exam-dop-c02-33.prompt: A fintech company publishes its internal package @corp/billing-utils to an npm repository in AWS CodeArtifact, and this repository has an upstream repository with an external connection to the public npmjs registry. The security team is concerned about a dependency substitution attack, in which an attacker uploads a higher version with the same name to the public registry so that builds pull a malicious version. The 80 developers must continue to publish internal packages directly, and must be able to download other public packages as usual. Packages are published and installed many times a day, so slowing down the development flow or adding a separate approval step is unacceptable. The build environments are a mix of developer PCs, per-team CI servers, and AWS CodeBuild, so it is hard to control client settings one by one. Internal package names all use the @corp scope, and the repository administrator is the security team. The build environments are a mix of developer PCs, per-team CI servers, and CodeBuild, so it is hard to control client settings one by one. An external audit last quarter pointed out the risk of dependency substitution attacks. The security team wants to be able to prove with logs that builds did not pull a malicious version even if a dependency substitution attack occurs. Which prevention measure is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Remove the external connection from the repository and change the development procedure so that developers download all public packages themselves and publish them manually to the internal repository.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the package origin controls of that internal package to allow publish and block upstream, so that even if a version with the same name is uploaded to the public registry, it cannot enter the repository.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify in the .npmrc on developer PCs and build servers that packages in the @corp scope are downloaded only from the internal repository, and distribute this setting in the team development guide document.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the upstream repository connection order so that the public repository has the lowest priority, and set a rule that internal package versions are always published with the latest tag.

exam-dop-c02-33.explanation: The correct answer is to set the package origin controls to allow publish and block upstream. With this setting, direct publishing continues to work and versions with the same name do not flow in from the public registry or upstream repositories, so the dependency substitution attack is blocked, and other packages are unaffected. Removing the external connection violates the requirement to download public packages as usual. Specifying the scope in .npmrc depends on client settings, cannot block inflow at the registry level, and leaves risk in any environment where the setting is missing. The connection order and tags are not a means of preventing an external version with the same name from flowing into the repository. The condition that client settings cannot be controlled eliminates the .npmrc approach.

exam-dop-c02-34.prompt: In the 60 accounts of a logistics group's organization, if S3 Block Public Access on a bucket is turned off, it must be turned back on automatically without human intervention. Even when a new account is added to the organization, the same detection and remediation must apply without separate work, and the security team manages the rules in only one place, the delegated administrator account. Remediation is done by turning on the Block Public Access settings, and the IAM role used to run remediation is not created by hand in each account but is deployed with the same name to all accounts with StackSets so that it is provided consistently. Currently the owner of each account receives an email alert and handles it manually, which takes hours. The security team has 3 people and cannot maintain per-account automation code. The remediation history must be viewable at once from the delegated administrator account, and rule changes must be made by editing one template and redeploying it. After remediation, a follow-up notice that tells the bucket's owning team the result is needed, but this notice is outside the scope of this question. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From the delegated administrator account, define in an organization conformance pack template an S3 Block Public Access AWS Config rule and an AWS Systems Manager Automation automatic remediation action, specify the StackSets-deployed role as the AutomationAssumeRole, and deploy it to the organization.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create AWS Config rules directly in each account, have the owner who receives the noncompliance notification by email turn the Block Public Access setting back on in the console, receive per-account reports of the results, and create the same rules manually in new accounts as well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deploy separately, with AWS CloudFormation in each account, an Amazon EventBridge rule that detects PutBucketPublicAccessBlock calls from AWS CloudTrail events and a Lambda function, and manage the deployment status of each account separately.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receive AWS Security Hub organization integration findings as a report once a day, have the security team correct the bucket settings of all accounts at once with a batch script, include new accounts starting from the next report, and keep the remediation history in the script logs.

exam-dop-c02-34.explanation: An organization conformance pack is the correct answer. A conformance pack bundles Config rules and remediation actions into a single template and deploys it to the entire organization, and remediation is performed by an SSM Automation document whose execution role is deployed to all accounts with the same name through StackSets and specified as the AutomationAssumeRole, which satisfies single-place management in the delegated administrator and automatic application to new accounts. Creating rules in each account and having owners remediate manually misses both the automatic remediation requirement and the automatic application to new accounts requirement. The CloudTrail call event approach sees only the call that turns protection off, and does not solve buckets that are already noncompliant or the per-account deployment management. Remediating with a script after a daily report requires human intervention and has a large delay. The condition that rules must be managed with a single template eliminates deploying event rules per account.

exam-dop-c02-35.prompt: A reservation platform automatically rotates the application account password of Amazon RDS for MySQL with AWS Secrets Manager every 30 days. The application uses a connection pool and rereads the secret every 5 minutes. High availability requirements are strict, so the possibility that a request that read the secret during rotation is denied authentication must be reduced as much as possible. Secrets Manager rotation continues to be used, and the cloned user may have the same permissions as the original user. Failed rotations must be retried automatically, and the company does not want to create a procedure to redeploy the application or restart the connection pool because of rotation. The operations team has 4 people and there is no separate maintenance window. The database is Multi-AZ, and the application servers run 20 tasks concurrently on Amazon ECS. The rotation Lambda function runs in the same VPC as the database, and a Secrets Manager VPC endpoint already exists. A requirement that the previous credentials the application was using must not be invalidated immediately during rotation has already been confirmed in the security review. The rotation schedule is set for the early morning of the first week of each month, but retries on failure must be automatic. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use the single user strategy and add a deployment procedure that restarts the connection pool so that the application reads the new secret right after rotation finishes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Read the secret value only once at application startup and keep it in an environment variable, and set a procedure in which the responsible person performs rotation manually at deployment time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use the alternating users rotation strategy and keep a separate superuser secret for cloning the user.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Limit the rotation schedule to a nighttime maintenance window only, and block application traffic during the maintenance time so that authentication denials do not occur.

exam-dop-c02-35.explanation: The alternating users strategy is the correct answer. This strategy updates two users in turn, so an application that read the secret during rotation still gets valid credentials, and after rotation both the previous user and the cloned user remain valid, so the chance of authentication denial is lowest; a separate superuser secret for cloning is required. The single user strategy has a risk of denial in the short interval after the password changes and before the secret is updated. Fixing the value in an environment variable and rotating manually abandons the automatic rotation requirement. A nighttime maintenance window and traffic blocking conflict with the high availability requirement. The condition that the company does not want to create a procedure to restart the connection pool eliminates the single user strategy.

exam-dop-c02-36.prompt: The AWS Security Hub delegated administrator account of an e-commerce organization aggregates findings from 70 accounts. A large volume of findings for a specific LOW-severity S3 control accumulates in 12 accounts in the development OU and clutters the security team's queue. The same findings in production accounts must still be shown as they are, and the control check itself must continue in all accounts. The history of suppressed findings must remain for audit purposes, and the security team wants to change the suppression criteria in one place. The security team has 2 people and cannot maintain additional code or per-account configuration. Security Hub is aggregated in the Seoul Region and the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard is turned on. The suppression target is a control related to access logging on development buckets, the 12 accounts in the development OU are identified by account ID, and there are 40 accounts in the production OU. The security team wants to be able to easily audit the scope of impact of the suppression rule in the console. The suppression rule must not be managed as code, and the security team must be able to check and modify it in the console. Which solution meets these requirements while minimizing the number of rules to manage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disable the control across the entire organization to stop generating findings, so that the same findings are no longer shown in the production accounts either.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deploy an Amazon EventBridge rule and a Lambda function in each development account to suppress findings with BatchUpdateFindings whenever a new finding is generated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have the security team filter and select the development account findings in the console once a week and manually suppress them by setting the workflow status.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the delegated administrator account, create an automation rule that changes findings matching the development account IDs, LOW severity, and the control ID to SUPPRESSED.

exam-dop-c02-36.explanation: An automation rule in the delegated administrator account is the correct answer. For new and updated findings, an automation rule changes the workflow status to SUPPRESSED when conditions such as account ID, severity, and control ID match, and when created once in the administrator account it applies to all member accounts (the rule operates only in the Region where it was created). Disabling the control stops the check itself and loses both the production account findings and the check requirement. Per-account EventBridge and Lambda would require deploying and maintaining code in 12 places. Weekly manual suppression leaves the queue cluttered in the meantime and repeats manual work. The conditions that production account findings must still be shown and the checks must continue eliminate disabling the control.

exam-dop-c02-37.prompt: A payment service team wants to verify, in a pre-production environment that matches production, that the payment success rate is maintained even if one of the three Availability Zones in the Seoul Region disappears. The experiment injects a failure that stops the Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone, and if the payment success rate Amazon CloudWatch alarm drops below 99%, the experiment must stop automatically before a human intervenes. The experiment procedure must be kept as a repeatable definition, and the results must be compared each time by using the same procedure. The experiment runs only in a production-like environment, and the permission to run the experiment is limited to an IAM role with the minimum scope. The team wants to repeat the same experiment every quarter and does not want to maintain its own fault injection code. All target EC2 instances have the tags Env=staging and Tier=payment and run in an Auto Scaling group. The payment success rate is measured continuously during the experiment, and the experiment results are compared at each quarterly retrospective. The experiment is performed during business hours after advance notice, and the target is limited to the payment service in the staging environment. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a Lambda function that calls the EC2 stop API and a Lambda function that polls the alarm state and restarts instances, tie them together with AWS Step Functions, and keep the experiment procedure as a state machine definition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have an engineer stop the instances in that Availability Zone manually in the console while watching the alarm dashboard, and manually restart the stopped instances if anything abnormal is seen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Remove that Availability Zone from the Auto Scaling group's Availability Zone list to terminate the instances, and manually run a CloudFormation stack update that adds the Availability Zone back if the alarm fires.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Define in an AWS FIS experiment template a stop action that selects the EC2 instances in the target Availability Zone by tag, specify the payment success rate alarm as a stop condition, and run the experiment.

exam-dop-c02-37.explanation: The correct answer is to define a stop action and a stop condition in an AWS FIS experiment template. FIS lets you define an experiment as a template that can be run repeatedly, and when the CloudWatch alarm specified as a stop condition crosses its threshold, the experiment stops automatically, which satisfies the requirement that it stops before a human intervenes. A stopped experiment cannot be resumed, but that is suitable for a safeguard. Manually stopping in the console violates the requirements for automatic stopping and a repeatable definition. Building it with Lambda and Step Functions requires implementing the safety mechanism and the restart logic yourself. Removing the Availability Zone from the group is a configuration change, not fault injection, and recovery is also manual. The condition that the company does not maintain its own fault injection code eliminates the Step Functions approach.

exam-dop-c02-38.prompt: A shopping app company deploys a service running on AWS Fargate with rolling updates (the Amazon ECS deployment controller) several times a day. Yesterday it deployed a new task definition, and because of a defect in which the container exits right after starting, the new tasks repeatedly failed and restarted, and the deployment remained in progress for a long time. Without adopting AWS CodeDeploy blue/green and while keeping the existing rolling update method, the company wants a deployment like this to automatically return to the last successfully completed deployment when it is judged to have failed. While the new tasks are failing, the existing tasks must continue to handle traffic, and no human judgment should be needed for the return. The development team does not want to change the structure of the deployment pipeline. The service uses ALB target group health checks, 10 tasks are distributed across 3 Availability Zones, and the deployment configuration is already a minimum healthy percent of 100% and a maximum percent of 200%. It must be possible to confirm from the service events which healthy version it returned to on rollback. The return to the previous healthy deployment must proceed without a separate approval process, and service notifications are maintained after rollback. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on the deployment circuit breaker with the rollback option so that a deployment is judged FAILED on repeated failures and returned to the last COMPLETED deployment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the deployment configuration to a minimum healthy percent of 100% and a maximum percent of 200% so that existing tasks are taken down only when all new tasks are healthy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Implement and connect your own rollback code in which a Lambda function specifies the previous task definition with UpdateService when a CloudWatch alarm fires.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch the service to the CodeDeploy blue/green deployment controller and use AppSpec hooks and alarm-based rollback to revert a failed deployment.

exam-dop-c02-38.explanation: The rollback option of the deployment circuit breaker is the correct answer. The circuit breaker marks a deployment FAILED when new tasks cannot reach RUNNING or repeatedly fail health checks and reach the threshold, and if the rollback option is on, it returns to the last COMPLETED deployment, so it can be used while keeping rolling updates. Adjusting the minimum and maximum percentages helps keep healthy tasks but has no failure judgment or automatic return, so the new tasks keep retrying. A self-built rollback Lambda function has implementation and maintenance burden. Switching to blue/green violates the constraint of not adopting it. The background that the percentage settings are already applied means adjusting the percentages has no new effect.

exam-dop-c02-39.prompt: A retail group must centrally manage operating system patching of 400 Amazon EC2 instances across 5 accounts and 3 Regions. A scan to collect compliance information must run every day, installation must run only at 2 AM on Sunday, and security updates must be auto-approved only after 7 days have passed since release. Reboots caused by patching are allowed only early on Sunday morning. For security audits, the patch compliance status per instance must be viewable in the Systems Manager compliance view of each account and Region. The infrastructure team has 3 people and wants to avoid creating maintenance windows and associations separately for each account and Region. The instances are a mix of Amazon Linux 2023 and Windows Server 2022, and all are registered as Systems Manager managed instances. The patch targets are instances tagged Env=prod, and changes to the patch policy must be made by the central team in one place. After the Sunday 2 AM installation window has passed, the instances that need a reboot must be identifiable in an inspection report. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create State Manager associations in each account and Region to run AWS-RunPatchBaseline as a Scan operation daily and as an Install operation at 2 AM on Sunday, and create a 7-day auto-approval baseline in each account and set it as the default.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a maintenance window in each account and Region and register an AWS-RunPatchBaseline task, group instances with the Patch Group tag, and create a 7-day auto-approval baseline by hand in each account and associate it with each group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Install an Ansible agent on the 400 instances to update packages by cron early on Sunday morning, and aggregate the compliance status of all accounts with a script that uploads per-instance results to Amazon S3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a patch policy with Systems Manager Quick Setup integrated with AWS Organizations, define the scan and install schedules separately, specify a patch baseline that auto-approves security updates after 7 days, and apply it to the target OUs and Regions.

exam-dop-c02-39.explanation: A Quick Setup patch policy is the correct answer. A patch policy integrates with Organizations and is applied to managed nodes across multiple accounts and Regions with a single configuration, can specify different schedules for scanning and installing, lets you choose the patch baseline per operating system so the 7-day auto-approval baseline can be used, and the compliance information produced by scans is reported for each account and Region pair, which meets the audit requirement. The maintenance window and Patch Group approach still requires repeating the setup for every account and Region combination. State Manager associations also have to be created for each account and Region, which increases repetitive work. Ansible does not use the Systems Manager patch baseline and compliance reporting features and has to be built yourself, so it has the highest operational overhead. The condition that settings must not be repeated for each account and Region puts the maintenance window and State Manager association approaches at a disadvantage.

exam-dop-c02-40.prompt: A securities company must deliver Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS, and Application Load Balancer metrics in three Regions to a third-party APM and an Amazon S3 data lake for long-term analysis in near real time. Currently a Lambda function polls the metrics with GetMetricData every 5 minutes, but the API call cost is high and delivery latency reaches several minutes. Only metrics in the EC2, RDS, and ALB namespaces need to be included, and a setup that operates a separate collection server in each Region is not allowed. The APM can receive data at an HTTP endpoint, and the data lake loads data into partitioned paths in S3. The observability team has 3 people and cannot easily maintain metric collection code. The metrics center on EC2 CPU, RDS connection count, and ALB request count, and the delivery targets are the three Regions of Seoul, Tokyo, and N. Virginia. The APM can accept the OpenTelemetry format, and the data lake may store data in the original format. Metric latency of about 1 minute in near real time is sufficient, and no metrics may be lost during delivery. The company will not add a separate processing step for metric format conversion and wants to handle it with the delivery services alone. Which solution reduces delivery latency and operational overhead the MOST?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduce the interval of the EventBridge scheduled rule to 1 minute so that the same Lambda function calls GetMetricData for EC2, RDS, and ALB metrics more often and sends the results to S3 and the APM separately, deploying the function in each Region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Additionally install the APM vendor's agent on each server and database to send metrics directly, configure the agent to upload to S3 separately, and supplement managed service metrics with the agent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create two CloudWatch Metric Streams in each Region with a filter that includes only the EC2, RDS, and ALB namespaces, and send one to Amazon Data Firehose for S3 and the other to Firehose for the APM's HTTP endpoint.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create an Observability Access Manager sink in a central account, allow the APM service to create a link to read CloudWatch metrics, and set up a separate export for S3.

exam-dop-c02-40.explanation: Metric Streams connected to Firehose is the correct answer. A stream exports metrics in near real time, a namespace filter can select only the EC2, RDS, and ALB metrics, and Firehose delivery streams for S3 and for the APM HTTP endpoint each deliver to their destinations, so the polling code and GetMetricData call cost go away. Reducing the polling interval to 1 minute actually increases the API call cost and leaves the code maintenance burden unchanged. Adding the APM agent to servers requires host changes, and the agent cannot collect managed service metrics such as ALB and RDS. An Observability Access Manager link is for sharing observability data between AWS accounts, so an external APM cannot create a link. The condition that no collection servers may be placed in each Region eliminates the agent approach.

exam-dop-c02-41.prompt: The operations team at a service company must apply a configuration change runbook to 200 Amazon EC2 instances tagged Env=prod in one account in the Seoul Region. The change must proceed in stages of 10% of the total at a time and must stop automatically if failed instances exceed 5%. In addition, before it is applied to the first target, one of two operations owners must approve, and the approval request must be announced through Amazon SNS. Connecting to the instances with SSH or placing a self-managed script server is not allowed. The work history must be retained for audit per execution step, and the operations team performs the change itself using a runbook created as code. The instances are already registered as SSM managed instances and the Automation execution role is also ready. The change runbook consists of steps that replace a configuration file and restart the service, and the approval request is delivered to an SNS topic subscribed to by the two operations owners. The change history must let auditors confirm, per execution step, who approved and on which instances a failure occurred. Instances that fail during the work are reprocessed separately later, and this requirement is limited to staged progress and stopping. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Place an aws:approve step (two approvers, minimum approvals of 1, SNS notification) as the first step of a Systems Manager Automation runbook, run the change runbook against the tag-based targets in the next step with aws:executeAutomation, and specify a maximum concurrency of 10% and a maximum error of 5%.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have an AWS Step Functions state machine process the instance list in batches of 20 in a Map state, implement yourself an approval step using a callback token and a failure counter that stops the execution when it exceeds 5%, and keep the per-step history in the state machine execution record.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run the script on the tag-based targets with Run Command with a maximum concurrency of 10% and a maximum error of 5%, and document a procedure to obtain verbal approval by email from one of the two operations owners before the run.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Distribute SSH keys to the instances and have a shell script on a bastion host run repeatedly in 10% batches, with the script exiting when the number of failures exceeds 5% and approval obtained by chat.
