exam-dop-c02-41.explanation: The correct answer is to place an aws:approve step in a parent runbook, run the child change runbook against the tag-based targets with aws:executeAutomation, and specify the maximum concurrency and maximum errors. aws:approve pauses execution until the required number of the designated approvers approve and sends a notification to the SNS topic; approval is obtained only once in the parent runbook, and the child execution's maximum concurrency of 10% and maximum error of 5% handle staged progress and automatic stopping. If the approval step were put in the execution against the targets itself, the child automation for each target would repeat the approval step. Run Command relies on verbal approval, so approval is not enforced by the system. Step Functions requires implementing and maintaining the approval and failure counter yourself, which has a large operational overhead. SSH and a script server directly violate the constraint that they cannot be used. The condition that SSH and a self-managed script server cannot be used eliminates the bastion approach.

exam-dop-c02-42.prompt: The trading system of a securities firm runs active-passive in two Regions, Seoul and Tokyo. By regulation, an operator must explicitly press a failover button when a Region fails, and the setup must prevent an incident in which the traffic of both Regions is turned off at once during a failure. In addition, the failover operation must not depend on modifying Route 53 records, which is a control plane API that can be affected during a failure. Failover drills are held every quarter, and the drills must be validated by using the same procedures and tools as during a real failure. Both Regions have identical configurations prepared behind an Application Load Balancer, and DNS is already operated in a Route 53 hosted zone. Cross-Region data replication is already configured, so this question covers only traffic failover. Normal traffic goes 100% to Seoul, and the operations team wants to judge the failover state by a value explicitly set by the operator, separate from ALB health checks. The failover procedure document used in the quarterly drills must be kept identical to what is used in a real failure. The results of the quarterly drills are evaluated by failover time and whether the safety rules work. Which configuration is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create routing controls per Region and routing control health checks in an Application Recovery Controller cluster, associate them with Route 53 failover records, and add a safety rule requiring that at least one remain on.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep Route 53 weighted records at Seoul 100 and Tokyo 0, and use a runbook in which the operator changes the weights to Seoul 0 and Tokyo 100 with the Route 53 API during a failure. The change is made with the Route 53 API, and after the change the operator directly checks the healthy state of both Regions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have the operator change the traffic dial of the AWS Global Accelerator endpoint groups to Seoul 0 and Tokyo 100 during a failure, and directly check the healthy state of both Regions before and after the change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Associate the health check of each Region's ALB with Route 53 failover records so that when the Seoul health check fails, traffic switches to Tokyo automatically without human intervention and returns when recovered.

exam-dop-c02-42.explanation: ARC routing controls and safety rules are the correct answer. A routing control is a simple on/off switch that shifts traffic from one Regional replica to another, works with Route 53 health checks to drive the failover records, and is operated through the data plane of a cluster made up of endpoints in five Regions, so it does not depend on the control plane. A safety rule that enforces at least one remaining on prevents the incident in which both are turned off at once. Changing weights is a control plane operation, which violates the dependency constraint. Automatic failover based on health checks violates the regulation that a person must perform the failover directly. A traffic dial is also a control plane operation and has no safety rules. The condition that the solution must not depend on the control plane API eliminates the weight change approach.

exam-dop-c02-43.prompt: A SaaS company manages a monorepo on GitHub (12 services) and operates a separate AWS CodePipeline pipeline for each service. Currently the pipelines run no matter where in the repository a push occurs, so the orders service pipeline runs unnecessarily dozens of times a day because of unrelated service changes, and cost is increasing. The company wants the pipeline to run only when files under services/orders/ change on the main branch, without operating a new Lambda function or Amazon EventBridge rule, and with minimal changes. A new service is added every quarter, so the same approach must be repeatable as services increase. The source is already integrated through a GitHub connection (AWS CodeConnections). The repository has 12 directories under services/ and a common libs/ directory, and the orders service pipeline does not need to react to changes in libs/. The pipeline consists of AWS CodeBuild and AWS CodeDeploy stages. The finance team pointed out that although the cost of a single pipeline execution is small, it adds up to a meaningful monthly cost when it accumulates dozens of times a day. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Migrate to separate repositories per service, create a repository dedicated to the orders service, and have the pipeline run when a push occurs to that repository.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the pipeline type to V2 and add a push trigger to the source action that uses the GitHub connection, specifying filters of main for the branch and services/orders/** for the file paths.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn off change detection on the source action of the V1 type pipeline, add a CodeBuild action after the source stage, and have it exit with an error code if the list of changed files does not include the orders service path.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create an Amazon API Gateway and a Lambda function that receive GitHub webhooks, inspect the changed file paths, and call StartPipelineExecution only when the paths match.

exam-dop-c02-43.explanation: The correct answer is to change the pipeline to type V2 and apply push trigger filters to the connection-based source action. Branch and file path filters are supported only in the V2 type, and when specified, the pipeline starts only for pushes that match the conditions, so no additional infrastructure is needed and the change is small. Exiting early with CodeBuild on V1 still incurs the pipeline execution and source stage cost and leaves a failure status. Adding API Gateway and Lambda conflicts with the constraint of not operating anything new. Migrating to separate repositories is a larger change than the requirement calls for and violates the minimal-change requirement. The condition of not operating new infrastructure eliminates the API Gateway and Lambda approach.

exam-dop-c02-44.prompt: The web application of an online education company runs in an Auto Scaling group (8 instances) behind an Application Load Balancer. Some instances fall into a deadlock and do not respond to requests, while the EC2 status checks pass and the ALB target group health check marks those instances as unhealthy and removes them from traffic. However, the instances remain and capacity decreases. The application takes about 4 minutes to initialize after boot. Traffic is normally 800 requests per second, and adding instances increases cost, so the problematic instances must be replaced quickly without needlessly increasing capacity. The replacement must be performed by Auto Scaling without human intervention, and the company does not want to build its own monitoring code. The ALB target group checks the /health path every 10 seconds, and the unhealthy threshold count is 2. The Auto Scaling group currently uses EC2 health checks with a grace period of 0 seconds, and a new instance always takes less than 4 minutes to come up healthy. Replacement instances are always created from the same AMI and launch template, and the ALB sends requests only to healthy instances even during replacement. Which setting is MOST appropriate to replace unhealthy instances automatically while keeping a new instance that is still booting from being terminated early?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Keep the Auto Scaling group health check type as EC2 and set the grace period to 0 so that an instance is replaced immediately when a problem occurs in the EC2 status checks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on the Elastic Load Balancing health check type in the Auto Scaling group and set the health check grace period to 300 seconds, which is longer than the initialization time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the health check interval and unhealthy threshold count of the ALB target group so that instances are judged unhealthy sooner, and keep the Auto Scaling group health check settings at their defaults.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on detailed instance monitoring and configure an EventBridge rule so that when a CPU utilization alarm fires, a Lambda function terminates that instance, replacing unresponsive instances yourself.

exam-dop-c02-44.explanation: The correct answer is to turn on the ELB health check in the Auto Scaling group and set the grace period longer than the initialization time. By default, Auto Scaling ignores ELB health check results and uses only EC2 status checks, so the ELB health check must be turned on for it to replace instances that the load balancer reports as unhealthy. The grace period must be longer than the initialization time so that an instance that is still booting is not caught by the check and replaced repeatedly. Adjusting only the ALB health check makes removal from traffic faster but no replacement occurs. A CPU alarm and Lambda termination cannot reliably indicate a deadlock through a metric and would have to be implemented yourself. Using only EC2 status checks cannot detect an application deadlock. The condition that the initialization time of a new instance is about 4 minutes calls for a grace period longer than the initialization time.

exam-dop-c02-45.prompt: A bank has a pipeline named MyFirstPipeline that has a manual approval action in the stage right before the production deployment. By regulation, only the release manager group can approve, and developers may view the pipeline status but must not be able to approve their own changes. The approval request must also be delivered by email. The approval history must let auditors confirm who approved and when, and even if the number of pipelines grows beyond 20 as services increase, approval permission settings must be easy to maintain. The developer group already has permission to view pipelines. The approval action is a single ManualApproval in the prod-deploy stage, and all pipeline names follow the prod- convention. Release managers sign in with roles imported from IAM Identity Center, and audit evidence is checked with the PutApprovalResult event in AWS CloudTrail. There are 5 release managers, and approval permission must not automatically follow when a new developer joins. The people who receive the approval request email may include development leads who do not have approval permission. Which configuration meets these requirements MOST appropriately while following the principle of least privilege?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attach the AWSCodePipeline_FullAccess managed policy to the release manager group, and separately attach to the developer group an explicit deny policy that denies only PutApprovalResult from that policy to block approval only. An explicit deny takes precedence over an allow, so the developer group's approval denial remains in effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify an SNS topic on the manual approval action and connect an email subscription, allow the codepipeline:PutApprovalResult permission to the release manager group only, with the approval stage and action ARNs of the pipelines as the resource, and give the developer role view permissions only.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grant the developer group AWSCodePipelineApproverAccess, and add a Lambda verification step after the approval action that fails the pipeline if the author of the change approved it, blocking self-approval.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Do not use the manual approval action; have a CodeBuild stage check for the existence of an approval file, and restrict with a bucket policy so that only release managers can upload the file to that S3 location.

exam-dop-c02-45.explanation: The correct answer is a manual approval action connected to SNS notifications, with the PutApprovalResult permission scoped to the approval action ARN and granted only to release managers. The approval permission can be limited to an individual action with a resource ARN in the pipeline/stage/action format, which follows least privilege. Granting a full access policy and blocking with a deny is a configuration that grants needlessly broad permissions. Using an approval file does not use the pipeline's standard approval feature, notifications, and audit records and is a self-built control with a large operational overhead. Giving developers approval permission and blocking self-approval afterward with Lambda violates the regulation that developers must not have approval permission in the first place. The condition that permission settings must stay easy to maintain as pipelines grow fits well with scoping the resources by the naming convention.

exam-dop-c02-46.prompt: An online bookstore has an active-passive configuration in which the Application Load Balancer in the Seoul Region is the primary endpoint and the ALB in the Tokyo Region is the standby endpoint. If the Seoul ALB has no healthy targets, DNS must automatically respond with the Tokyo ALB. The company wants to minimize creating and managing separate health check resources, and failover must occur without human intervention. The RTO is within 5 minutes, and depending on a procedure in which a person edits DNS records directly at night would delay the response. DNS is already operated in a Route 53 hosted zone, and both ALBs are in the same account. Both ALBs are internet-facing in their respective Regions, and the domain is in a Route 53 hosted zone. The Seoul ALB target is a single Amazon ECS service, Tokyo keeps only standby capacity normally, and it is acceptable for traffic to return to Seoul automatically when Seoul recovers. The Tokyo data is replicated asynchronously from Seoul, and this question covers only the DNS failover method. The time it takes to fail back after the Seoul ALB's healthy targets recover is not important. Which Route 53 configuration has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create two alias records (primary and secondary) with the failover routing policy that target the ALB in each Region, set Evaluate target health to Yes, and do not associate a separate health check.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create latency-based alias records in the two Regions with Evaluate target health turned off, and prepare a runbook in which the operator deletes the Seoul record if Seoul fails.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put both IP addresses of the Seoul ALB and the Tokyo ALB as values in a single simple routing record, and set the TTL as short as possible so that clients use whichever responds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Configure an EventBridge rule and a function so that when a CloudWatch alarm that monitors the ALB's healthy host count goes to 0, a Lambda function modifies the Route 53 record to point to the Tokyo ALB.

exam-dop-c02-46.explanation: The correct answer is a failover alias record with Evaluate target health turned on. An alias record that targets an AWS resource such as an ALB does not require creating a separate health check; if Evaluate target health is set to Yes, Route 53 follows the target's health and responds with the secondary record when the primary record is unhealthy. A simple routing record does not evaluate health, so an unhealthy IP is included in the response, and lowering only the TTL does not produce automatic failover. A latency record with Evaluate target health turned off cannot detect a failure and requires manual deletion. Modifying records with an alarm and Lambda must be implemented yourself, so the operational overhead is large. The condition of minimizing separate health check resources supports the configuration that uses the alias record's Evaluate target health.

exam-dop-c02-47.prompt: The large-file upload API of a photo printing service runs in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and a single upload request takes up to 90 seconds. Every time a scale-in or an unhealthy instance replacement occurs, uploads in progress are cut off and 5xx errors occur. The deregistration delay of the target group is set to 30 seconds, which is shorter than the default. Scale-in happens several times a day, and interrupted uploads lead to customer complaints. The application code cannot be changed, and the maximum time for one request to finish does not exceed 90 seconds. The ALB forwards HTTP/1.1 requests to the target group, and the scale-in policy is target tracking based on CPU utilization. An upload is a single HTTP request that completes within one request and has no resume feature, and the maximum upload time of 90 seconds is a value agreed as a service level objective. The client does not automatically retry when an upload fails, so the interruption itself must be prevented. The instance that is terminated during scale-in may always have an upload request in progress. Which action is MOST appropriate to prevent upload interruption while meeting these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the Auto Scaling group health check grace period to 120 seconds so that an instance selected for termination keeps serving longer until it finishes in-flight requests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the target group deregistration delay to 120 seconds, which is longer than the longest request time of 90 seconds, so that Auto Scaling waits to terminate a terminating instance until it finishes in-flight requests.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the termination policy to NewestInstance so that the most recently launched instances are terminated first, keeping the older instances that handle uploads for a long time from being terminated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the target group health check interval to 90 seconds so that an instance with an upload in progress stays in a healthy state, and also increase the unhealthy threshold count so that fewer replacements occur.

exam-dop-c02-47.explanation: The correct answer is to set the deregistration delay longer than the longest request time. With connection draining on, Auto Scaling waits until in-flight requests finish or the maximum wait time passes before terminating the instance, so increasing the delay to 120 seconds lets all 90-second requests finish, and the interruption goes away without any code change. The health check grace period is a setting that delays the start of checks for newly launched instances and is unrelated to waiting at termination. Adjusting the health check interval changes only how fast an instance is judged unhealthy and does not wait for in-flight requests at termination time. Changing the termination policy only changes which instance is terminated and does not solve the problem of requests being cut off on whichever instance is terminated during scale-in. The condition of a single request with no resume feature means a setting that waits for in-flight requests at termination time is needed.

exam-dop-c02-48.prompt: A healthcare company rotates the password of an Amazon RDS database in a private subnet with an AWS Secrets Manager Lambda rotation function. The VPC has no internet gateway and no NAT gateway, and the database is not exposed externally. The rotation function code uses the AWS-provided template as is, and the database has no public IP. By security regulation, traffic to the database and to Secrets Manager must not traverse the internet, and adding a new NAT gateway has not been approved. The rotation period is 30 days. The rotation function's subnets span 2 Availability Zones, and the database security group currently allows only port 3306 from the application subnets. The function code uses the AWS-provided template without modification, and because approving code changes to the rotation function is difficult, the company does not want to add custom code other than the template. How the application connects with the new password after rotation is outside the scope of this question. Which TWO configurations that let the rotation function connect to the database and call Secrets Manager meet these requirements in the SAFEST way? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leave the Lambda function outside the VPC and allow port 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0 in the inbound rules of the database security group so that the rotation function can connect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store the database password in plaintext in a Lambda environment variable and update the function configuration each time it is rotated, removing the Secrets Manager call.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC and change the database subnet routing to public so that Lambda reaches the database and Secrets Manager over the internet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a Secrets Manager interface endpoint in the VPC so that Lambda reaches the service without traversing the internet.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Connect the rotation Lambda function to the same VPC subnets as the database, and use security groups to allow only the connection between Lambda and the database.

exam-dop-c02-48.explanation: The correct answers are connecting Lambda in the same VPC and a Secrets Manager interface endpoint. The rotation function must reach both the database and the Secrets Manager endpoint; placing it in the same VPC as the database and allowing the connection with security groups lets it connect without exposing the database, and in a VPC with no internet, an interface endpoint lets it reach the service privately. Attaching an internet gateway and making the database subnet public puts the database at risk. Keeping the password in a plaintext environment variable defeats the protection of Secrets Manager. Allowing 0.0.0.0/0 inbound leaves the database open to the whole world. The condition that adding a NAT gateway has not been approved eliminates the configurations that go over the internet and supports the endpoint approach.

exam-dop-c02-49.prompt: The order API of a delivery platform deploys a Lambda function with an AWS SAM template. A new version must initially receive only 10% of invocations, and after watching the error alarm for 10 minutes, the rest must be shifted. Before the shift begins, a smoke test function must validate the new version, and if an alarm fires, the deployment must be rolled back to the previous version without human intervention. This function receives hundreds of invocations per second, and even a brief rise in error rate leads to lost orders, so the number of customers affected by the new version must be limited during the first 10 minutes. The team wants to meet this requirement only by modifying the existing SAM template, without adopting a new deployment tool. The function is invoked behind Amazon API Gateway, and CloudWatch alarms for the Errors and Throttles metrics already exist. The SAM template is deployed from a CI pipeline that has a service role that can use AWS CodeDeploy, and the smoke test function has already been written as a separate SAM resource. This function is deployed three times a week, and having a person watch the deployment progress every time is hard to sustain. What is the SIMPLEST solution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use the canary deployment setting of the API Gateway stage to send 10% of traffic to the new API deployment, have an operator promote the canary in the console after 10 minutes, and delete the canary deployment to roll back if there is a problem; in this method, the entire API deployment, not a Lambda alias or version, is the canary target.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify AutoPublishAlias on the function, set DeploymentPreference to Canary10Percent10Minutes, and specify the smoke test function in the PreTraffic hook of Hooks and the error alarm in Alarms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set DeploymentPreference to AllAtOnce, run the smoke test in a PostTraffic hook, and have the AWS CloudFormation stack rollback revert to the previous version if the test fails.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deploy the new version as a separate function, split two API endpoints with Route 53 weighted records at 10 to 90, and configure a CloudWatch alarm action to invoke a Lambda function that reverts the weights.

exam-dop-c02-49.explanation: The correct answer is to use DeploymentPreference in SAM. AutoPublishAlias creates an alias, Canary10Percent10Minutes shifts 10% first and moves the rest after 10 minutes, the PreTraffic hook validates before the shift, and CodeDeploy rolls back automatically when an alarm in Alarms fires. API Gateway canary works at the API deployment level, not at the Lambda version level, and promotion and rollback are manual operator tasks. AllAtOnce does not shift 10% first, so it does not meet the required staged shift, and PostTraffic validates after the shift is finished. Using a separate function and Route 53 weights can implement the requirement, but you would have to build and operate the records and the alarm-reaction logic yourself, so it is not the simplest. The conditions that no new tool is adopted and only the SAM template is modified, and the requirement for a shift at the Lambda alias level, support DeploymentPreference.

exam-dop-c02-50.prompt: A travel platform team uses AWS CodeDeploy to deploy an application to 30 Amazon EC2 instances. The ApplicationStop script of the last successful revision has an error and always returns a nonzero exit code. The new revision includes a fix to this script, but deployments keep failing at the ApplicationStop stage. The problem must be solved by deploying this revision without re-creating the instances or the deployment group. Production traffic is flowing to the target instances, so manually connecting to each instance to fix the script is not allowed. A hotfix must be deployed today. The deployment group selects instances by EC2 tags, and automatic rollback is turned off. The new revision is already uploaded to Amazon S3, the fixed ApplicationStop script has been verified locally, and the hotfix must be deployed today. Some files left by the previous deployment do not conflict with the new revision, so the file overwrite problem is irrelevant to this requirement. Deployment logs are checked in the CodeDeploy console, and the agent version is the latest. Which action is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delete the deployment group, re-create it with the same name, and deploy the new revision so that the information about the previous revision is reset and the script does not run.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reinstall the CodeDeploy agent on each instance to reset the agent state so that the new revision's AppSpec and scripts are also used at the ApplicationStop stage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase the timeout of the ApplicationStop hook in the new revision's AppSpec to 3600 seconds so that the previous revision's script has enough time to handle the error and exit normally. Also analyze the logs and adjust the time value so that the previous revision's script exits normally within the time limit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When creating the deployment, specify the option that ignores failures of the ApplicationStop lifecycle event (--ignore-application-stop-failures) and deploy the new revision that includes the fixed script.

exam-dop-c02-50.explanation: The correct answer is to deploy with the option that ignores ApplicationStop failures. ApplicationStop runs the AppSpec and script of the last successful revision, not of the current revision, so even if the script is fixed in the new revision, the old script with the error runs in the first deployment and fails. If you deploy once while ignoring the failure, the fixed script is used from then on. Increasing the timeout does not fix the defect that the script always returns a nonzero code, and that script belongs to the previous revision, not the new revision's AppSpec. Re-creating the deployment group changes the cleanup information that was managed under the existing deployment group ID and can cause file conflict errors. Reinstalling the agent has nothing to do with which revision's script is used. The condition that the deployment must be done today without connecting to instances or re-creating the group supports the ignore-failure option.

exam-dop-c02-51.prompt: At an online shopping mall, 40 Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer serve a web application. The company uses CodeDeploy in-place deployments, and the deployment lifecycle takes about 3 minutes per instance. Even during deployment, at least 75% of all instances must always be in a healthy serving state, and the entire deployment must finish within 30 minutes. None of the predefined deployment configurations meets both conditions. Traffic is highest during the daytime and there is little spare capacity per instance, so if service capacity runs short during deployment, order failures increase. The team has no budget to add instances. The instances span three Availability Zones, and CodeDeploy is configured to deregister instances from the ALB target group before deployment and register them again after deployment. Most of the lifecycle time is the application shutdown time in BeforeInstall and is similar across instances. If an instance fails the health check between the start and end of deployment, that instance is treated as failed at that stage. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use CodeDeployDefault.HalfAtATime but increase the instances to 60 so that service capacity remains sufficient even while half are being deployed at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime and split the deployment group into 4, configuring parallel actions in the pipeline so that four deployments start at the same time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce but remove all instances from the ALB before the deployment starts to show a maintenance page, and register them again when the deployment ends.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a custom deployment configuration that specifies a minimum healthy host value of 75%, apply it to the deployment group, and turn on the load balancer connection and automatic rollback on deployment failure in the deployment group.

exam-dop-c02-51.explanation: The correct answer is a custom deployment configuration with a minimum healthy hosts value of 75%. Deploying 10 instances at a time, which is 25% of 40, takes about 3 minutes for each of 4 batches and finishes in about 12 minutes, with at least 75% always in service. HalfAtATime deploys half at the same time, so the healthy percentage drops to 50% and violates the 75% condition; adding instances does not change the percentage criterion and only increases cost. OneAtATime deploys 40 instances sequentially, taking about 120 minutes and violating the 30-minute limit, and splitting groups to parallelize makes the configuration complicated. AllAtOnce deploys to all instances at the same time and directly violates the 75% service requirement. The condition that there is no budget to add instances eliminates solving it by adding capacity.

exam-dop-c02-52.prompt: The audit team of a manufacturing group needs to identify, within one day, which currently running EC2 instances across 70 accounts and 4 Regions of the organization were created from AMIs that are not on the approved list. It wants to query from a single account and avoid logging in to each account or running scripts that repeatedly call service APIs. The AWS Config recorder is recording EC2 instances in all accounts. The results are submitted as audit evidence, and the audit team has no permission to log in to individual accounts and must query all account data from only one account. This check is repeated every quarter, so it would be good if the query can be reused. The list of approved AMI IDs has about 120 entries and is managed in one account as a Systems Manager parameter. The query results must include the account ID, Region, instance ID, and AMI ID, and there are about 6,000 instances. The audit team downloads the query results as CSV and submits them as evidence, and query cost is not a concern. The target instances do not include terminated ones, and only the current configuration state is needed. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run a script that iterates over each account and Region calling DescribeInstances, and merge the results to create a report that compares them with the approved list.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an organization AWS Config aggregator in the delegated administrator account that includes all accounts and Regions, and use an advanced query to find instances whose imageId is not on the approved list.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Query the RunInstances event history of the organization trail with Amazon Athena in 90-day units to estimate the currently running instances and AMIs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Check the number of failed EC2-related controls in the AWS Security Hub organization summary dashboard to find instances with unapproved AMIs.

exam-dop-c02-52.explanation: A Config aggregator and an advanced query are the correct answer. An aggregator gathers configuration data from multiple accounts and Regions in one place, and an advanced query reads the current resource state with SQL-like syntax, so you can find instances by an imageId condition without logging in to accounts or calling service-specific APIs. A script that iterates over accounts and Regions calling DescribeInstances is the approach the question asks to avoid. RunInstances events are past launch records, so the current running state would have to be estimated, and it is hard to distinguish terminated instances. The number of failed Security Hub controls does not provide information for matching against the approved AMI list. The condition that the same query can be reused every quarter also supports a saveable advanced query.

exam-dop-c02-53.prompt: At an e-commerce company, applications in multiple accounts each write JSON logs to their own Amazon CloudWatch Logs log groups. The security team wants to gather the logs of all accounts in an Amazon S3 bucket in a separate log archive account within minutes, but the current script that runs CreateExportTask daily in each account has a large delay and does not meet the requirement. The logs come from 40 accounts at hundreds of GB per day, there must be no loss in transit, and the company does not want to grant S3 write permissions to any account other than the archive account. The application and log agent configuration cannot be changed. The logs come from 40 accounts in the Seoul Region, and the archive account is also in the Seoul Region. The security team queries S3 with Amazon Athena, so it wants files to be loaded under time-based prefixes, and the ingestion delay must be within 5 minutes. One JSON line is one event, and some log groups have different retention periods, so the archive account wants everything to accumulate in the same format. The archive account's bucket is open for write-only access and the source accounts have no read permission. Which configuration meets the near-real-time delivery requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Place a Lambda function in each account that polls the log groups with GetLogEvents every minute and saves directly to the archive account's S3 bucket with PutObject.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the export task schedule from daily to hourly and have each account call CreateExportTask with an EventBridge scheduled rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a Logs destination in front of Amazon Data Firehose in the archive account and deliver to S3 through subscription filters on each account's log groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the agent configuration so that the CloudWatch agent on each instance assumes an IAM role in the archive account and writes directly to log groups in the archive account.

exam-dop-c02-53.explanation: The combination of a Logs destination in the archive account and subscription filters is the correct answer. A subscription filter sends log events to Firehose in near real time and Firehose loads them into S3, so it satisfies both the latency requirement and the requirement of no application changes. A polling Lambda function requires maintaining code and checkpoints in every account, so the operational overhead is large, and the latency is bound by the polling interval. An export task is an asynchronous batch job, so even a shorter schedule does not meet the near-real-time requirement. Having the agent write to log groups in another account requires changing the settings on all hosts and building the S3 loading path separately. The condition that the agent and the application cannot be changed eliminates changing the agent configuration.

exam-dop-c02-54.prompt: In the Workloads OU of a telecom company's AWS Organizations organization there are 60 accounts, and accounts will continue to be added. The security team wants to deploy, with AWS CloudFormation, an IAM role for delivering audit logs and AWS Config rules to the Seoul and Tokyo Regions of all accounts. When a new account joins the OU, deployment must happen automatically, and if deployments fail in 3 or more accounts in a Region, the operation must stop immediately. Management account credentials are not used for day-to-day operations, and the deployed stack must be the same template in all accounts. If manual work arises per account, it becomes hard to prove consistency in an audit. The StackSet template consists of one IAM role and two Config rules and is deployed to the Seoul and Tokyo Regions at the same time. When the template changes, the security team wants to update it in one place and have it reflected in all accounts, and failed accounts can be retried separately later. The audit team wants to view the deployment status of each account on a single screen. The target Regions are only Seoul and Tokyo, and no additional Regions are planned. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Place CloudFormation deployment actions for each account in parallel in AWS CodePipeline, and when a new account is created, update the CDK code to add an action to the pipeline and redeploy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In a delegated administrator account, create a StackSet with service-managed permissions that targets the OU, turn on automatic deployment, and set the failure tolerance to 2.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use a StackSet with self-managed permissions, manually create a StackSet execution role in each account, have a Lambda function add a StackSet instance on every new account creation event, and set the failure tolerance to 2.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a service-managed StackSet in the management account that targets the OU but turn off automatic deployment, have the responsible person add newly created accounts to the target list every week, and set the failure tolerance to 2.

exam-dop-c02-54.explanation: The correct answer is a service-managed StackSet in a delegated administrator account with automatic deployment turned on and the failure tolerance set to 2. With service-managed permissions, StackSets creates the necessary IAM roles and, through automatic deployment, creates stacks in new accounts that join the OU, and using a delegated administrator means management account credentials do not need to be used day to day. Failure tolerance is calculated per Region, so it continues when up to 2 accounts fail and stops at the third failure. Self-managed permissions require creating roles and handling events yourself, and turning off automatic deployment means new accounts are not deployed automatically and the management account must be used. Per-account pipeline actions require code changes every time accounts are added. The conditions of automatic deployment to new accounts and not using management account credentials support service-managed permissions and a delegated administrator.

exam-dop-c02-55.prompt: A CI pipeline pushes images to an Amazon ECR private repository in the tooling account of a financial group, and dozens of new images are pushed every day. Amazon ECS tasks in 15 workload accounts in the same AWS Organizations organization must pull these images, and the repository settings must not need to be edited each time a new workload account is added to the organization. Storing separate copies of the images in each account is not acceptable because of cost. The security team requires that access be strictly limited so that accounts outside the organization cannot pull the images. The platform team has 3 people, so onboarding an account must not involve manual work. The ECS tasks in the workload accounts run on AWS Fargate, and the task execution roles are created with the same naming convention in each account. The repository and all workload accounts are in the Seoul Region, and image pull speed is not a concern. Some other repositories in the tooling account are exposed to external partners under a separate policy, and this must not be mixed with that policy. Each workload team is responsible for approving changes to the task execution role on the pulling side. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Manage a repository policy that lists the workload account IDs as individual Principals with an AWS CloudFormation StackSet, and update the target list and policy statements and redeploy every time a new account is created. Also configure a CI job in which the pipeline reads the target list and redeploys the StackSet when a new account is created.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an ECR read-only IAM user in the tooling account, store the access keys in AWS Secrets Manager, and have the tasks in each account log in to the tooling account registry with these keys to pull images.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an ECR repository in each workload account and replicate images to each account with replication rules from the tooling account repository so that tasks pull from the repository in their own account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the tooling account repository policy, allow ecr:BatchGetImage and ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer with the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition specifying the whole organization, and grant the authorization token and pull permissions to the task execution role in each account.

exam-dop-c02-55.explanation: The correct answer is to allow pulls for the whole organization by using the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition in the repository policy. When a new account joins the organization, it gets access without a policy change, the images are stored only in the tooling account so there is no replication cost, and each task execution role must have the permission to obtain an authorization token through its IAM policy. Listing account IDs requires a policy update for every new account, which violates the requirement. Per-account replication multiplies image storage cost by the number of accounts, which is a prohibited condition. Sharing long-term access keys carries a heavy key management and rotation burden and goes against security best practices. The condition that repository settings must not be edited when a new account is added supports the organization ID condition.

exam-dop-c02-56.prompt: The platform team at a game publisher wants to let 30 development teams create Amazon RDS and security group stacks themselves. Developers must not have IAM permissions for RDS, EC2 security groups, or AWS CloudFormation directly, and they must be able to choose the DB instance class only from three approved options. The product must be usable from multiple development accounts in AWS Organizations. New development teams join every quarter, so this setup must be maintained without manual work by the platform team as the number of teams grows. Developers prefer to select a product from a list in the console and enter only values. Development teams cannot decide encryption and backup retention period themselves when creating RDS and use values fixed in the template. For a new version of the product, the platform team edits and publishes the template and the development teams choose to update, and the development accounts are under the development OU. The platform team must be able to change only the template constraint and publish it when the approved instance classes change. All DBs created by the development teams are placed in private subnets in the Seoul Region. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Give developers only the permission to create CloudFormation stacks and have the stack create resources with a service role, but developers write the templates themselves and the instance class is checked in code review.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a new account for each development team with AWS Control Tower Account Factory, include the RDS and security group stacks in the account creation template, and have developers modify them directly in the account.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Register a CloudFormation product in an AWS Service Catalog portfolio, specify an IAM role for provisioning as a launch constraint, limit the instance class to the three options with a template constraint, and share the portfolio with the organization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Give developer roles full permissions for RDS, security groups, and CloudFormation in each development account, and limit the allowed scope by using an SCP that denies creating DBs with unapproved instance classes.

exam-dop-c02-56.explanation: The correct answer is a configuration that uses Service Catalog launch constraints and template constraints. A launch constraint specifies the IAM role that Service Catalog assumes when provisioning a product, so end users can launch the product without holding permissions for the underlying services. A template constraint limits parameter values such as the instance class to an allow list, and sharing the portfolio makes it available in multiple accounts. Granting developers permissions directly violates the requirement that they must not hold them. Having developers write their own templates means the system cannot enforce the allowed classes. Account Factory is an account provisioning tool, and its purpose is not to provide a product list and restrict values. The condition that developers must not be given permissions directly supports the configuration that uses a launch constraint.

exam-dop-c02-57.prompt: A ticket booking company collects Amazon API Gateway access logs (JSON) in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The company wants to continuously check whether 5xx responses are concentrated on a small number of client IPs and to receive an alarm when the contribution of the top IPs grows. There are tens of thousands of unique IPs, and log ingestion reaches hundreds of GB per day. The company wants to view the top contributors by log field as a real-time time series without people running queries repeatedly. During an incident the responder has no time to build per-IP aggregations by hand, so the alarm must react automatically to changes in the top contributors. The log format is already unified as JSON, so no change is needed on the ingestion side. The API Gateway access logs are in JSON format and include the clientIp, status, and routeKey fields. The alarm only needs to fire when the 5xx count of the single top contributor exceeds a certain value, and the service runs in a single Seoul Region. It is enough for the alarm to fire when the top contributor's 5xx count exceeds a certain value as a 5-minute average. The rule must remain in place after the alarm clears so that it is ready for the next anomaly. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run a Logs Insights query manually in the console every 5 minutes to aggregate 5xx counts per IP, and have the responsible person check the result to judge whether the threshold was exceeded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a metric filter that uses the IP value as a dimension to produce a 5xx metric, and create one alarm for each individual metric that is generated for every unique IP.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a Contributor Insights rule on the log group with the IP field as the key and status 5xx as the filter, and set an alarm on the rule metric.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trace all 5xx requests with an AWS X-Ray sampling rule, and have the responsible person compare error rates per client IP in the service map.

exam-dop-c02-57.explanation: A Contributor Insights rule is the correct answer. It uses a log field as the contributor key to produce the top N contributors and the number of unique contributors as a real-time time series, and an alarm can also be set on the rule metric, so no one needs to run queries repeatedly. Running Logs Insights periodically is not real time and requires continuous human involvement. A metric filter that uses the IP as a dimension requires a separate metric and alarm for every unique IP, and with tens of thousands of them cost and management burden explode. X-Ray is a request-level tracing tool and is not suited to aggregating the top contribution of client IPs as a time series. The condition that there are tens of thousands of unique IPs eliminates the metric filter approach that uses the IP as a dimension.

exam-dop-c02-58.prompt: The integration test stage of an AWS CodeBuild project at an insurance company needs the staging database password. The security team requires that the password must not remain in plaintext in the project environment variables or in the source repository, and that builds must always use the latest value without changing the build configuration even when the password is rotated automatically every 90 days. This build runs dozens of times a day, and multiple developers can view the project settings. Builds must not fail because the password was rotated, and no one should have to fix the settings. The buildspec is in an AWS CodeCommit repository, and the project runs in CodeBuild in the Seoul Region. The staging DB password is stored encrypted in AWS Secrets Manager with a customer managed KMS key, and rotation is performed by a Lambda function integrated with Amazon RDS. All developers can view the project settings, so the password value must not be exposed on the settings screen. The security team will check the password rotation history during audits, and the rotation history is viewed in Secrets Manager. Which actions are needed to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Store the password as a SecureString in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, read it with the parameter-store entry in the buildspec, and create a schedule for the responsible person to update the value every 90 days.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store the password as a Secrets Manager secret, enable automatic rotation, and map it to an environment variable with the secrets-manager entry under env in the buildspec.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grant the secretsmanager:GetSecretValue permission on that secret to the CodeBuild service role, and if a customer managed key is used, also grant decrypt permission on that key.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put the password in the project environment variables as the PLAINTEXT type, and restrict CodeBuild console view permissions to the security team role only so that no one else can see the value.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commit a file in which the password is encrypted with AWS KMS to the source repository, decrypt it during the build, and re-encrypt and commit the file every time it is rotated.

exam-dop-c02-58.explanation: The correct answers are to store the password in Secrets Manager with automatic rotation enabled and map it in the buildspec, and to grant the build service role permission to read the value. The secrets-manager mapping in the buildspec retrieves the current version (AWSCURRENT) at build time by default, so no settings change is needed even after rotation, and retrieval fails if the service role lacks permission. A Parameter Store SecureString stores the value securely but has no automatic rotation feature, so a person has to update it, which does not meet the automatic rotation requirement. A plaintext environment variable can be exposed in plaintext in the console and CLI, so it is a prohibited approach. Committing an encrypted file leaves a secret in the source repository and requires manual work on every rotation. The automatic rotation requirement eliminates the Parameter Store approach, and the ban on plaintext exposure eliminates the environment variable approach.

exam-dop-c02-59.prompt: A stack update for a logistics company's production stack failed and a rollback started, but someone had already deleted in the console the RDS parameter group that needed to be restored during the rollback, so the rollback also failed and the stack went into the UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state. In this state the stack cannot be updated. The parameter group that caused the problem cannot be recovered, but the stack must be recovered safely without deleting the stack or the remaining resources. While recovering, the other resources of the production stack, the Auto Scaling group and the Application Load Balancer, are still serving traffic, so they cannot be deleted or re-created. The incident happened in the morning and must be recovered today. The stack was in the middle of an update that replaces the parameter group in the template with a new name, and what was deleted is the parameter group with the old name. The console deletion cannot be undone, and the team plans to retry the update on the same day after recovery. The database and storage resources of the production stack are healthy and must not be touched during recovery. After recovery, the team plans to check the differences between the template and the actual resources with drift detection. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delete the stack and create it again from the same template to provision all resources anew, and restore the data from the snapshot created at deletion to recover the service.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a change set that contains only a change adding the parameter group and run it on the stack in the UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state so that the missing resource is restored and the rollback then continues.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run continue update rollback while specifying that the parameter group resource that failed to roll back be skipped, return the stack to UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, make the template and the actual resources consistent, and then update again.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run the stack update again with the same template so that CloudFormation automatically re-creates the missing parameter group and the rollback is completed.

exam-dop-c02-59.explanation: The correct answer is to run continue update rollback while skipping the failed resource. A stack in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED cannot be updated, but the rollback can be continued and returned to UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, and if the cause cannot be fixed, the resource that failed to roll back can be skipped to complete it. The skipped resource no longer matches the template, so it must be made consistent before the next update. Deleting and re-creating the stack creates all the remaining resources anew, which is an excessive recovery scope. In this state, stack updates and change set execution are not possible, so updating again or running a change set does not work. The condition that the Auto Scaling group and the ALB cannot be deleted eliminates deleting and re-creating the stack.

exam-dop-c02-60.prompt: Under financial regulation, a securities group must retain management event audit logs for all accounts for 7 years and must be able to prove that the logs have not been tampered with or deleted. This is a newly built environment, and member account administrators must not be able to turn off or modify the trail. The logs must be producible immediately when a regulator requests them, and delete permission on the log store must not be granted to anyone during normal times. Audits are performed every year by an external auditor, and log retention is done in a separate archive account to reduce cost. The organization is AWS Organizations with all features enabled and has 80 accounts. Logs are stored in a dedicated Amazon S3 bucket in the archive account in the Seoul Region, and the regulator requires evidence showing that the logs have not been tampered with to be submitted together with the logs. The organization is AWS Organizations with all features enabled and has 80 accounts. After logs are delivered, access to the archive bucket must be allowed only for the audit role. Log storage cost is within the approved budget, and deletion for cost reduction is not considered. Which solution meets these requirements in the SAFEST way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an individual trail in each account and have each account administrator retain logs in the account's own bucket, with a lifecycle rule that deletes them after 7 years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an organization trail with log file integrity validation turned on in the management account, deliver it to S3 in the archive account, and apply S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for 7 years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an organization trail and store it in an SSE-S3 bucket with only S3 versioning turned on to protect against deletion and overwriting, without using integrity validation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Send the trail events of all accounts to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, set the log group retention to 7 years, and use this as the means of tamper prevention and integrity proof.

exam-dop-c02-60.explanation: An organization trail with integrity validation turned on and Object Lock in compliance mode is the correct answer. An organization trail cannot be deleted or have its settings changed in member accounts, log file integrity validation proves tampering and deletion with hashes and signed digest files, and compliance mode Object Lock prevents anyone from deleting objects during the retention period. A per-account trail can be turned off by the account administrator, who can also erase the logs. Versioning alone allows someone with delete permissions to delete versions and does not prove tampering. Log group retention is not a tamper-proof means such as signed digests. The requirement to prove tampering needs log file integrity validation, and the condition that delete permission is not granted to anyone even during normal times supports compliance mode.

exam-dop-c02-61.prompt: A fintech company's container images are pushed to Amazon ECR by an AWS CodeBuild pipeline. The audit requirements are that, in the production repository, no tag can be overwritten with a different image once it has been pushed, and that during an incident it must be possible to roll back to exactly the image that was deployed previously. The current pipeline pushes both a git commit hash tag and a latest tag with every build, and the Amazon ECS task definition references latest. In the past, an image with the same tag was overwritten and the cause of an incident could not be reproduced, so the auditor requires evidence that tags and image contents always correspond one-to-one. The company does not want to change the pipeline structure significantly. The repository is in a single Seoul Region, and an average of 200 production images are pushed per month. Deployment updates the ECS task definition through AWS CodePipeline, and rollback works by updating the service again to point to the image of the previous deployment. The development repository is excluded from this requirement. The pipeline's image tag convention uses both the build number and the commit hash, and this convention itself will not be changed. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST amount of change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a lifecycle policy to retain previous images with the same tag for a certain period, keep copies in another repository with replication rules, and restore from the copy when a problem occurs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the repository to immutable but specify only the latest tag as an exclusion filter so that latest can still be overwritten, and keep the ECS task definition referencing latest as it does now.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on tag immutability for the repository, change the pipeline to push only the commit hash tag, and update the ECS task definition in the deployment stage to reference the commit hash tag.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Attach an IAM policy that denies ecr:PutImage to developer roles so that people cannot push directly, and allow only the pipeline role to push.

exam-dop-c02-61.explanation: The correct answer is to turn on tag immutability and use only the commit hash tag. In an immutable repository, pushing with an existing tag returns ImageTagAlreadyExistsException, so continuing to push latest would make the pipeline fail, while using only unique tags means no tag is overwritten and the exact image of the previous deployment can be referenced for rollback. A configuration that exempts only latest violates the requirement that no tag can be overwritten. An IAM policy that blocks only developer pushes cannot prevent the pipeline from pushing again with the same tag. Lifecycle policies and replication are after-the-fact retention means and cannot prevent tag overwriting itself. The auditor's requirement for evidence that tags and images correspond one-to-one eliminates the approach that exempts latest.

exam-dop-c02-62.prompt: Amazon GuardDuty at an e-commerce company produced a backdoor communication finding for an EC2 instance running in an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer. The automated response workflow must preserve forensic evidence while minimizing service impact, must not terminate the suspected infected instance, and must keep the group's service capacity. The collected evidence will be used for follow-up investigation and regulatory reporting, so the disk state at the time of the incident must be preserved separately, independent of later changes. This process must run automatically, without paging anyone, even at night. The group is behind an Application Load Balancer and normally has little spare capacity. The instance belongs to an Auto Scaling group spread across 3 Availability Zones in the Seoul Region and has two EBS volumes (root and data). The automated response is run by AWS Step Functions after Amazon EventBridge receives the GuardDuty finding, and analysis is performed in a separate forensics account. The execution history of the response workflow is used as evidence in the incident report, so the result of each step must be retained. Which TWO actions should the workflow perform? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Terminate the instance immediately and let Auto Scaling replace it with a new instance, minimizing the time the suspected infected instance remains in service.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reboot the instance to remove the malicious process residing in memory, and then leave it in the group as is to continue serving.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create snapshots of the EBS volumes attached to the instance and preserve them as evidence for analysis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Detach the instance from the Auto Scaling group and deregister it from the load balancer, and let a replacement instance launch without reducing capacity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immediately reset the passwords of all IAM users in the entire organization to block possible credential leakage all at once.

exam-dop-c02-62.explanation: The correct answers are preserving EBS snapshots and detaching the instance from the Auto Scaling group. A snapshot leaves the disk state at that point in time as separate evidence without stopping or terminating the instance, and detaching the instance from the group deregisters it from the load balancer so traffic stops, and if you choose not to decrease capacity, a replacement instance launches and service capacity is maintained. Immediate termination loses evidence and violates the requirement not to terminate. A reboot erases memory evidence, and the malicious code on the same disk remains, so the infection continues. Resetting passwords of all users in the entire organization is an excessive measure unrelated to this instance compromise and greatly affects services and users. The requirements for automatic execution without paging anyone and for not terminating the instance eliminate immediate termination.

exam-dop-c02-63.prompt: The development team at a game company wants to use CDK Pipelines to create a pipeline in the shared services account (111111111111) that deploys stacks to the Seoul Region of the staging account (222222222222) and the production account (333333333333). All deployments must be made only through roles that the pipeline assumes, without storing long-term credentials. The security team requires that in the target accounts, no principal other than the pipeline account be able to assume the deployment roles. The three accounts belong to the same organization, and CDK bootstrapping has not been done even once. The first deployment is scheduled for tomorrow. The CDK app is written in TypeScript, and the pipeline receives the source through a GitHub connection in the shared services account in the Seoul Region. The target accounts do not yet have a place to upload assets (Lambda code, container images), and the same CDK app stacks are deployed to staging and production. The pipeline runs automatically whenever a code change is merged, and no manual deployment procedure is wanted. What must be done to satisfy all the requirements before the first deployment? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an IAM user in each target account, store the access keys in AWS Secrets Manager in the pipeline account, and have the deployment stage read these keys to sign in to the target accounts and deploy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When bootstrapping the target accounts, specify the pipeline account ID in the --trust option and specify the policies that AWS CloudFormation will use at deployment with --cloudformation-execution-policies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create the CDK bootstrap stack in the two target accounts with CloudFormation StackSets using service-managed permissions, and use the pipeline account as is without bootstrapping it separately.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create the same AWS CodePipeline pipeline in each target account to subscribe to the same source repository at the same time, and have the pipeline in the shared services account handle only the build.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bootstrap the Seoul Region of the pipeline account and the two target accounts with cdk bootstrap so that the roles and asset buckets used for deployment are prepared in each environment.

exam-dop-c02-63.explanation: The correct answers are bootstrapping all the relevant environments and specifying --trust so that the target accounts trust the pipeline account when they are bootstrapped. CDK Pipelines requires bootstrapping both the environment where the pipeline is created and the environments where stacks are deployed, and the bootstrap of a target environment must specify the pipeline account ID with --trust so that the pipeline in that account can assume the roles and deploy; the execution policies determine the deployment permissions of CloudFormation. Long-term access keys violate the constraint of not storing long-term credentials. Creating a pipeline in each target account breaks the structure of deploying from the shared account. A configuration that does not bootstrap the pipeline account omits the required environment preparation. The background that the target accounts do not yet have a place to upload assets makes bootstrapping the target environments necessary.

exam-dop-c02-64.prompt: The payment API request count metric of a payment processor shows a pattern in which traffic concentrates during weekday daytime and drops sharply on weekends. A fixed-threshold alarm misses weekend drops if tuned to the weekday peak and produces repeated false positives on weekdays if tuned to weekends. The company wants to receive alarms only when the metric leaves its normal range for the time of day and day of the week, without people recalculating thresholds periodically. The alarm must detect both sharp drops and sharp increases, and the operations team does not want to adjust thresholds by hand. The metric has already been accumulating in Amazon CloudWatch for several weeks. The metric period is 1 minute, and there are special event days such as promotions about twice a year. Alarm evaluation at 5-minute intervals is sufficient, and the operations team wants to see the normal range band on a graph when the alarm fires. The metric has already been accumulating for several weeks. After the alarm fires, the on-call engineer checks the metric and the normal range together through the Amazon SNS notification. The alarm must work with one rule for both weekdays and weekends, and the company does not want separate alarms per day of the week. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set a high fixed threshold based on the weekday peak value and disable the alarm actions on weekends with an EventBridge scheduler.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have a Lambda function read last week's metrics with GetMetricData every week, calculate the mean and standard deviation, and update the threshold with PutMetricAlarm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enable CloudWatch anomaly detection on the metric and create an anomaly detection alarm that goes to ALARM when the value leaves the expected range band.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the request count metric statistic from the 1-minute average to p99, set the threshold once, and keep it fixed afterward.

exam-dop-c02-64.explanation: An anomaly detection alarm is the correct answer. The anomaly detection model learns seasonality such as time of day and day of the week as well as trends, builds an expected range band, and raises an alarm only when the value leaves that band, so thresholds do not need to be recalculated. A fixed peak-based threshold plus disabling on a weekend schedule misses weekend drops and intra-day variation, and managing the schedule becomes a new burden. Recalculating weekly with Lambda is self-built code and has limits in reflecting changing patterns because it uses last week's statistics. Changing the statistic to p99 does not solve the time-of-day problem because the threshold stays fixed. The background that several weeks of data have already accumulated helps the anomaly detection model learn the day-of-week pattern.

exam-dop-c02-65.prompt: GuardDuty is enabled in the 50 accounts of a telecom organization, and there is a security delegated administrator account. The company wants to build a response that automatically isolates the affected instance when an EC2-related finding with high or higher severity occurs. The company does not want to deploy rules to each member account or create cross-account event bus connections. The response must start within a few minutes of the finding, and the isolation action must be performed only with a least-privilege role in the target account. The number of accounts will keep growing, and the security team has 3 people. Findings occur in GuardDuty in the Seoul Region, and the SSM Agent is installed on the instances in member accounts. The isolation action is an Automation runbook that replaces the security group with an isolation security group, and an AutomationAssumeRole with the same name is deployed in every member account. Forensic analysis of the instance after isolation is performed in a separate security account and is not included in the scope of this question. The isolation targets are limited to findings that have high or higher severity and point to an EC2 instance. Which solution has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Put a rule with a severity condition on the default event bus of the delegated administrator account, and isolate with Automation that assumes the role in the account indicated by accountId.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deploy the same EventBridge rule to each of the 50 member accounts with StackSets, and configure each rule's target to forward events to the event bus of the delegated administrator account.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Export GuardDuty findings to Amazon S3, query high-severity items once a day with Amazon Athena, and have the responsible person run an isolation script.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place a Lambda function in each member account to poll GuardDuty GetFindings every 5 minutes and isolate the instances in that account if there are items of high or higher severity.

exam-dop-c02-65.explanation: A rule on the default event bus of the delegated administrator account is the correct answer. In the delegated administrator account, its own EventBridge rule receives the finding events of member accounts as well, and the target account can be identified with detail.accountId, so there is no need to deploy anything per member account. Deploying rules and forwarding targets to each member with StackSets creates and maintains unneeded configuration in 50 places. Exporting to S3 and daily Athena queries introduce a delay of a day before isolation, which is unsuitable for automated response. A polling Lambda function per member requires operating code and schedules in every account and adds a 5-minute delay. The condition that rules must not be deployed to each member account eliminates the StackSets approach.

exam-dop-c02-66.prompt: The payment API of a shopping app company runs as an Amazon ECS Fargate service. When deploying a new version, the team wants to run integration tests through a test listener before the version receives real user traffic. If the tests pass, only 10% of the traffic must be sent first and observed for 5 minutes, after which the rest is shifted, and if the tests fail or a 5xx rate alarm fires, the deployment must return to the previous version without human intervention. A separate server or state machine for deployment orchestration cannot be operated. The service runs 24 hours a day, so scheduling a maintenance window and blocking traffic is not an option, and the deployment history must remain in the CodeDeploy deployment records for audit. The service uses ALB production listener 443 and test listener 8443, and the integration test has already been written as a Lambda function that calls 8443. When the new version stabilizes, the old tasks must be cleaned up, and the service runs in a single Seoul Region. Payment processing must not be interrupted even during deployment windows, and the previous version must be able to receive traffic until the point of rollback. Which configuration meets all of these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Specify CodeDeployDefault.ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes in a CodeDeploy ECS blue/green deployment group, run the integration test with Lambda in the AfterAllowTestTraffic hook of the AppSpec, and connect the 5xx rate alarm as the deployment group's automatic rollback alarm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run an AWS Step Functions state machine from a CodePipeline invoke action to change the target group weights of the ALB listener rule in stages from 10% to 100%, and write it yourself so that the state machine restores the weights if an alarm fires.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use an ECS service rolling update with a minimum healthy percent of 100% and turn on the deployment circuit breaker rollback so that it returns to the previous task definition revision if the new tasks fail the ALB health check.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specify CodeDeployDefault.ECSAllAtOnce in a CodeDeploy ECS blue/green deployment, run the integration test in the BeforeAllowTraffic hook, and if a problem is detected, manually adjust Route 53 weighted records to return traffic to the previous service; after rollback, the responsible person also manually redeploys the previous service.

exam-dop-c02-66.explanation: The correct answer is a combination of CodeDeploy ECS blue/green deployment with ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes, the AfterAllowTestTraffic hook, and alarm-based automatic rollback. Test listener validation, the 10% 5-minute canary, and alarm rollback are all managed features, so no separate server or state machine is needed. Rolling updates with a circuit breaker only detect health check failures, so there is no test listener validation and no 10% first shift. ECSAllAtOnce moves all traffic at once, violating the requirement for a 10% first shift, and the rollback is a manual adjustment that requires human intervention. Changing weights with Step Functions can be implemented, but you must write and operate the state machine yourself, which conflicts with the constraint that no state machine can be operated. The condition of not operating a state machine and the requirement for CodeDeploy deployment records eliminate the Step Functions approach.

exam-dop-c02-67.prompt: Under the security policy of a financial group, all Amazon EC2 servers must run from a golden AMI with the latest patches applied. The platform team wants, whenever a new version of the Amazon Linux 2023 base AMI is released, to build a new AMI without human intervention after it passes tests with a CIS check script, and deploy it automatically to 12 workload accounts in the Seoul and Tokyo Regions. An AMI that fails testing must not be deployed to any account. The cost of image building and testing must be incurred only once, and the company wants to eliminate the procedure in which workload teams create or copy AMIs themselves.
