The platform team has 3 people and cannot easily maintain build orchestration code. A new version of the base AMI comes out once or twice a month, and the golden AMI includes installation of an internal agent and a CIS check. The target accounts belong to the same organization, AMIs are delivered by account sharing, and retiring older AMIs is not part of this requirement. The internal agent version included in the AMI is taken from a parameter managed by the security team, and the build pipeline reads this value. Which configuration meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a separate Image Builder pipeline in each workload account so that each builds and tests AMIs on its own schedule, and have the platform team review the per-account results every week and ask the accounts that fail to take action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Build the AMI with Packer in a CodeBuild stage of AWS CodePipeline, and if the test script succeeds, run Region copy and account sharing with the AWS CLI; the responsible person checks for new base AMI versions and starts the pipeline manually.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In an EC2 Image Builder image pipeline, specify the parent image with a version wildcard (x.x.x), set the schedule to run only when there are dependency updates, and define together the test components and the distribution settings that target the two Regions and 12 accounts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Implement it so that an EventBridge rule periodically runs a Lambda function that launches a temporary EC2 instance from the latest base AMI, completes configuration and testing with a script, and then calls CreateImage, CopyImage, and the account-sharing API in order.

exam-dop-c02-67.explanation: The correct answer is a configuration in which a single Image Builder pipeline handles building, testing, and distribution as managed features. With a version wildcard for the parent image and a schedule conditioned on dependency updates, the pipeline runs automatically only when a new base AMI is released, an image that fails testing is not distributed, and the distribution settings deliver it to multiple Regions and accounts at once. Implementing it yourself with Lambda and EventBridge means maintaining both the orchestration and the error handling. The Packer approach has a person check for new base AMIs and start it, which violates the requirement for automation without human intervention. Having a pipeline in each account means operating 12 separate pipelines, which increases the burden and reduces test consistency. The condition that build and test cost is incurred only once eliminates the per-account pipeline approach.

exam-dop-c02-68.prompt: A team at a media company performs CodeDeploy in-place deployments to Amazon EC2 instances. The new revision is set up so that the AfterInstall script creates the file /etc/app/feature.conf, but the ValidateService stage failed and an automatic rollback ran. After the rollback, the previous revision was deployed, but feature.conf remains on the instances and changes the behavior of the previous version. The operator wants to find the cause and prevent recurrence. The deployment procedure including the scripts is already used in the same way by several services, so changing to blue/green to replace instances is not part of this scope. There are 40 instances, and manually connecting to delete the file would not be a recurrence prevention measure. The previous revision in the rollback deployment already runs a service stop script in the BeforeInstall hook, so there is a place to put cleanup logic. feature.conf is not in the files section of the new revision's AppSpec and is created only by the script, and manually connecting to 40 instances to delete it is not a recurrence prevention measure. The operator wants to guarantee that the previous version operates without that setting even after a rollback. Which cause and action BEST fit this situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rollback reinstalls the last successful revision as a new deployment, and CodeDeploy deletes only the files installed by the previous deployment that are listed in the cleanup file, so files created by scripts remain. Add cleanup logic that deletes the file to the BeforeInstall hook script of the revision that is redeployed during rollback.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The content overwrite option for the deployment is set to Retain, so feature.conf was preserved. Changing the overwrite option to Overwrite when creating the deployment removes the file on rollback. This option must be specified each time a deployment is created and is applied the same way to later deployments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The timeout of the ValidateService hook script is short, so the rollback deployment was interrupted midway. Increase the hook's timeout value so that the rollback deployment runs through all lifecycle events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The CodeDeploy agent must be restarted after a rollback ends for the cleanup file to take effect. When the rollback completes, automatically run an operation that restarts the agent on all instances with Systems Manager.

exam-dop-c02-68.explanation: The correct answer is to understand how rollback works and add cleanup logic to the script. CodeDeploy handles a rollback as a new deployment of the last successful revision, and before a new deployment it deletes only the files installed by the previous deployment that are listed in the cleanup file. Files that a script creates at runtime are not subject to cleanup and therefore remain, and since a rollback deployment runs the scripts of the revision being rolled back to, the deletion must be done directly in that revision's BeforeInstall hook. The overwrite option is how files that already existed at the target location are handled and does not delete files created by a script. A hook timeout would appear as a deployment failure and does not explain a file that remains after a successful rollback. There is no documented behavior in which restarting the agent applies the cleanup file. The fact that files created by scripts are not subject to CodeDeploy cleanup is the reason the cleanup logic must go in the script.

exam-dop-c02-69.prompt: A healthcare data company's organization uses Amazon S3 buckets, IAM roles, AWS KMS keys, and Amazon SQS queues in three Regions. The company wants to continuously find and notify the security team whenever a resource-based policy change opens access to accounts outside the organization or to anonymous users. The zone of trust is the entire organization, and the solution must not require creating separate check rules per service and must have the lowest operational overhead. Policy changes happen several times a day, resources of new services keep growing, and the security team must know within 24 hours of detection. The security team has 2 people, so a method where people review policies every quarter is hard to sustain. The target resources are hundreds of S3 buckets, thousands of IAM roles, and dozens of KMS keys and SQS queues, and there are a few intended shares with external partners outside the organization. Intended shares must be filterable by archiving, and notifications may be received through finding creation events. The security team must be able to mark whether an external sharing item in the findings list is intended after review. The analysis results are collected separately per Region, and the security team does not prioritize viewing them on a single screen. Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust in each Region in use, and deliver the findings to Amazon SNS through Amazon EventBridge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on the AWS Config managed rule related to S3 public access, and for the remaining services have the responsible person visually review the resource policies every quarter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enable Amazon Macie to check sensitive data and external sharing status of the buckets, and check IAM roles and KMS keys together in the Macie findings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty and receive notifications to the security team when an abnormal access finding occurs, treating it as a resource policy change.

exam-dop-c02-69.explanation: An external access analyzer is the correct answer. This analyzer uses the organization as the zone of trust, analyzes the policies of multiple resources such as S3, IAM roles, KMS keys, and SQS, and creates a finding for every access opened to an external principal; because analyzers are per Region, one must be created in each Region in use. Config rules require separate rules per service, and having people review the rest conflicts with the continuous detection requirement. Macie is a sensitive data detection service for S3 and does not look at IAM role and KMS key policies. GuardDuty centers on threat behavior detection and has only some findings related to S3 bucket policies; it does not continuously analyze whether the policies of IAM roles, KMS keys, and SQS queues are open to external parties, and there is no basis for treating an abnormal access finding as a policy change. The requirement for external access analysis that includes IAM roles and KMS keys eliminates the S3-specific service.

exam-dop-c02-70.prompt: A shopping platform deploys its Lambda-based order service with the AWS CodeDeploy Canary10Percent5Minutes configuration. If the error rate rises in the new version, traffic must be returned to the previous version before a person can look, and the error rate is already managed with a CloudWatch alarm (Errors metric). Many deployments happen at night and no one can be on standby, and when the alarm threshold is exceeded the service must return to the previous version within a few minutes. The company does not want to change the alarm configuration it already uses and must keep changes to the deployment pipeline minimal. The service is defined in a SAM template that splits traffic at the alias level. The deployment group uses the Lambda compute platform and the service is defined in a SAM template that splits traffic at the alias level. The alarm evaluates the Errors metric as a 5-minute sum, the threshold has already been set based on operating experience, and there are a few deployments a day, mostly at night. It has been decided that, starting with this deployment, the procedure in which a person runs the rollback when the alarm fires will be eliminated. If a deployment is in progress when the alarm fires, the weights must immediately go back to the previous version. Which solution meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Write a runbook in which, five minutes after a deployment starts, the responsible person checks the alarm state and manually switches the weights to the previous version alias.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Receive the alarm state change event through Amazon EventBridge and implement code in which a Lambda function directly returns the weights to the previous version with UpdateAlias.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add the alarm as a monitoring alarm on the deployment group, and turn on the deployment group's automatic rollback configuration so that it rolls back automatically when the alarm exceeds the threshold.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put validation logic in the PreTraffic hook Lambda function and judge that rollback after the shift is unnecessary because all errors are filtered out before traffic moves.

exam-dop-c02-70.explanation: Alarm monitoring and automatic rollback configuration on the deployment group is the correct answer. When an alarm crosses its threshold or the deployment fails, CodeDeploy rolls back to the last healthy revision as a new deployment, so simply attaching the existing alarm rolls back without human intervention. A runbook for manual switching by the responsible person conflicts with the requirement to return before a person can look and reacts slowly. Returning the alias with EventBridge and Lambda can conflict with the weights that CodeDeploy controls and also requires self-built code. The PreTraffic hook validates only before the traffic shift, so it cannot detect an error rate increase that occurs after the shift. The conditions of not changing the existing alarm and minimizing pipeline changes support alarm monitoring on the deployment group.

exam-dop-c02-71.prompt: The order processing Lambda function of a delivery app company calls PutMetricData synchronously on every request, which increases response time and occasionally causes throttling. Order throughput is several hundred requests per second, and the function's latency target is 200 ms or less. The team wants to use the metrics in alarms while keeping code changes small, and when a problem occurs wants to look up detailed attributes of the request (order ID, user ID) from the same log event. Unique values such as the order ID must not be made metric dimensions. It is sufficient for metrics to be reflected in alarm evaluation in 1-minute units, and the logs are already collected in CloudWatch Logs. The function is written in Node.js and already outputs structured JSON logs. The two metrics needed are OrdersProcessed and OrderLatencyMs, and the alarm is evaluated with a single service name dimension. The key goal of this change is to use the metrics in alarms without increasing the function's synchronous latency. The function's memory setting and timeout are left as they are, and only the logging approach is changed. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Batch the PutMetricData calls that were made for every request into a single call right before the function ends, and include the order ID in the dimensions for detailed tracking.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a metric filter that uses the order ID and user ID from every log line as dimensions so that a metric is created for each unique value, and set alarms only on the metrics that are needed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Record the latency in AWS X-Ray annotations in the Lambda function and configure X-Ray group notifications so that an alarm fires based on the annotation value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Output structured logs in the EMF format so that CloudWatch extracts the metrics, and keep the order ID and user ID as log properties rather than dimensions.

exam-dop-c02-71.explanation: EMF is the correct answer. The function only outputs a JSON log that contains the metric definitions, and CloudWatch extracts the metrics asynchronously, so the synchronous call latency and throttling of PutMetricData disappear, and unique values remain in the log as properties rather than dimensions and can be queried with Logs Insights. Batching still leaves an API call in the code, and including the order ID as a dimension creates a metric for every unique value and increases cost. A metric filter with unique-value dimensions explodes the number of metrics for the same reason. X-Ray annotations are for searching traces and are not for producing a base metric for alarms. The fact that the logs are already structured JSON means the code change to switch to EMF is small.

exam-dop-c02-72.prompt: A fintech company updates an AWS CloudFormation stack that includes an Auto Scaling group and an Application Load Balancer every week. There have been two incidents in which everything was fine right after an update but a 5xx rate alarm fired about 20 minutes later, and each time an operator manually reapplied the previous template. The company wants to monitor the alarm for 30 minutes after an update finishes and have the stack roll back to its previous state automatically, without human intervention, if the alarm fires. Updates are performed outside business hours and no one is on standby, so no human judgment may be involved from detecting the failure to recovery. The 5xx rate alarm has already been created in CloudWatch. The stack is in the Seoul Region, and the 5xx rate alarm to use as the rollback trigger has already been created in CloudWatch. Stack updates are run from a CI pipeline, and the usual update takes about 15 minutes. The rollback must return the entire stack state to before the update, and partial recovery of only some resources is not allowed. If an update triggers the alarm again, root cause analysis must be possible within the same day. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a change set before the update to review the impact, run the change set, have an operator watch the alarm dashboard for 30 minutes, and cancel the stack update if anything abnormal appears.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify both DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy as Retain on the Auto Scaling group so that the existing group remains even if an update causes resource replacement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set a stack policy that denies updates to the Auto Scaling group and ALB resources, and temporarily lift the policy whenever a change is needed and reapply it after the update.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specify the 5xx rate CloudWatch alarm as a rollback trigger in the rollback configuration of the stack update, and set the monitoring time to 30 minutes.

exam-dop-c02-72.explanation: The correct answer is to specify the CloudWatch alarm as a rollback trigger in the rollback configuration and set the monitoring time to 30 minutes. After resource deployment finishes, CloudFormation watches the alarm for the specified monitoring time, and if the alarm goes to ALARM, it automatically rolls back the entire stack operation. The monitoring time can be set from 0 to 180 minutes, so it meets the 30-minute requirement. A stack policy is a means of blocking updates to specified resources and is unrelated to alarm-based rollback. Reviewing a change set and monitoring manually cannot cancel an update once it has already finished, and it involves a person. A deletion policy only preserves a replaced or deleted resource and does not trigger a rollback. The condition that rollback must happen without human judgment eliminates the manual monitoring approach.

exam-dop-c02-73.prompt: A manufacturing company runs legacy applications on 60 VMware VMs (a mix of Windows and Linux) in its on-premises data center and wants to set up disaster recovery for them in AWS. The applications cannot be modified, the RPO is a few seconds, the RTO is within 1 hour, and normal-time AWS cost must be minimized. Recovery drills are held every quarter and must be repeatable without affecting production, and the impact on production performance of the source servers must be minimal. The recovery procedure is started by a person using predefined settings. The data center and AWS are already connected with AWS Direct Connect. Some of the 60 source servers run Windows Server 2016, which is an operating system supported by the replication agent. A staging subnet for replication can be created in AWS in advance, and DNS cutover after recovery is handled separately. The temporary instances used in recovery drills must be cleaned up after the drill so that costs do not continue to accrue. No person is involved in application initialization after the recovery servers boot. Which solution is MOST suitable to meet these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Back up the VMware VMs several times a day with AWS Backup and store them in a vault in an AWS Region, and when a failure occurs, restore servers from the backups to resume the service.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run the same number of EC2 instances as on premises at all times in the AWS Region, continuously synchronize files and data with rsync, and shift only traffic when a failure occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Install the AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery agent on the source servers to perform continuous block-level replication to a staging area subnet, and launch recovery instances only for drills and real failures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Upload a nightly snapshot of each VM to Amazon S3, and document a procedure to create an AMI with VM Import/Export and launch new EC2 instances when a failure occurs. In this process, the boot verification and network configuration of the converted AMI are performed manually by the responsible person at the time of the failure.

exam-dop-c02-73.explanation: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery is the correct answer. It replicates the source servers' data continuously at the block level, so the RPO is on the order of a few seconds; it keeps replication in a staging area made of low-cost storage and minimal compute and launches recovery instances only for drills or failures, so normal-time cost is low, and it also supports drills that do not affect production. Nightly snapshots mean a day of data loss, which violates the RPO of a few seconds, and import and conversion also take a long time. Running the same number of instances at all times directly violates the cost minimization requirement, and the rsync setup must also be managed yourself. Backups several times a day lose the data between intervals and do not satisfy an RPO of a few seconds. The Direct Connect link is only a replication path and does not change the judgment that continuous replication is needed for an RPO of a few seconds.

exam-dop-c02-74.prompt: The license server of a semiconductor design company runs on a single EC2 instance (using only an EBS root volume and no instance store volumes) that is tied to its instance ID and a fixed private IP. If a system status check fails because of an underlying hardware problem, the instance must be recovered automatically with the same instance ID and IP. OS errors inside the instance are handled separately. Recovery must be attempted automatically, and the operations team does not want to take manual action early in the morning. Reissuing the license takes several days, so creating a new instance is not an option. The instance is of a current-generation type that supports EC2 automatic recovery, and its EBS root volume is encrypted. After recovery, the attached network interface and the fixed IP must remain the same, and alarm notifications are also received through Amazon SNS. Because this server is a single instance, a high availability cluster configuration is not permitted under the license. When recovery occurs, the operations team only needs to receive the SNS notification, and no separate approval is required. Which solution meets these requirements with no additional server cost?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure the EC2 recover action on a StatusCheckFailed_System alarm (the default simplified automatic recovery for supported instances serves the same purpose).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure a CloudWatch alarm on the StatusCheckFailed_Instance metric that performs the EC2 reboot action so that the instance is restarted when a failure occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wrap the instance in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 1 so that it is replaced with a new instance if it fails the health check.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create AMIs regularly, and when a failure occurs have a Lambda function launch a new instance and attach the existing private IP to it.

exam-dop-c02-74.explanation: The recover action connected to the system status check is the correct answer. Recovery moves the instance from the faulty host to another host and keeps the instance ID, the private and Elastic IP addresses, the metadata, and the attached EBS volumes as they are. An instance status check alarm is a metric that looks at OS-level problems and does not resolve a host hardware problem, and a reboot takes place on the same host. Auto Scaling replacement creates a new instance ID, which conflicts with the license requirement. Launching from an AMI also changes the instance ID and adds the burden of Lambda and AMI management. The condition that reissuing the license takes several days eliminates approaches that create a new instance.

exam-dop-c02-75.prompt: The internal order system of a retail company consists of web and application servers in Seoul and Amazon Aurora MySQL. Management requires an RTO of 30 minutes and an RPO within a few seconds, and compute cost in the DR Region must be minimized during normal operation. A person may start the work of bringing up the service in the DR Region during a Regional failure, but the procedure must be automated, and the work of turning on the application servers in the DR Region during a failure can be automated with a template. DR drills are held twice a year. The budget is most sensitive to DR Region compute cost. The Aurora cluster has three db.r6g.2xlarge instances, and the application servers are 12 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The DR Region is Osaka, and IaC is AWS CloudFormation. No traffic is served in the DR Region during normal operation, and the storage cost in the DR Region is acceptable. DNS cutover during recovery is handled by a Route 53 change and is outside the scope of this question. Which DR strategy and configuration is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pilot light: continuously replicate data to the DR Region with an Aurora global database, keep the application servers off with only the AMI and the IaC template prepared, and when a failure occurs, launch the servers from the template and scale them out.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Warm standby: always run a scaled-down full environment in the DR Region, replicate with an Aurora global database, and have part of the traffic handled even in normal times using Route 53 weighted distribution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Backup and restore: copy daily DB snapshots and AMIs to the DR Region, and when a failure occurs, restore a cluster from the snapshot and create new servers from the IaC template to resume the service.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multi-site active/active: operate full capacity in both Regions at the same time and have both Regions handle user requests by using the write forwarding feature of the Aurora global database.

exam-dop-c02-75.explanation: Pilot light is the correct answer. Data is replicated continuously with an Aurora global database, which satisfies an RPO of a few seconds, and the application servers are only prepared with the AMI and IaC and kept off, so normal-time compute cost is lowest; during a failure, an automated procedure started by a person turns the servers on and scales them to aim for the 30-minute RTO. Backup and restore uses daily snapshots, which violates the RPO of a few seconds, and restore time is also long. Warm standby meets the requirements but runs a scaled-down full environment at all times, which is excessive compared with the requirement to minimize compute cost. Multi-site active/active maintains full capacity in both Regions and is the most expensive. The condition that DR compute cost is the most sensitive eliminates warm standby and multi-site.

exam-dva-c02-1.prompt: A company's CI pipeline pushes a container image to Amazon ECR on every commit. A single repository in one account holds images for twenty services, and tens of thousands of untagged images and old development images have accumulated, increasing storage costs every month. Development tags start with dev-. Release-tagged images that start with v must not be deleted because of audits. Only two infrastructure engineers are on the team, and they do not want to maintain a separate cleanup script. The cleanup rule should be applied once to the entire repository regardless of service, and deleted images do not need to be recoverable. Currently, cleanup is done manually and occasionally by using a crontab on the CI server. Which cleanup method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Write a script that runs in an AWS Lambda function on a schedule, lists the images, selects the old images, and deletes them directly. Run the function by using Amazon EventBridge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delete and re-create the repository, and then push only the release images again from another repository to remove all unnecessary images.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use an ECR lifecycle policy that expires untagged images after a set period and expires images with the development prefix tag beyond a set count. Exclude images with the v prefix from the rules.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable tag immutability on the repository so that the same tag cannot be overwritten, which causes old images to be cleaned up automatically.

exam-dva-c02-1.explanation: A lifecycle policy is a managed ECR feature that automatically expires images according to rules, so there is no code or scheduler to operate, and a tag prefix condition can protect the release images. A Lambda deletion script does the same job, but you have to build and maintain it yourself. Re-creating the repository carries the risk and effort of moving the release images and also requires changing pipeline references. Tag immutability only prevents overwriting; it does not delete images.

exam-dva-c02-2.prompt: A company deploys a web application by using an AWS CodeDeploy in-place deployment to an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group (12 instances) behind an Application Load Balancer. Deployments happen several times a day, including during business hours, and no staff are on call overnight. After the new version is installed, the deployment must check that the /health endpoint returns 200. If the check fails, the deployment must roll back to the last successful version without human intervention. The health check must be at the application level, not a port response, and the company wants to keep the existing deployment group configuration. Currently, deployments proceed one instance at a time and take less than 15 minutes. Changing the entire deployment process to a new tool is difficult given the schedule. Which configuration meets these requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Put a health check script in the ValidateService hook and enable automatic rollback on failure for the deployment group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Put a health check script in the BeforeInstall hook of the AppSpec file and, if it fails, skip the install step so that the existing version is kept.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Connect only Amazon SNS notifications to the deployment group, without a CloudWatch alarm, and have an engineer manually redeploy the previous revision when the notification is received.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put a health check script in the ApplicationStop hook of the AppSpec file and, if there is no response, run the install script of the previous revision.

exam-dva-c02-2.explanation: ValidateService is a hook that runs after installation and service start are complete, so it is the right place to check the state of the new version. If the script fails, the deployment fails, and automatic rollback redeploys the last successful revision. BeforeInstall runs before the new version is installed, so there is nothing to check yet. Manually redeploying after an SNS notification requires human intervention, which conflicts with the requirement. ApplicationStop is the step that stops the existing version and is not meant for validating the new version.

exam-dva-c02-3.prompt: An AWS Lambda function at a fintech company reads a SecureString parameter from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store by using GetParameter (with WithDecryption set to true) to obtain a database connection string. The parameter is encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key in the same account, and other workloads also use this key. The key policy is set to allow delegation of permissions to IAM policies in the account. The function only reads the value, and the security team requires giving the execution role only the least privilege. The function code calls the parameter by a fixed name, and the parameter is in one location. The company has a single account, and the VPC endpoint configuration is already complete, so networking does not need to be considered. Which TWO least-privilege permissions should be granted to the function's execution role? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a statement to the execution role's policy that allows ssm:GetParameter on the ARN of the parameter.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a statement that allows kms:Encrypt on the customer managed key so that the function can re-encrypt the value it reads.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a statement to the execution role's policy that allows kms:Decrypt on the ARN of the customer managed key that was used for encryption.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a statement that allows secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on all secrets in the account so that the function can read values broadly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Add a statement that allows ssm:PutParameter on the entire parameter path so that the function can read and update the value.

exam-dva-c02-3.explanation: To read and decrypt a SecureString, both the ssm:GetParameter permission to read the parameter and the kms:Decrypt permission to decrypt the value are required. PutParameter is an unnecessary write permission for a function that only reads. kms:Encrypt is needed when storing a value, not when reading it. Secrets Manager permissions are for secrets in a different service, so they are unrelated to retrieving a Parameter Store parameter, and their scope is also too broad.

exam-dva-c02-4.prompt: A logistics company's inventory service stores inventory items in an Amazon DynamoDB table. During peak season, inventory changes are frequent. When two AWS Lambda functions that read an item, change the quantity, and save it run concurrently on the same item, the last write overwrites the earlier change, quantities are lost, and customers complain. The team does not want to introduce a new lock table or lock service and does not want to change the table structure significantly. Because call frequency is high, retry logic is acceptable, but a design that significantly increases user response latency must be avoided. The table is in on-demand mode, and each item is smaller than 1 KB. Which method safely detects concurrent modifications with the FEWEST changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change reads to ConsistentRead, calculate the quantity after reading the latest quantity, and overwrite the same item with PutItem to reduce the gap between the read and the write.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have each function send an unconditional Put for the same item inside TransactWriteItems so that the two writes are processed serially.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a version attribute to the item, write by using an UpdateItem condition expression only when the version matches the version that was read, increment the version, and re-read and retry on failure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Collect the inventory change requests with DynamoDB Streams, have a single Lambda function apply them in order, and remove the original write path.

exam-dva-c02-4.explanation: The correct answer is optimistic locking by using a version attribute and a conditional UpdateItem. If another write has changed the version since the read, the condition fails, so a lost update is detected, and only the failing side needs to re-read and retry, so no separate lock infrastructure is required. A strongly consistent read only guarantees the latest value at the moment of the read and does not prevent another write from slipping in between the read and the write. Putting an unconditional Put in a transaction does not change the fact that the last write wins. Streams are a record of changes made after a write, so they cannot remove the write path, and this approach significantly changes the structure.

exam-dva-c02-5.prompt: A resize AWS Lambda function in an image processing service is configured with 512 MB of memory. It is invoked tens of thousands of times a day, so even small cost differences add up. The average run time is 8 seconds, and the function uses almost 100% of the CPU. Max Memory Used in the REPORT log is 180 MB. Users complain that processing delays are long, and the operations team wants to reduce the delay while minimizing any increase in monthly cost. The code is already optimized with no bottlenecks and will not be modified. The function runs outside a VPC, concurrency is sufficient, and the cold start time is negligible compared with the total of 8 seconds. Requests invoke the function asynchronously through Amazon S3 events. Which is the MOST cost-effective way to determine the memory setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because actual usage is 180 MB, lower the memory to 256 MB to reduce the GB-second price, and ignore any change in run time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure provisioned concurrency to create execution environments in advance so that the 8-second processing time becomes shorter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use AWS Lambda Power Tuning to measure run time and cost for each memory setting, and choose the setting with the lowest cost.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the function timeout so that processing is not cut off midway, assume this reduces processing time, and leave the memory as is.

exam-dva-c02-5.explanation: The correct answer is to use Lambda Power Tuning to measure run time and cost for each memory setting and choose from the results. Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory, so for a CPU-bound function, increasing memory can significantly reduce run time, and the cost can stay the same or even drop. Power Tuning is the tool that confirms this by measurement. Lowering memory also reduces CPU, making the function slower and conflicting with the latency requirement. Provisioned concurrency is meant to mitigate cold starts and has no effect on the processing time itself. Increasing the timeout has nothing to do with processing speed.

exam-dva-c02-6.prompt: The task definition of an Amazon ECS Fargate service specifies an AWS Secrets Manager secret in the secrets field so that it is injected as a container environment variable. After a new deployment, the task fails to start and a permission error occurs when retrieving the secret. The application code calls only Amazon S3, and that permission already exists in the task role. The secret value must be injected as an environment variable when the container starts, and the security team does not allow excessive permissions. The service is scheduled to launch next week, so the schedule is tight, and other services in the same cluster are already working normally. The secret is in the same account and the same Region and is not encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. Which is the MOST appropriate solution that uses least privilege?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the secret to the task role so that the container can read the secret when it starts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the task execution role to resolve all permission errors, including secret retrieval, at once.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the Principal in the secret's resource-based policy to a wildcard so that all principals in the account can retrieve the value.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Allow secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the secret on the task execution role, and also add kms:Decrypt if necessary.

exam-dva-c02-6.explanation: Values injected through the secrets field are retrieved by the ECS agent by using the task execution role before the container starts, so granting GetSecretValue (and kms:Decrypt if needed) for the secret to the execution role is enough. The task role is the role used by the application code inside the container, so it is not used for injection at the startup stage. An administrator policy breaks the principle of least privilege, and a wildcard Principal exposes the secret far too broadly.

exam-dva-c02-7.prompt: At a company, the network team manages a VPC stack with AWS CloudFormation, and several application teams must each reference the subnet IDs of that VPC from their own stacks. All stacks are in the same account and Region and have different lifecycles. The subnet IDs rarely change after deployment, but each team has a different deployment schedule, so a change to one stack must not have to wait for the deployment of another stack. Stack changes happen a few times a month and are deployed automatically in a CI pipeline, and the teams do not want to operate any additional services. The subnet IDs in the VPC stack will be shared between stacks going forward. Which method avoids hardcoding the subnet IDs in templates and has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restructure all application stacks as nested stacks with the VPC stack as the parent, and have the parent pass the subnet IDs as parameters.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Document a procedure in which the application teams look up the subnet IDs in the console on every deployment and enter them directly as template parameters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Export the subnet IDs from the Outputs of the VPC stack and import them in the application stacks by using Fn::ImportValue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put a custom resource in each application stack so that a Lambda function finds the IDs with EC2 DescribeSubnets at deployment time and returns them.

exam-dva-c02-7.explanation: Export and Fn::ImportValue let stacks in the same Region and account reference output values directly, so no hardcoding or manual entry is needed. Nested stacks are a structure in which the parent and children share a single lifecycle, so they do not fit a situation where teams and lifecycles differ. Manual entry is error-prone and has a high operational burden. A custom resource requires creating and maintaining Lambda code, which is excessive for a simple reference.

exam-dva-c02-8.prompt: An AWS CloudFormation stack includes an Amazon EBS volume (AWS::EC2::Volume) that holds data. This volume is managed only by this stack and is not referenced by other stacks, and stack deletion permissions are open to many operators. Recently, a stack in a development environment was deleted by operator mistake, so the data at the time of deletion must be recoverable. However, to reduce costs, the company does not want to keep the volume itself indefinitely, and normal stack deletion must not be blocked. The volume totals 500 GiB, the recovery requirement is for the data as of just before the stack deletion, and a recovery time of up to several hours is acceptable. Snapshot storage costs are much lower than the cost of keeping the volume. Which method requires the FEWEST changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Specify DeletionPolicy Snapshot on the volume so that a snapshot is created before the stack is deleted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify DeletionPolicy Retain on the volume resource so that the volume remains as is even if the stack is deleted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enable termination protection on the stack so that deletion requests fail until an administrator disables it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leave the deletion policy at its default and separately configure an Amazon EventBridge schedule rule so that a Lambda function creates volume snapshots every week.

exam-dva-c02-8.explanation: If DeletionPolicy is set to Snapshot, CloudFormation creates a snapshot of the volume when the stack is deleted and then deletes the volume, so the data at the time of deletion is preserved and the volume cost goes away. Retain leaves the volume in place, so costs continue and the volume moves outside the stack's management. Termination protection blocks deletion itself, which conflicts with the conditions. Periodic snapshots preserve data only up to the time of the last run, not the time of deletion, and they also require separate operation.

exam-dva-c02-9.prompt: Several internal payment services running on Amazon ECS call an Amazon API Gateway REST API in the same account. The callers are AWS workloads, not end users, and the team does not want to operate a new token issuing server or user directory. The call volume is not high, but the APIs that each service can call must differ, and the team does not want to increase the work of distributing and rotating credentials to each service. All calls are made from ECS tasks in the same VPC, and each service already has its own task role. The API has a Regional endpoint, and the services are written with the AWS SDK. Which authorization method controls permissions per caller and has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create dedicated service users in an Amazon Cognito user pool, attach a Cognito authorizer, and have the services call by using the tokens they receive when they sign in.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a Lambda token authorizer and implement it yourself so that it validates a secret string shared by the services and sent in a header.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set the method to AWS_IAM authorization, allow execute-api:Invoke on the task roles, and use SigV4 signing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Issue API keys through a usage plan, distribute them to each service, and turn on only the API key required setting on the method to identify callers.

exam-dva-c02-9.explanation: IAM authorization verifies SigV4 signatures with the caller's IAM credentials, so no separate authentication server is needed, and the task role policies can divide the call permissions per service. The Cognito user pool approach requires operating a user directory for services and token refresh. A Lambda authorizer that validates a shared secret means you take on the code and secret rotation yourself. API keys are for usage control and are not designed to be used as an authorization or strong authentication mechanism.

exam-dva-c02-10.prompt: In an order processing system, an AWS Lambda function that processes messages from an Amazon SQS queue opens connections to an Amazon RDS database. When events surge and the queue builds up, the concurrent executions of this function rise into the hundreds, exceed the database's maximum of 100 connections, and cause connection errors. Scaling up the database will be reviewed next quarter, and until then the team wants to control this on the function side first. The change must not affect other functions in the same account, and the team wants to cap the concurrent executions of this function at no additional charge. Queue messages may be delayed but must not be lost, and the queue's visibility timeout and retry configuration are already set appropriately. This function is also invoked directly through an API in addition to SQS, so a cap on the concurrent executions of the entire function is needed regardless of the invocation path. The team wants to solve this through configuration only, without code changes. Which is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set provisioned concurrency of 100 on this function to reserve 100 pre-initialized execution environments so that no more than that are created.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set reserved concurrency of 100 or less on this function to cap the concurrent executions of that function and separate it from the concurrency pool of other functions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower the account-wide concurrent execution quota to 100 so that the concurrent executions of all functions stay within the database connection limit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shorten the function timeout to reduce connection hold time, hoping the connection count does not exceed the limit even as concurrent executions increase.

exam-dva-c02-10.explanation: The correct answer is to set reserved concurrency on this function. Reserved concurrency limits the maximum concurrent executions of the function to prevent downstream resources such as a database from being overloaded, separates the pool from other functions, and has no additional charge. Provisioned concurrency sets the number of pre-initialized environments, is meant to mitigate cold starts, incurs charges, and does not prevent scaling beyond that number. The account quota is a service quota, is not something to lower for this purpose, and affects all functions. Shortening the timeout does not guarantee a cap on concurrent executions. For reference, the maximum concurrency setting on the SQS event source mapping also limits concurrent invocations per queue at no additional charge, but it applies only to invocations coming from that event source and cannot block direct invocations. This question requires a function-wide cap regardless of the invocation path, so reserved concurrency is correct. The two settings are independent, so when they are used together, the mapping's maximum concurrency should be set to no more than the reserved concurrency so that messages are not throttled.

exam-dva-c02-11.prompt: A fintech app must encrypt the Korean resident registration number attribute of an Amazon DynamoDB item before storing it, so that plaintext is not exposed to the DynamoDB service or to principals that have table read permissions. Other attributes are used as query conditions, so they must remain plaintext, and the company wants to manage the key in AWS KMS. Regulations require that decryption of this attribute be auditable through AWS CloudTrail. The application is written in Java, and the development team has three people who do not want to implement the encryption logic themselves. Key usage records must be kept by using the default AWS auditing mechanism, without building a separate service. The table has tens of millions of items, and reads are mostly primary key lookups. Which method meets the requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use the AWS Database Encryption SDK to specify that only that attribute is encrypted on the client side, and use a KMS keyring.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change encryption at rest for the table to a customer managed KMS key so that all attributes are encrypted with that key inside DynamoDB.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enforce TLS on connections to DynamoDB and use a VPC gateway endpoint policy so that only allowed roles can access the table.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Block access to the resident registration number attribute by using the IAM condition key dynamodb:Attributes, and restrict all callers to reading only hash values.

exam-dva-c02-11.explanation: The Database Encryption SDK provides attribute-level client-side encryption, so only the specified attribute is stored as ciphertext and the others can stay plaintext, and plaintext is not visible to the service or to principals with read permissions. Server-side encryption returns the decrypted value to callers that have permissions, so it does not meet the requirement. TLS and endpoint policies only control the transport and access path and do not hide the stored value itself. Restricting attribute access so that only hashes are read differs from the requirement to store the original value in a protected form.

exam-dva-c02-12.prompt: An online store's order history screen has become slow, and the team is reviewing the Amazon DynamoDB table design. Each customer can accumulate up to several thousand orders, and the screen shows each customer's orders from most recent first. Customers must also be able to look up orders for a specific period (for example, from January 1 to March 31). Queries should use only Query, not Scan, and the team wants to avoid increased read costs from reading many items and discarding them with filters. Writes must not concentrate on a particular date. There are hundreds of thousands of customers, and a single customer does not place many orders per day. Each screen shows the 20 most recent orders. Which design is MOST appropriate when the problem is solved by primary key design alone, without adding secondary indexes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use the order date as the partition key and the customer ID as the sort key, and for per-customer lookups, Query all partitions for the relevant dates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use only the order ID as the partition key, store the customer ID and date as regular attributes, and filter with a FilterExpression.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use the customer ID as the partition key and a value combining the date and the order ID as the sort key, and query by using a BETWEEN key condition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use only the customer ID as the partition key, store the date as a regular attribute, and sort the results of a per-customer Query in the application.

exam-dva-c02-12.explanation: The correct answer is a design with the customer ID as the partition key and a value combining the date and the order ID as the sort key. A customer's orders sit in a single item collection sorted by date, so a sort key condition such as BETWEEN reads only the period needed, and ScanIndexForward=false returns the most recent orders first. Using the order date as the partition key concentrates writes on particular dates and scatters per-customer lookups across multiple partitions. A key of the order ID alone requires a Scan for per-customer lookups. Storing the date only as an attribute means reading all of a customer's orders and then filtering or sorting, which increases read cost.

exam-dva-c02-13.prompt: A mobile app uploads files directly to Amazon S3 without going through a server. An AWS Lambda function (using its execution role) creates a presigned PUT URL for uploads with a validity period of 7 days and passes it to the app. Uploads succeed right after the URL is issued, but after a few hours they fail with an ExpiredToken error, according to inquiries. Bucket permissions and CORS are correct, and users often take photos and upload them later. The app is native, and the team wants to make server-side changes in only one place, the Lambda function. The target object key is a path separated by user ID, and for security reasons the URL should be valid only as long as necessary. What is the cause, and what is the MOST appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The signature expiration condition in the S3 bucket policy must be relaxed, so add a condition that allows s3:signatureAge and leave the URL validity period as is.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The URL also expires when the role's temporary credentials expire, so shorten the URL validity period to fit within the credential lifetime and issue a new URL just before the upload.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The IAM role lacks the s3:PutObject permission, so add write permissions on the entire target bucket to the execution role's policy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The PUT method is missing from the bucket CORS configuration, so add PUT to AllowedMethods to allow browser uploads.

exam-dva-c02-13.explanation: The correct answer is to understand the relationship between the temporary credential lifetime and the URL validity period, and to issue a new URL just before the upload. According to the official documentation, a presigned URL created with temporary credentials becomes invalid at whichever comes first: the specified validity period or the time the credentials expire. If the URL is signed with role credentials, the URL also expires when the role session ends, even if 7 days is specified (7 days is the maximum possible with IAM user credentials and SigV4). Because the upload succeeded right after issuance, insufficient permissions are not the cause. A missing CORS setting would block the request from the start in a browser and does not explain signature expiry. The signatureAge condition is meant to reject old signatures, so it is not something that relaxes anything, and it does not fix credential expiry.

exam-dva-c02-14.prompt: An IAM role for a development team has an identity-based policy that allows s3:*, and the same role has a permissions boundary set with a policy that allows only s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket. The bucket has no bucket policy, and the organization's SCPs do not block Amazon S3. The security team has formally approved uploads for this role, but developers' PutObject calls are blocked with AccessDenied. The role is shared by several developers, and its other permissions must be kept as they are now. The boundary policy is not attached to any other role and is dedicated to this role, and an IAM administrator can apply changes immediately. Which method resolves the problem with the SMALLEST change scope?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Explicitly add another statement that allows s3:PutObject to the role's identity-based policy to make the upload permission clear, and update the policy version.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a statement that allows s3:PutObject to the permissions boundary policy so that uploads are included in the intersection of the boundary and the identity policy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Include an allow for s3:PutObject in the session policy passed when assuming the role to temporarily expand permissions beyond the boundary.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the role in addition to allow all actions, including those for Amazon S3.

exam-dva-c02-14.explanation: A permissions boundary is the maximum permissions that an identity-based policy can grant, so the effective permissions are the intersection of the boundary and the identity policy. Adding PutObject to the boundary creates an intersection with the identity policy that already allows s3:*, and uploads open up. Writing the same allow again in the identity policy does not change the situation, because it is already allowed and is blocked by the boundary. A session policy can only reduce permissions and cannot widen them beyond the boundary. Attaching an administrator policy does not solve it either, because the boundary still acts as the upper limit.

exam-dva-c02-15.prompt: An online shopping company is building an order workflow with AWS Step Functions that runs payment approval, inventory deduction, and shipping request in order across different services. For high-value orders, the workflow waits up to 3 days for approval from a person by using a callback token, and non-idempotent tasks such as payment must run exactly once. The execution history must be kept as audit material so that responsibility can be traced when failures occur, and the company handles thousands of orders per day. The team does not want to operate a workflow engine itself. The approvers for high-value orders are integrated by pressing a button in an internal approval tool, which returns the token. The entire processing of a single order takes from a few minutes to up to 3 days. Which workflow type is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use an Express asynchronous workflow. It is advantageous for high-volume processing, and execution status is checked in Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use a Standard workflow. It supports executions of up to 1 year, an exactly-once execution model, and waiting for a callback token.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Connect an Express synchronous workflow to Amazon API Gateway to receive the result in the call response, and also wait for the approval step in the same execution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Implement a chain in which a Lambda function directly invokes the next Lambda function, and handle the approval wait by repeated polling inside the function.

exam-dva-c02-15.explanation: The correct answer is a Standard workflow. Standard workflows run for up to 1 year and use an exactly-once execution model, which suits non-idempotent tasks such as payment, and they support the callback (.waitForTaskToken) pattern and execution history lookup. Express workflows run for up to 5 minutes, asynchronous ones use at-least-once execution, and they do not support the callback pattern, so they violate both the 3-day approval wait and the run-only-once requirement. A Lambda chain with polling cannot wait 3 days inside a function that has a maximum run time of 15 minutes, and you would have to implement state management and error handling yourself, which is a heavy operational burden.

exam-dva-c02-16.prompt: The buildspec of an AWS CodeBuild project builds an image with docker build and then pushes it to Amazon ECR. The project uses a Linux container environment, the source is in AWS CodeCommit, and the ECR repository has already been created in the same account and Region. The build currently fails with an error that it cannot connect to the Docker daemon, and it is expected that even after this error is fixed, a permission error will occur in the later push step. The team wants to fix only the CodeBuild settings without moving the build environment to a new service. Under security policy, the build environment image is the AWS managed Ubuntu standard image as is, and the ECR login is handled in the pre_build phase of the buildspec. Which TWO actions are needed to resolve the problem? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the source provider to Amazon S3 so that the buildspec can read the Docker context from the local file system.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add the ecs:UpdateService permission to the CodeBuild service role so that the pushed image can be applied to the service immediately.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the build environment image to a Windows Server image to use an environment in which the Docker daemon runs by default.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable privileged mode in the project environment so that the Docker daemon can run inside the build container.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Allow the CodeBuild service role ECR push permissions such as ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, image layer upload, and PutImage.

exam-dva-c02-16.explanation: To build a Docker image inside CodeBuild, privileged mode must be turned on in the environment, and to push to ECR, the service role must have the authorization token, layer upload, and PutImage permissions. Switching to a Windows image is not a solution to the daemon connection problem. ecs:UpdateService is a permission needed in the deployment stage and is unrelated to pushing images. The source provider has nothing to do with Docker daemon access or ECR permissions.

exam-dva-c02-17.prompt: A startup's mobile backend uses an Amazon API Gateway REST API with an AWS Lambda proxy integration. After deploying a new endpoint, clients receive a 502 Bad Gateway response with Malformed Lambda proxy response. The Lambda logs show a normal completion with no errors, and the function returns a dictionary in the form {"message":"ok","items":[1,2,3]} as is. Other endpoints of the same API work normally, and there are no timeout-related logs. The frontend team expects a JSON body and must also receive CORS values in the response headers. The backend is written in Python. Which fix is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the function timeout beyond the API Gateway integration timeout so that the response is not cut off by delays.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the handler return format so that the response is returned in a structure of statusCode, headers, and a string body.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add permission for the API Gateway service principal to invoke the function to the Lambda function's resource-based policy so that the invocation is not denied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on a cache cluster on the stage so that API Gateway returns a cached response even if the function's response format is wrong.

exam-dva-c02-17.explanation: The correct answer is to change the handler to return a statusCode, headers, and body (string) format. In a Lambda proxy integration, API Gateway requires the function to respond in a defined JSON format, and it returns 502 Bad Gateway for any other format. The function being recorded as a normal completion is consistent with this explanation. A timeout is a setting for solving delay problems and is unrelated to a format error. If invocation permission were missing, the function itself would not be invoked and no normal completion would appear in the logs. A cache is meaningful only when there is a response with the correct format and cannot hide a format error.

exam-dva-c02-18.prompt: A team that runs the post-payment stages serverlessly has an order processing AWS Lambda function that reads messages from an Amazon SQS standard queue with a batch size of 10. Daily volume is high, so reducing the batch size would significantly increase invocation costs. Currently, if even one message in a batch fails to process, the function throws an exception, and the remaining 9 messages also reappear in the queue and are processed twice, and some messages have already been processed twice. The function code can be modified. Processing takes about 1 second per message, and the function timeout is 30 seconds. Most failures are caused by transient external API errors, and a retry succeeds. Which is the MOST appropriate method to retry only the failed messages while keeping a batch size of 10 and making minimal changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lower the batch size to 1 so that the function is invoked separately for each message, and also increase the function concurrency limit to handle the increased number of invocations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on ReportBatchItemFailures on the event source mapping, and have the handler return only the messageId values of the failed messages as batchItemFailures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower the visibility timeout of the source queue to 0 seconds so that only the failed messages become visible again immediately and the remaining messages are deleted as is.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Specify an SQS standard queue as the DLQ in the Lambda function configuration so that the entire batch in which a failure occurred is stored in a separate queue and an operator reprocesses it later.

exam-dva-c02-18.explanation: The correct answer is to set ReportBatchItemFailures on the event source mapping and return only the failed messageId values as batchItemFailures. This deletes the successful messages from the queue and makes only the failed messages visible again, so the batch size of 10 is kept while duplicate processing is prevented. Reducing the batch size to 1 breaks the condition of the question (keep a batch size of 10) and only increases the number of invocations and the cost. Setting the visibility timeout to 0 seconds does not change the behavior of returning the entire batch that ended in an exception and makes the same messages be received repeatedly right away. A function-level DLQ is for asynchronous invocations; for an SQS event source, the DLQ must be placed on the queue side, and in either case the whole batch is stored, so it does not prevent reprocessing of successful messages.

exam-dva-c02-19.prompt: A mobile game service queries a global secondary index (GSI) keyed on playerId right after saving a score to the Amazon DynamoDB base table, but the score just written is sometimes missing from the results. When the team turns on ConsistentRead to fix this, a ValidationException occurs. The results screen shown right after score submission must always show the latest score, and the overall ranking list screen can be a few seconds late. The table is in on-demand mode, and the team does not want to migrate data to a new table. The GSI has playerId as the partition key and is sorted by score, and the screen right after submission already knows the primary key of the item that was just saved. Which solution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For the screen right after submission, call GetItem on the base table by using the primary key and ConsistentRead, and use the GSI only for the list that tolerates delay.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the read capacity units of the global secondary index so that the index catches up with changes to the base table more quickly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put a DAX cluster in front of the global secondary index to get index query results back from the cache consistently.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the projection of the global secondary index to ALL so that all attributes are in the index and the base table does not need to be read separately.

exam-dva-c02-19.explanation: The correct answer is to query the base table by primary key with a strongly consistent read on the screen right after submission, and to use the GSI only for lists that tolerate delay. Reads from GSIs and streams support only eventual consistency and do not support strongly consistent reads, which causes the ValidationException; only the base table and LSIs support strongly consistent reads. Increasing read capacity does not change the consistency model. DAX is a cache layer and cannot make the guarantee of the latest value any stronger. Changing the projection to ALL only reduces table lookups; the index data is still eventually consistent.

exam-dva-c02-20.prompt: A cost alarm goes off at 2 a.m. because the number of AWS Lambda invocations suddenly spikes. The cause is a recursive structure in which the function sends its processing results to an Amazon SQS queue, and that queue invokes the same function as an event source. Reviewing and deploying the fix is expected to take several hours, and costs must be stopped in the meantime. The function configuration and the messages in the queue must be preserved, and other functions in the same account must keep working normally. The function is connected through an SQS event source mapping, the code path that caused the recursion has already been identified, and only preparing the fix remains. The messages that have accumulated must be processed normally after the fix. Which is the MOST appropriate way to immediately stop only further executions of this function before the fix is deployed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set the function's reserved concurrency to 0 so that all new invocations are throttled and not executed, and remove the limit after the fix.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delete the function so that no invocations occur, and when deploying the fix, create a new function with the same name and reconnect it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the function timeout to 1 second so that each invocation ends quickly, and wait for the recursion to die down naturally.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower the account-level Lambda concurrent execution quota on the Service Quotas screen to limit the execution of all functions.

exam-dva-c02-20.explanation: The correct answer is to set reserved concurrency to 0. With reserved concurrency set to 0, all invocations of that function are throttled and not executed, so the cost increase can be stopped immediately before the code is fixed, the function configuration remains intact, and you only need to remove the setting after the fix. Deleting the function means you have to re-create the configuration and connection settings. Reducing the timeout does not stop the invocations themselves, so the recursion continues. Lowering the account quota stops other functions too, and service quotas are not meant to be lowered arbitrarily.

exam-dva-c02-21.prompt: A compliance requirement states that all access to a specific Amazon S3 bucket must be encrypted in transit and that HTTP requests must be denied. The bucket is shared by several teams, dozens of applications access it by using SDKs, and code deployment schedules differ by team, so the code of each application cannot be modified. SSE-S3 default encryption is already applied to the bucket. The audit is next month, and the security team wants to apply the control once, centrally, without coordinating with each team. Both uploading and downloading objects are done through existing IAM roles, and whether VPC endpoints are used differs by team. Which method meets this requirement with the FEWEST changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enable SSE-S3 default encryption on the bucket so that all objects are encrypted at rest and transport is also protected.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a statement to the bucket policy that denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put a condition that allows only HTTPS requests into each team's application IAM policy, ask the teams to deploy the policies, and check whether they have been applied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on bucket versioning so that objects written over unencrypted transport can be rolled back to a previous version.

exam-dva-c02-21.explanation: If the bucket policy explicitly denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false, no caller can access the bucket over HTTP, and no client code change is needed. SSE-S3 encrypts data at rest and does not enforce the transport channel. Putting a condition in each team's IAM policy requires changes and coordination for every team and cannot block principals that are missed. Versioning is only a recovery feature and does not prevent plaintext transport.

exam-dva-c02-22.prompt: The operations team has been receiving the same failure alarm repeatedly for several hours. In an AWS Lambda function that uses an Amazon SQS standard queue as its event source, a particular message always causes an exception and keeps being received again. An SQS queue was specified as the DLQ in the function settings, but no messages accumulate in that queue. The problem message must be kept for later root cause analysis, and processing of normal messages must continue. About 50,000 messages a day arrive in the source queue, the problem messages are a small number of malformed messages, and the alarm is set in Amazon CloudWatch on the function's error count. Which is the MOST appropriate action to isolate the problem message after a set number of attempts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the on-failure destination of the event source mapping to an SQS queue and set the function's maximum retry attempts to 2 to configure the same isolation effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduce the message retention period of the source queue to 1 minute so that messages that could not be processed disappear from the queue on their own.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the function-level DLQ target to an Amazon SNS standard topic so that failure events are delivered at the same time to a subscribed email address and queue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Connect a DLQ to the source queue with a redrive policy that specifies maxReceiveCount, so that a message received a set number of times is moved to the DLQ.

exam-dva-c02-22.explanation: The correct answer is to connect a DLQ to the source queue with a redrive policy that has maxReceiveCount. When SQS is used as the event source, the DLQ must be configured on the queue itself, not on the Lambda function; a function-level DLQ applies only to asynchronous invocations, which is why the queue is empty now. The on-failure destination and maximum retry attempts are asynchronous invocation settings and are not an isolation mechanism for an SQS event source mapping. Reducing the retention period makes normal messages disappear along with the problem message, leaving no data to analyze. Changing the function-level DLQ to SNS does not change the situation, because it applies only to asynchronous invocations.

exam-dva-c02-23.prompt: A fintech company's point transfer API processes, in a single Amazon DynamoDB table, a balance deduction for the sender (only when the balance is at least the amount), a balance increase for the recipient, and the addition of a history item. Because of financial regulations, all three operations must either all succeed or all fail, and intermediate states must not be visible externally. Even if the client resends the same request because of a network timeout, a double transfer must not occur. All items are in one table in the same Region, and the team does not want to add a separate coordination service. Traffic is at the level of hundreds of requests per second, and a single transfer touches three items. The app uses the AWS SDK directly, and the client sends a unique request ID with every request. Which implementation is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Send two Updates and one Put in a single BatchWriteItem call, and resend if UnprocessedItems appears in the response.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Put two conditional Updates and one Put in a single TransactWriteItems call, and resend with the same ClientRequestToken.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Call the three operations in order with UpdateItem and PutItem, and if one fails midway, perform compensating calls that undo the operations that already succeeded.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Collect write results with DynamoDB Streams, and have a Lambda function correct the differences periodically if the balance totals do not match.

exam-dva-c02-23.explanation: The correct answer is to put two conditional Updates and one Put in a single TransactWriteItems call and secure idempotency with ClientRequestToken. A transaction either fully succeeds or fully fails and can also use condition expressions, and if it is resent with the same token, it returns success without any change within the token validity time (10 minutes). BatchWriteItem as a whole is not atomic and cannot specify condition expressions. The compensating call approach exposes intermediate states externally, and the compensation itself can fail. Correcting after the fact with Streams means there are moments when the balance is wrong, so it does not meet the atomicity requirement.

exam-dva-c02-24.prompt: A payment service runs as an Amazon ECS service on Fargate (desired task count of 4) and is connected to Application Load Balancer health checks. Deployments are done several times a day as rolling updates, and no one is on standby at night. The number of healthy tasks must not drop during a deployment, and if new tasks repeatedly fail to start, the service must return to the last healthy deployment without human intervention. A large change such as switching the deployment method to AWS CodeDeploy is difficult this quarter. The ECS service already uses the rolling update deployment controller, and task definition updates are made automatically in the CI pipeline. The cluster has sufficient Fargate capacity quota. Which configuration meets the requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set minimumHealthyPercent to 50 and maximumPercent to 100, and enable the circuit breaker with the rollback option.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set minimumHealthyPercent to 100 and maximumPercent to 200, and enable the deployment circuit breaker with the rollback option.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set both minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent to 100, and if it fails, have an engineer manually roll back to the previous task definition in the console.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch the service to the CodeDeploy blue/green deployment controller and configure rollback with two target groups and a separate AppSpec file.
