The allowed domains include a payment processor API and a package repository, and most of them are behind a CDN, so their IP addresses change often. Blocked requests must be logged so that the security team can review them once a month. Which method meets these requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall to block DNS queries for domains other than the approved ones so that instances cannot connect to other domains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Register the approved domain names in the security group outbound rules and deny other destinations to control HTTPS traffic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put the IP ranges of the approved domains in an allow list in the network ACL and update the rules with AWS Lambda whenever the IP addresses change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a domain allow list rule group in AWS Network Firewall, leave all other traffic blocked by default, and place it in the outbound path.

exam-saa-c03-42.explanation: The correct answer is the domain allow list in Network Firewall. It identifies the domain from information such as the SNI of the HTTPS connection and blocks traffic not on the list by default, so rules do not need to be changed when IP addresses change, and direct connections by IP address are also blocked. DNS Firewall filters only DNS queries, so connecting directly by IP address bypasses it. Security groups cannot specify domain names as rule targets. Network ACLs are stateless filters based on IP ranges, so following domains whose IP addresses change often would require building automation yourself, and there is also a rule quota. The condition to block direct IP connections eliminates the option that looks only at the DNS stage, and the condition that IP addresses change eliminates IP-based rules.

exam-saa-c03-43.prompt: A new ticketing event service uses an Amazon DynamoDB table, and its traffic is unpredictable. Average utilization is normally below 5% of capacity, but within seconds after an event starts it spikes to dozens of times the average. The size of each event never exceeds twice the peak of the previous event, and throttling must not occur at those times. The table is currently provisioned for the peak, which is expensive. Traffic spikes happen once or twice a day, and the team cannot assign staff to capacity planning. The table is 20 GB, and both reads and writes increase during events. There is no hot partition problem in which requests concentrate on a single item. Which method is the MOST cost-effective without increasing the operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so that it is billed only per request and handles the surging traffic without extra configuration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep provisioned mode, purchase 3-year reserved capacity to lower the unit price for the peak capacity, and set a capacity utilization alarm in Amazon CloudWatch.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apply Application Auto Scaling to provisioned mode to adjust capacity automatically with a target utilization of 70%.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place a DAX cluster in front of the table and reduce the table's provisioned capacity to the average usage level so that it absorbs the write load.

exam-saa-c03-43.explanation: The correct answer is on-demand capacity mode. It is billed for requests made without capacity planning, so the idle cost of a table with low average utilization disappears, and it immediately accommodates up to twice the previous peak traffic, so surges of a similar size that repeat each time are handled without throttling (a surge exceeding double can be throttled within 30 minutes, so the precondition of this problem is important). Reserved capacity is effective for steady traffic, and with 5% utilization it would mean buying peak-sized capacity for a long term, which is very wasteful. Auto scaling takes time to react, so throttling can occur with traffic that spikes within seconds. DAX only caches reads and does not absorb write load, so reducing capacity would block writes. The two conditions of a spike that rises within seconds and no capacity-planning staff expose the weakness of approaches that set capacity in advance.

exam-saa-c03-44.prompt: A platform team wants to let 300 developers create AWS Lambda execution roles themselves in the development account. However, developers must not be able to escalate their privileges by creating roles with greater permissions than their own, and the team wants to avoid an approach in which the security team approves every request. Developers must deploy new functions several times a day without prior approval, and the security team has 2 staff members. The security team wants to define the maximum permission scope of roles once. Developers create roles only within their own account, and the roles need only things like Amazon S3 read access and Amazon DynamoDB access. The security team already has one managed policy that defines the allowable permission scope. Which method is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grant iam:CreateRole but add a condition that allows it only when the specified permissions boundary policy is attached together, to limit the maximum permissions of the role.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grant developers the IAMFullAccess managed policy, set an alarm on AWS CloudTrail events, and revoke excessive permissions after the fact when they are seen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Define an approval procedure in a document in which developers request role creation, and the security team receives the request as a ticket, reviews it, and creates the role on their behalf.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deny all of iam:* with an SCP in the development account, and create the necessary roles in a separate management account and share them across accounts.

exam-saa-c03-44.explanation: The correct answer is a delegation approach that enforces a permissions boundary as a condition. If a condition on iam:PermissionsBoundary is attached to the iam:CreateRole allow, every role the developers create has only permissions within the boundary, so privilege escalation is prevented and no per-request approval from the security team is needed. IAMFullAccess lets developers create administrator permissions for themselves, and an alarm is only an after-the-fact response. A ticket approval process is the structure the requirements said to avoid. Denying all of iam:* with an SCP makes it impossible for developers to create roles at all, which contradicts the requirements. The requirement to define the maximum permissions once and let developers create freely within that scope is the classic use case for a permissions boundary.

exam-saa-c03-45.prompt: A financial company must retain 120 TB of transaction records for 7 years under regulations. The data is retrieved only during audits, which happen once a year and are announced one week in advance, so it is enough if the data can be obtained within one day of a request. During the retention period, no one, including the root user, must be able to delete or overwrite objects. Once stored, the data is never modified, and about 2 TB of new data is added each month. The stored data consists of compressed files averaging 200 MB per object, and uploads are done in a monthly batch. Retention costs account for a large part of the annual IT budget, so management has asked for savings. Which storage approach is the MOST cost-effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Upload to Amazon S3 with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode specifying a 7-year retention, and use a lifecycle rule to transition the objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep the data in S3 Standard-IA, have an administrator manually delete the objects after 7 years without using Object Lock, and review storage costs monthly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keep the data in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval so that it can be retrieved immediately in milliseconds during audits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Store the data on Amazon EBS Cold HDD (sc1) volumes attached to EC2 instances and keep snapshots for 7 years.

exam-saa-c03-45.explanation: The correct answer is the combination of Object Lock in compliance mode and a transition to Glacier Deep Archive. Compliance mode prevents anyone, including the root user, from deleting or overwriting objects during the retention period, and since retrieval once a year with restoration within a day is sufficient (standard retrieval takes within 12 hours), the cheapest archive class is the right fit. Standard-IA has a higher unit price per GB and, without Object Lock, cannot prevent deletion during retention. Glacier Instant Retrieval is for archives that need immediate access, so it is more expensive than required and has no deletion protection. EBS sc1 requires keeping volumes and EC2 instances running, and snapshots can also be deleted, so costs and management burden are much higher. The regulatory condition that deletion is impossible even for root and the retrieval condition that restoration within a day is acceptable decide the lock mode and storage class respectively.

exam-saa-c03-46.prompt: A data analytics team queries CSV logs that accumulate in Amazon S3 at 300 GB per day by using Amazon Athena. Most queries use only a specific date range and a few columns, but a BI tool runs the same queries hundreds of times a day, and each time it scans all of the data, so it is slow and the scan-based charges are also large. The BI tool's SQL cannot be modified, and data transformation can be run as a once-a-day batch. The team does not want to add any new always-on infrastructure. Only 90 days of logs are queried, and there are 60 columns, but queries usually use only 5. The average scan per query is tens of GB, and BI dashboard responses take several minutes. Which method improves performance and cost the MOST effectively while keeping the query shape?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compress the CSV files with gzip and change only the compression format in the Athena table definition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Load the data into an Amazon Redshift cluster and run subsequent queries in Redshift.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on Transfer Acceleration for the S3 bucket to speed up Athena data reads.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Convert the data to Parquet with date partitions by using an AWS Glue job and update the table.

exam-saa-c03-46.explanation: Athena charges in proportion to the amount of data scanned, so columnar Parquet reads only the needed columns, and date partitions make it read only the matching paths, greatly reducing scan volume and time while the SQL can be used unchanged. gzip compression reduces the scan volume to some extent, but it does not allow column-level reads or partition pruning. Loading into Redshift adds new infrastructure and a loading pipeline and does not fit the requirement of keeping the query shape. Transfer Acceleration is a feature for client upload and download paths and has nothing to do with Athena scans. The conditions that the SQL cannot be changed and that always-on infrastructure must not be added point to changing only the storage format and partitions.

exam-saa-c03-47.prompt: An e-commerce company serves static assets through Amazon CloudFront, and the objects in the origin S3 bucket are encrypted with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key, and the bucket is not public. Users must not be able to access the S3 URL directly and must receive content only through CloudFront. User requests come from all over the world, and static files are downloaded millions of times a day. The key policy can be modified by the security team. There is one CloudFront distribution, which previously used an OAI, but object reads started to fail when SSE-KMS was introduced. The company wants to rework the origin access method. Which configuration meets these requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an OAI and allow only the OAI in the bucket policy; CloudFront will then decrypt and deliver SSE-KMS objects, so no key policy change is needed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Open the bucket to the public, have CloudFront add a secret Referer header, and use that header value as a condition in the bucket policy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an Amazon S3 presigned URL for each object, set a short expiration behind CloudFront, and restrict direct access.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Associate an OAC with the distribution, allow only the cloudfront.amazonaws.com principal for that distribution in the bucket policy, and also allow decryption in the key policy.

exam-saa-c03-47.explanation: The correct answer is the OAC configuration plus an allow in the key policy. OAC supports SSE-KMS objects, and allowing only a specific distribution in the bucket policy blocks direct access to the S3 URL. However, the KMS key policy must also allow the CloudFront service principal to decrypt. OAI does not support objects encrypted with SSE-KMS. The Referer header approach opens the bucket to the public and is bypassed if the header is exposed, so it is not secure. Presigned URLs must be issued and managed for as many objects as there are and are not a means of blocking direct access. CloudFront must read SSE-KMS objects, so an allow in the key policy is needed in addition to the bucket policy.

exam-saa-c03-48.prompt: 300 web servers of an advertising platform generate thousands of JSON logs per second, and the logs are later queried with Amazon Athena. The company wants to convert them to Parquet format at roughly 1-minute intervals and store them in Amazon S3 by date. The small data team does not want to operate consumer application code or shard management itself, and the cost of keeping a cluster running at all times is also a burden. The schema of the logs is already defined in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Each log record averages 1 KB, and new fields are occasionally added. Records that fail conversion must be collected under a separate S3 prefix and checked later. Which method has the LEAST operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ingest into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and have a KCL consumer application on EC2 write Parquet files to Amazon S3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run an always-on Spark Structured Streaming job on an Amazon EMR cluster and store the output in Amazon S3.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on format conversion in an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream and specify a date prefix for the S3 destination.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Invoke an AWS Lambda function for each log record and store each one directly in Amazon S3 as an individual Parquet object.

exam-saa-c03-48.explanation: Amazon Data Firehose is a serverless delivery service that handles buffering, JSON-to-Parquet conversion (using the schema of an AWS Glue table), and storing with an S3 date prefix through configuration alone, so there is no need to operate shards or consumer code. Data Streams with a KCL application requires shard management and operating EC2 consumers. An always-on EMR streaming job has large operational and cost burdens. Saving per record with Lambda causes an explosion of small files that degrades later analysis performance, and retries for failures and partitioning would also have to be implemented yourself. The condition of not operating shards, consumer code, or clusters points to a serverless delivery service.

exam-saa-c03-49.prompt: A SaaS company receives events on an Amazon EventBridge custom event bus, and an AWS Lambda function that is a rule target processes them. An archive has been configured on this bus for the past month. Because of a bug in the deployed processing logic, about 6 million events were processed incorrectly over the last 3 days, and after the fix the same events must be processed again. The processing logic is idempotent, so the result is overwritten even if it receives the same event again, and the event publishers are owned by another team and cannot be modified. The archive retention period is indefinite, and all 6 million incorrectly processed events are included in the archive. Reprocessing must finish within one day, and no separate development staff has been assigned. Which method solves the problem with the LEAST effort?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extract the events from Amazon CloudWatch Logs and call the publisher's API again with a script.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Specify that 3-day time range in the archive, replay it to the bus, and let the targets process the events again.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add an Amazon SQS dead-letter queue to the rule target and run reprocessing on the messages from the last 3 days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the asynchronous invocation retry count of the Lambda function so that past events are invoked again.

exam-saa-c03-49.explanation: The original events are stored in the EventBridge archive, so replaying a specified time range lets the fixed target process the same events again without touching the publishers. Extracting events from logs and calling the publisher's API again is impossible without modifying the publishers and requires a lot of manual work. A dead-letter queue accumulates only events that failed delivery, so events that were delivered successfully but processed incorrectly are not in it. Asynchronous invocation retries only try failed invocations a few more times and do not recreate past events that already completed successfully. The fact that the processing logic is idempotent means there are no side effects even if the same events are delivered again.

exam-saa-c03-50.prompt: A security team wants to turn on Amazon GuardDuty in all 60 existing accounts in AWS Organizations and in all accounts created in the future, and wants to view the findings in one existing security operations account. The organization keeps creating new accounts, and people logging in to each account to do the work must be avoided. The security team has three members and is not allowed to deploy agents on EC2 instances. The security account is separate from the log archive account, and the findings are connected to a notification system through Amazon EventBridge. Some accounts use only the Asia Pacific (Seoul) Region because of a Region restriction SCP. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Send an invitation to each member account and configure the connection by having the person in charge of each account accept it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Designate the security account as the GuardDuty delegated administrator.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Install a GuardDuty agent on the EC2 instances in each account and send the logs to the security account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Set auto-enable for new accounts in the organization and also enable the existing member accounts in bulk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Specify only the AWS CloudTrail logs of the management account as input and exclude other accounts from analysis.

exam-saa-c03-50.explanation: The correct answers are designating a delegated administrator and configuring organization auto-enable. When the security account is the delegated administrator, the findings of all member accounts can be viewed in one place, and with auto-enable and bulk enablement, both existing and new accounts can be turned on without logging in. GuardDuty analyzes log sources directly without agents, so no installation on instances is needed. The invitation method requires acceptance in each account, which does not match the requirement to avoid manual work. Looking only at management account logs cannot detect threats in member accounts. Viewing in one place and enabling both existing and new accounts are separate requirements, so the actions are also split into two.

exam-saa-c03-51.prompt: A security team sees several cases per month in which developers accidentally make an Amazon S3 bucket public, and it wants the public setting to be removed automatically as soon as a violation occurs. Three of the accounts need public buckets for static websites, so exceptions must be made. AWS Config is already turned on in all accounts. Maintenance of custom code must be minimized, and each account has dozens of buckets, so checking them one by one by hand has reached its limit. If possible, the time from detection to remediation should be within a few minutes, and automatic remediation records must be kept for audit purposes. The team judged that completely removing the permission to change S3 settings from developers is not realistic. Which method is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Receive AWS CloudTrail events with Amazon EventBridge and deploy to each account a self-written AWS Lambda function that checks and fixes bucket ACLs and policies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run an Amazon Macie discovery job every day to find public buckets and notify the owner so that they change the settings manually.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Check the bucket permissions check results of AWS Trusted Advisor once a week and block public access on violating buckets manually.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Detect public read access with an AWS Config managed rule, connect an AWS Systems Manager Automation document for automatic remediation, and exclude the exception accounts from the target.

exam-saa-c03-51.explanation: The correct answer is the combination of an AWS Config managed rule and an automatic remediation action. The managed rule continuously evaluates the public read status, the attached Automation runbook reverts the setting without custom code, and the exception accounts can be excluded from the rule's scope. A self-built Lambda approach requires deploying and maintaining code in every account. Macie is a sensitive data discovery service and does not revert public settings. If a person checks Trusted Advisor once a week, the requirement for immediate remediation is not met. A managed configuration that satisfies all three conditions, automatic remediation, minimal code, and allowed exception accounts, is needed.

exam-saa-c03-52.prompt: A company is moving two on-premises Windows file servers (with DFS replication) to AWS. 150 users at headquarters and branch offices use SMB shares and NTFS permissions based on Active Directory, and AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory is already integrated with the on-premises Active Directory. During an Availability Zone failure, the system must switch over automatically to another Availability Zone, and the company wants to leave server patching and replication management to AWS. Changes on the user side must be minimized, and the migration must be completed in one weekend day. The shared data is about 4 TB, and users mainly open and save office documents. Users must continue to connect with the same share names and paths. What should the company choose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Install the file server role on EC2 Windows instances in two Availability Zones and configure DFS replication yourself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a Multi-AZ Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system and join it to Active Directory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a Multi-AZ Amazon EFS file system and mount it on the Windows instances over NFS.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keep the data in an Amazon S3 bucket and provide it over SMB through an S3 File Gateway on EC2.

exam-saa-c03-52.explanation: Multi-AZ FSx for Windows File Server natively supports SMB, Active Directory integration, and NTFS permissions, fails over automatically to a standby file server during an Availability Zone failure, and AWS manages patching and replication, so all constraints are met. Configuring DFS replication on EC2 yourself means continuing to operate patching and replication monitoring. EFS is NFS-based, so it is not supported on Windows instances and NTFS permissions cannot be used. S3 File Gateway is a cache over object storage, so file locking and permission behavior differ, and you would also be responsible for the availability of the gateway EC2 instance. The condition of keeping SMB and NTFS permissions as they are eliminates the NFS and object-based options.

exam-saa-c03-53.prompt: An order service that processes about 500,000 orders per day directly calls three systems in sequence when an order completes: payment settlement, inventory update, and notification sending. If one of them is slow or down, the order fails. The three systems are operated by different teams and are sometimes down for hours at a time because of deployments. Events must not be lost even if one system is down for several hours, and each system must receive all of the same order events. Changes to the order service should be minimized to a single place in the publishing code. Each system takes a few seconds on average to process one event, and the processing order does not matter among them. Even the slowest system can catch up on several hours of events after recovery. Which configuration is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The order service publishes to an Amazon SNS topic, and the HTTP endpoints of the three systems subscribe directly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The order service publishes once to an Amazon SNS topic, and a dedicated Amazon SQS queue for each system subscribes to it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The order service publishes to a single Amazon SQS standard queue, and the three systems poll the same queue together.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add an exponential backoff retry loop to the order service that repeats calls to failed systems for up to 1 hour.

exam-saa-c03-53.explanation: The publisher needs to send to Amazon SNS only once, and with a dedicated Amazon SQS queue for each subscriber, messages are retained in the queue even if one system is down for several hours and are processed after recovery, which provides both decoupling and loss prevention. With direct HTTP subscriptions, delivery is abandoned once the retry policy ends, so events can be lost during long outages. If three systems share one queue, each message is delivered to only one system and the other two never receive the event. A retry loop in the order service is still synchronous coupling, so order processing is delayed, and events are lost if the service restarts. The condition that all three systems must receive the same events and the condition of tolerating outages of several hours require fan-out and queue retention respectively.

exam-saa-c03-54.prompt: A securities firm runs a 1.5 TB single-process in-memory analytics engine on Amazon EC2. The entire dataset must be loaded into memory, the engine is structured so that it cannot be split across multiple servers, and its average CPU utilization is low, at 20% or less. There is almost no disk I/O, and the instance is expected to be used continuously for more than a year. No schedule has been set for modifying the software. Memory usage is 1.3 TB at peak and is expected to grow by about 15% over the next year. The server is in a single Availability Zone in the Asia Pacific (Seoul) Region and is launched anew from an AMI in the event of a failure. Considering cost efficiency relative to performance, which instance family should the company choose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use several compute optimized instances, such as the C family, grouped together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use storage optimized instances, such as the I family.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Distribute the engine across several general purpose instances, such as the M family.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use memory optimized instances, such as the X family.

exam-saa-c03-54.explanation: When the entire dataset must be loaded into memory and CPU utilization is low, memory optimized instances such as the X family, which have a high ratio of memory per vCPU, are the most cost-effective. Compute optimized instances have a high vCPU ratio, so they waste CPU relative to memory. Storage optimized instances are for workloads where local disk I/O is important, and this analytics engine has almost no disk I/O. Splitting across several general purpose instances would distribute the single engine's dataset, which requires changing the application structure and also costs more. The condition that the engine cannot be split eliminates the options that distribute across multiple servers, and the low CPU utilization eliminates the vCPU-centric families.

exam-saa-c03-55.prompt: A startup's B2B analytics dashboard uses Amazon Aurora MySQL. The database is about 300 GB with a read-heavy workload, and during business hours the load rises to 10 times its normal level, while it is nearly zero at night and on weekends. There is no DBA and two developers operate the system, so manually adjusting the instance size is difficult, and fixing a large instance sized for the peak is a cost burden. The company also wants to minimize connection drops during changes. Most queries are SELECT statements, and writes occur only in the nightly ETL. The average number of connections during business hours is around 200, and the application uses the cluster endpoint as it is. Which method has the LEAST operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a provisioned db.r6g.4xlarge instance sized for the peak load, fixed 24 hours a day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Switch to Aurora Serverless v2 and set an ACU range so that it scales out and in automatically.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Build your own scheduled AWS Lambda job that changes the instance class before and after business hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Always keep 15 Aurora read replicas and distribute all queries to the replicas.

exam-saa-c03-55.explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 increases and decreases capacity almost continuously in ACU units according to the load, so it handles the peak without a DBA and reduces costs during idle times. Fixing a large instance means paying peak rates even at night and on weekends. Changing the instance class with a script causes brief interruptions and failover during the change, and you must maintain the scheduling logic yourself. Keeping 15 read replicas running at all times costs even more and does not reduce the write load. The conditions of minimizing interruptions during changes and having no DBA eliminate the manual class-change approach.

exam-saa-c03-56.prompt: A design company stores about 40 TB of working files in S3 Standard. Restore requests usually arrive within a week after an incident. Incidents in which employees accidentally overwrite or delete files occur once or twice a month, and it must be possible to restore a previous version within 30 days. Storage costs must not grow without limit because of previous versions, and the company does not want to introduce a separate backup tool. There is only one IT person, so manual copy or cleanup procedures are hard to operate. The bucket has about 100 million objects with an average object size of 400 KB. Most restore requests are caused by overwrites, with about one deletion per month, and the versions to be restored are within the last 30 days. Which configuration is the MOST cost-effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on bucket versioning only and keep all previous versions forever without lifecycle rules.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on bucket versioning and add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent objects after 30 days.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Switch the bucket to the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class to reduce the cost of objects that are not used often.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Copy the entire bucket to a second bucket every night with AWS DataSync to maintain daily copies.

exam-saa-c03-56.explanation: Versioning keeps previous versions on overwrites and deletions, which makes recovery possible, and expiring noncurrent objects after 30 days meets the recovery-period requirement while limiting the cost of previous versions. Keeping all versions without a lifecycle rule makes costs grow continuously. Intelligent-Tiering is a means of saving costs based on access patterns, not a means of recovering from overwrites. Copying 40 TB every day with DataSync incurs large transfer and additional storage costs, and with only daily copies the point-in-time recovery resolution is also low. The condition that manual work cannot be operated also eliminates the daily copy approach.

exam-saa-c03-57.prompt: A company plans to keep running six Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL db.r6g.2xlarge instances continuously for more than 3 years and has no plans to change the engine or Region. The company already purchased Compute Savings Plans last quarter, but its RDS bill did not decrease. RDS currently accounts for 35% of the total monthly AWS cost, and management wants commitment-based savings. The Multi-AZ configuration must be kept because of availability requirements, and DB operations must remain with AWS. The six instances have relatively constant CPU utilization 24 hours a day, and only minor version engine upgrades are planned. The finance team can choose the commitment type and the upfront payment ratio. Which method reduces RDS costs in the MOST cost-effective way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Purchase RDS Reserved Instances for the relevant engine and Region and apply the commitment discount to instance usage hours.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the hourly commitment amount of the Compute Savings Plans so that RDS instance hours are also included in the discounted usage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Move the RDS instances to EC2 r6g, install PostgreSQL yourself, and apply EC2 Instance Savings Plans.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change all instances from Multi-AZ to Single-AZ to eliminate the standby instance cost and shorten the backup retention period.

exam-saa-c03-57.explanation: The correct answer is RDS Reserved Instances. Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2, AWS Fargate, and AWS Lambda usage and do not apply to RDS, so increasing the commitment amount does not reduce RDS costs. Reserved Instances fit long-term databases with a fixed engine and Region, and they also offer size flexibility within the same family. Installing on EC2 yourself means taking on patching, backups, and failover, which greatly increases the operational burden. Removing Multi-AZ reduces costs but lowers availability, which is a change in the opposite direction of the requirements. The conditions of keeping Multi-AZ and managed operations eliminate the options that downgrade the configuration or install it yourself.

exam-saa-c03-58.prompt: A fintech company runs its service on an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster in us-east-1. Because of regulations, the company must keep a recovery environment in ap-northeast-2 to prepare for a failure of an entire Region, with an RPO of a few seconds and an RTO within a few minutes. The cluster is about 3 TB, and writes occur continuously. The team has three members and does not want to operate replication scripts or conversion jobs itself. The secondary cluster in Seoul is not used during normal operation and is promoted only during a failure. Overall write TPS averages 3,000, and DR drills are performed twice a year. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copy automated snapshots to the Seoul Region every hour and, if a Regional failure occurs, create a new cluster and restore it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply changes to a separate Aurora cluster in Seoul with an AWS DMS ongoing replication task.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add Seoul as a secondary Region to an Aurora global database and promote the secondary cluster during a failure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create an Aurora cluster in Seoul, configure binlog replication yourself, and promote it during a failure.

exam-saa-c03-58.explanation: An Aurora global database replicates to another Region at the storage layer, usually with less than 1 second of lag, and fails over by promoting the secondary cluster, so it meets an RPO of a few seconds and an RTO within a few minutes with low operational burden. Copying hourly snapshots has an RPO of up to 1 hour, which does not fit, and restoring a new cluster also takes a long time. DMS ongoing replication requires task monitoring and schema management, which increases the operational burden, and its lag is not consistent. Binlog replication must be configured and monitored yourself, and its replication lag is larger than storage replication, so it is hard to guarantee the RPO target. The RPO of a few seconds eliminates the snapshot approach, and the condition of not operating it yourself eliminates the DMS or binlog approaches.

exam-saa-c03-59.prompt: A company must interconnect 45 VPCs across 12 accounts and an on-premises data center connected over AWS Direct Connect. It has been building a mesh with VPC peering, but it has become hard to manage. The IP ranges do not overlap, transitive routing between VPCs is required, and changes when a new VPC is added must be minimized. The network team has three members and wants to manage routing policy centrally. Direct Connect is already connected through a Direct Connect gateway, and traffic between development and production environments must be isolated. Two or three new VPCs are added each month. Which configuration is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add VPC peering between every pair of VPCs to build a full mesh and manage the route tables.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a separate Site-to-Site VPN connection to on premises for each VPC and route through it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure a hub-and-spoke design in which the VPCs and Direct Connect are attached to an AWS Transit Gateway.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a PrivateLink endpoint service in each VPC and configure them to consume each other.

exam-saa-c03-59.explanation: A Transit Gateway connects VPCs and on premises to a single hub and provides transitive routing, and a new VPC only needs to be attached to the hub, so changes are minimized. VPC peering does not support transitive routing, and a full mesh of 45 VPCs would need as many as 990 connections, which makes management even harder. Creating a VPN for each VPC makes connection count and bandwidth management complex, and transitive routing between VPCs would also have to be designed yourself. PrivateLink is a way of exposing specific services and does not suit connecting entire VPC networks. Central management, transitive routing, and easy VPC addition point to a hub structure.

exam-saa-c03-60.prompt: An internal tool runs a CSV conversion job only three or four times a day, for 2 to 3 minutes each time. It currently keeps a t3.large EC2 instance running 24 hours a day and processes the job with cron, with CPU utilization below 1%. The results are stored in Amazon S3, and the input files are at most about 50 MB. The company also wants to reduce management tasks such as server patching, and the conversion logic is a single Python script. The job runs at fixed times during business hours, and a delay of a few minutes causes no problem. There are 40 such tools, so even though each individual cost is small, the total cannot be ignored. Which alternative is the MOST cost-effective while requiring only small code changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apply a 3-year Reserved Instance to the same instance to lower the hourly rate, leave the cron setup as it is, and add only a utilization alarm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduce the instance to t3.nano and keep cron running 24 hours a day, minimizing the hourly rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Move the conversion logic to an AWS Lambda function invoked by Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, so that charges apply only for the time it runs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Move the conversion job to an AWS Fargate service, always run at least one task, and set the CPU to 0.25 vCPU.

exam-saa-c03-60.explanation: The correct answer is the combination of EventBridge Scheduler and Lambda. The job takes about 10 minutes a day and each run fits within the 15-minute limit, so charges apply only for the execution time and number of requests, there is virtually no idle cost, and no server management is needed. A Reserved Instance leaves the waste of keeping a 1%-utilization instance running as it is and adds a commitment on top. A t3.nano is still a structure that runs 24 hours a day, so there is still idle cost, and it may run short of memory. An always-on Fargate task is also billed whenever it is running, so the same problem remains. Every always-on structure leaves idle cost, so a serverless approach that bills only for the time it runs is right.

exam-saa-c03-61.prompt: A cost analysis SaaS vendor must read billing information in its customers' accounts. Customer security teams prohibit sharing long-term access keys and also want to prevent the confused deputy problem, in which the vendor mistakenly uses its role for another customer's request. The vendor has a service contract with them and must follow the principle of least privilege under the contract. There are 300 customers, so a separate authentication system cannot be built for each customer. The vendor fetches cost data once a day, and customers do not trust any external principal other than the vendor's account. The customer accounts are Organizations members and need only billing read permission. Which is the MOST secure method that meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a read-only IAM user and hand its access keys to the vendor, state in the contract that the keys must be rotated every 90 days, and review key usage with AWS CloudTrail.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a read-only IAM role in the customer account that trusts the vendor account, and add to the trust policy an external ID condition that the vendor assigns for each customer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a read-only role that trusts only the vendor account ID, and have all customers use the same role name and policy structure without an external ID.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Issue a temporary session of the customer's root user to the vendor so that it can connect to the billing console, and limit the session duration to 1 hour.

exam-saa-c03-61.explanation: The correct answer is a cross-account role with an external ID condition. The vendor receives temporary credentials through AWS STS without long-term keys, and requiring a unique external ID per customer as a condition of the trust policy prevents the confused deputy problem, in which another customer tricks the vendor into using this role. Handing over an IAM user and access keys violates the policy of prohibiting long-term key sharing. A role without an external ID allows cross-account access but misses a step, so the confused deputy risk remains. Sharing a root session grants excessive permissions and is not an allowed approach. Prohibiting long-term keys and preventing the confused deputy problem require role delegation and an external ID respectively.

exam-saa-c03-62.prompt: A regulatory auditor requires proof that the organization-wide API records to be retained for the next 3 years have not been modified or deleted during retention. An organization trail is already being delivered to an Amazon S3 bucket in the log archive account. The verification may be applied from the logs delivered going forward, tampering must be verifiable without additional development, and the auditor has read-only permission and must be able to reproduce the verification procedure personally. Write permission to the log archive account bucket is held by only two security administrators, and the log retention period is 3 years. The auditor plans to repeat the same verification every year. What should the company do to meet this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enable log file integrity validation on the trail and use the signed digest files to check whether the logs have been tampered with or deleted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Encrypt the trail logs with SSE-KMS and restrict the deletion permission in the key policy so that tampering cannot occur.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Also deliver the logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, specify a long retention period, and periodically compare the two copies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on versioning on the log bucket to preserve objects before modification and manually compare the version list during audits.

exam-saa-c03-62.explanation: The correct answer is AWS CloudTrail log file integrity validation. When it is turned on, CloudTrail creates a hash for each delivered log file and delivers signed digest files to the same bucket every hour, and the auditor can reproduce with a CLI validation command that the logs have not been modified, deleted, or forged. It applies from logs delivered after it is enabled, so it must be turned on now. SSE-KMS is only encryption at rest and does not tell you whether tampering has occurred. Comparing CloudWatch Logs copies is manual, and the copy could be changed in the same way. Versioning preserves previous objects but is not a means of automatically proving tampering. The condition that applying it from the logs delivered going forward is acceptable means that turning the feature on now satisfies the requirement.

exam-saa-c03-63.prompt: The delivery tracking system of a logistics company generates about 8 million events per day. Events of the same order (received, shipped, delivered) must be processed exactly once in the order in which they occurred, while events of different orders must be processed in parallel. The consumers are 20 Amazon EC2 workers, and the development team does not want to write code that manages queues per order. Each event averages 2 KB, and several hundred per second arrive at peak. Messages that repeatedly fail processing must be moved to a separate queue for a person to check. Which messaging configuration is MOST appropriate when building queue-based asynchronous processing that meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use an Amazon SQS standard queue, include a timestamp in each message, and have the consumers sort the messages before processing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Register each of the 20 workers as a subscriber to an Amazon SNS standard topic to fan out all events.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue with the order ID as the message group ID and use deduplication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dynamically create an Amazon SQS standard queue for each order and have one worker poll each queue in sequence.

exam-saa-c03-63.explanation: An SQS FIFO queue guarantees order within the same message group ID and ensures one-time processing with deduplication, and different groups can be consumed in parallel by multiple workers, so using the order ID as the group ID satisfies all the requirements. A standard queue does not guarantee order or deduplication, so consumer-side sorting cannot handle messages that arrive late. Fan-out with an SNS standard topic means all workers receive the same events, so they are processed in duplicate and with no order. Creating a queue per order causes an explosion of queues to manage and a single-worker bottleneck that harms parallelism. To satisfy both per-order ordering and parallelism across orders, order guarantees at the message group level are needed.

exam-saa-c03-64.prompt: A B2B software vendor wants customers to use, privately from the AWS accounts of its 300 customers, an API that runs behind a Network Load Balancer in the vendor's VPC. The CIDR ranges of customer VPCs may overlap with each other and with the vendor's VPC, and the vendor does not want to expose the entire customer networks to each other. Traffic must not traverse the internet, and the vendor must not have to change its network configuration each time customers are added. Customers create an endpoint in their own account, and the vendor reviews and accepts the connection requests. The API exposes only HTTPS port 443, and the average call volume per customer is a few dozen requests per second. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational burden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Establish VPC peering between each customer VPC and the vendor VPC and add routes to each other's CIDR in the route tables.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a Transit Gateway, attach all customer VPCs, separate the route tables to divide the access scope, and approve an attachment each time a customer is added.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a VPC endpoint service with the NLB as the target, and have customers create an interface endpoint in their own VPC and approve each connection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the NLB to internet-facing and register a fixed IP address for each customer in a security group allow list to control access.

exam-saa-c03-64.explanation: The correct answer is an endpoint service based on AWS PrivateLink. Consumers access only the one service through an interface endpoint, so overlapping CIDRs are not a problem and the entire network is not exposed, and the vendor does not need any routing changes even as the number of customers grows. VPC peering cannot be established when CIDRs overlap and results in connecting entire networks. A Transit Gateway also cannot route overlapping CIDRs. An internet-facing NLB with an IP allow list does not meet the private access requirement and increases the burden of managing customer IP addresses. The two conditions of overlapping CIDRs and service-level exposure eliminate all of the approaches that connect entire networks.

exam-saa-c03-65.prompt: An e-commerce company is designing disaster recovery (DR) with an RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 1 hour. The database is an Amazon Aurora database of about 2 TB, and the application servers are configured automatically from AMIs and infrastructure as code (IaC) templates, so they can be launched anew in the DR Region at the time of a failure. Normally the DR Region does not receive user traffic, and its cost should be as low as possible. DR drills are held every six months. The database change rate averages a few MB per second and can be replicated continuously to the DR Region. The application server AMIs are copied to the DR Region regularly. Which DR strategy is the MOST cost-effective and meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Warm standby: run a scaled-down full stack in the DR Region at all times and scale it out with Auto Scaling during a failure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pilot light: continuously replicate only the database to the DR Region and launch the servers from AMIs and IaC during a failure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Backup and restore: copy nightly snapshots to the DR Region and restore the database from a snapshot during a failure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Active-active: both Regions process requests and traffic is distributed with latency-based routing.

exam-saa-c03-65.explanation: Data can meet the 5-minute RPO through continuous replication, and since the servers may be launched at the time of failure, a pilot light that keeps only the core data tier running meets the requirements with the lowest normal-operation cost. Warm standby spends more on always-running servers for faster recovery than the requirement needs. Restoring from nightly snapshots has an RPO of almost a day and cannot meet the 5-minute target. Active-active operates both Regions in full, so it is the most expensive and also requires designing for write conflicts. The condition that servers may be launched anew at the time of failure makes a strategy of always-on servers unnecessary, and the 5-minute RPO requires continuous replication.

exam-sap-c02-1.prompt: An insurance company is migrating an Oracle 19c database (about 8 TB) that runs on self-managed on-premises servers to Aurora PostgreSQL. The database contains hundreds of PL/SQL packages and stored procedures, so the company must first determine which parts convert automatically and which require manual work before converting. The claims system continues to generate writes during business hours, so service interruption during cutover must be within 30 minutes. The on-premises environment and AWS are already connected with AWS Direct Connect, and the DBA team has approved enabling ARCHIVELOG mode and supplemental logging on the source server. The migration schedule is 3 months, and the 4 DBAs have little PostgreSQL experience. The company does not want to use custom-developed replication scripts because of the maintenance burden. The target schema contains about 1,200 tables and indexes, and write volume triples during month-end settlement. The source Oracle database will be kept for 2 weeks after the migration for rollback. Management requires the migration to be completed before quarter-end, but because the goal is to reduce licensing costs, the company will not purchase a new commercial conversion tool. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use DMS Schema Conversion to generate a conversion assessment report, convert and apply the schema and code, and then replicate with a task that combines a DMS full load and change data capture (CDC). Cut over when the lag is minimal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Export the Oracle tables to CSV files, upload them to Amazon S3, and bulk load them into Aurora PostgreSQL. Plan a schedule that stops application writes over a weekend until the load is complete, and set the cutover downtime accordingly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run only a DMS full load task to copy the 8 TB at once. Run the Oracle DDL and PL/SQL code as is on Aurora PostgreSQL without a conversion tool, and manually apply the changes that occurred during the copy just before cutover.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable Babelfish on the Aurora PostgreSQL cluster to run the Oracle clients and PL/SQL packages without changes. Move the data with a DMS full load and cut over immediately, skipping the assessment phase.

exam-sap-c02-1.explanation: The correct answer is the combination of DMS Schema Conversion and a DMS full load plus CDC. Schema Conversion uses a conversion assessment report to show which parts convert automatically and which require manual work, and it converts schema and code objects from Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL, but it does not move data. The data is moved with a DMS full load and CDC. Oracle CDC requires ARCHIVELOG mode and supplemental logging, which the conditions allow. Because CDC continuously applies changes, the cutover downtime can be kept short. A bulk CSV load cannot capture writes that occur during the migration, which causes a long outage. Using only a full load and running the Oracle DDL as is fails because of PostgreSQL syntax differences and also misses the changes. Babelfish is a feature for SQL Server clients and T-SQL, so it cannot run Oracle PL/SQL. Because the DBAs are not familiar with PostgreSQL and the schedule is 3 months, the combination of Schema Conversion, which first confirms the conversion scope through a report, and managed replication is the safest. Given the constraints of 4 DBAs with little PostgreSQL experience and a 3-month schedule, the combination that first confirms the conversion scope through a report and uses managed replication is the safest.

exam-sap-c02-2.prompt: A research institute needs to move 60 TB of data from an on-premises NAS (NFS) to Amazon S3 and then periodically synchronize subsequent changes. The NAS holds 40 million files, 80% of which are smaller than 1 MB, and researchers continue to modify files during the migration. The company has a 1 Gbps AWS Direct Connect connection, but bandwidth is almost unavailable during business hours, so transfers must run only at night. Security policy requires that transfers not traverse the public internet. Integrity between the source and the destination must be verified after the transfer. The maintenance contract for the NAS device ends in 3 months, so the migration must be finished within that time. The IT team has 2 people and does not want to develop or maintain scripts. The NAS is not a read-only archive but a shared store where researchers write new data every day, and there is no budget to purchase a new dedicated transfer server. After the migration, the research team plans to analyze the data in S3 with Amazon Athena. Consistency between the source NAS and S3 must not be broken because it would affect the reproducibility of research results, so verification results must be recorded for every file that has been transferred. Which method meets these requirements MOST appropriately?

choices.label: A
choices.text: On a Linux server that mounts the NAS, run the aws s3 sync command nightly with cron, and write a separate checksum comparison script to verify the source and destination after completion. Run the checksum comparison script once after the transfers finish and resend any mismatched files.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deploy an AWS DataSync agent on premises and create a task from the NFS location to the S3 location. Configure a nightly schedule and a bandwidth limit, enable transferred data verification, and connect through a VPC endpoint over Direct Connect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deploy an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises, move the NAS users to the gateway share, and let the gateway upload to S3 in the background. Consider the migration complete.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create an Amazon EC2 instance in a VPC, mount the NAS over VPN, copy the data to an Amazon EBS volume with rsync, and then copy the data from EBS to S3 in a two-step process.

exam-sap-c02-2.explanation: The correct answer is DataSync. The agent transfers data in parallel from NFS to S3, and DataSync provides task scheduling, bandwidth limits, repeated synchronization of changes, and data integrity verification out of the box. It can also transfer without the public internet by using a VPC endpoint, so no script development is needed. Cron with s3 sync requires custom development of bandwidth limiting and verification, which violates the requirements. File Gateway is a hybrid cache solution that moves users to a new share, not a bulk migration tool. The approach through EC2 and rsync involves many steps and adds intermediate EBS cost and operational work. Because the IT team has 2 people and cannot maintain scripts, DataSync, which provides scheduling, bandwidth limits, and verification out of the box, is more suitable than the other options. Because of the 2-person team that cannot maintain scripts and the nightly bandwidth limits, DataSync, which provides scheduling, bandwidth limits, and verification out of the box, is more suitable than the other options.

exam-sap-c02-3.prompt: A bank is building a new loan review workflow on AWS. After documents are verified, the step that waits for a staff member's approval can last up to 3 weeks, and the next step proceeds only after the approval result arrives. The payment step must run exactly once under any circumstances, and for auditing, the input and output of each step of each execution must be queryable for 90 days. Approvers use an approval system in the company data center, and this system can send REST calls over Direct Connect to AWS to deliver the result. There are several hundred reviews per day, and the development team of 5 uses Python and Java. The audit team wants to trace, per execution, who the approver was and the time of the decision, and the document verification step calls several Lambda functions in sequence. Regulators perform inspections every quarter. The credit score calculation has already been separated into its own microservice and is outside the scope of this design, and sending the approval result can be retried if it fails. Which design is MOST appropriate to reduce the burden of writing state management code yourself?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run an AWS Step Functions Express workflow asynchronously and set a long Wait state for the approval step to keep the execution alive for up to 3 weeks until the staff approval result arrives. Record the input and output of each step in Amazon CloudWatch Logs for auditing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Implement a sleep loop inside a Lambda function that periodically checks whether approval has been given, and run the function repeatedly by using an Amazon EventBridge rule that reinvokes it every 15 minutes to wait.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In a Step Functions Standard workflow, use the callback pattern (waitForTaskToken) for the approval step so that the next step continues when the staff approval system returns the result with the task token.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put review requests in an Amazon SQS delay queue so that a consumer processes them 3 weeks later, store the approval result in Amazon DynamoDB, and have the consumer check it and then invoke the next step.

exam-sap-c02-3.explanation: The correct answer is a Standard workflow with the callback pattern. Standard workflows provide executions of up to 1 year, an exactly-once execution model, and execution history lookup, so they safely orchestrate steps that cannot be duplicated, such as payments, and waitForTaskToken waits with a token until the external approval arrives. Express workflows last at most 5 minutes, do not support the callback pattern, and use an at-least-once execution model. A Lambda sleep loop requires you to write the state management code yourself and the execution is easily interrupted while waiting. An SQS delay queue supports a delay of at most 15 minutes, so it cannot support 3 weeks. Because there are only several hundred reviews per day, throughput is not a concern, and because the execution time is 3 weeks, the maximum execution time and the exactly-once execution model are the deciding factors. The constraints of a 3-week execution time and a payment step that must run exactly once eliminate Express and the sleep loop.

exam-sap-c02-4.prompt: A retailer is moving an on-premises SFTP server (OpenSSH) used by 20 partners to AWS. Partners connect with a user name and a public key. The partner companies have no staff who can change connection settings, so a host key change warning must not appear, and the domain name (sftp.example.com) cannot be changed either. Received files must be collected in Amazon S3 for downstream processing, and uploaded files must start a downstream processing pipeline through S3 events. Each partner must be able to see only its own folder. The current server is a single aging machine, and patching and incident response continually consume staff time, so the company wants to reduce the server operating burden, and the migration must be completed within one month. Three of the partners upload hundreds of small files per day, and one uploads large files of 20 GB each. The user accounts and public key list from the existing server are already organized and can be moved as is. Partner contacts review connection history in a monthly security check, and after the migration each partner keeps the same user name and authentication method. Which method is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP server with an S3 backend, import the existing host key, register each user's public key, and make sftp.example.com in Amazon Route 53 point to the server endpoint.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Install an OpenSSH server on an Amazon EC2 instance, store the data on Amazon EBS and periodically copy it to S3, and attach an Elastic IP address and change DNS. Configure folder-level access restrictions with Linux user permissions and directory modes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Issue S3 presigned URLs to the partners and instruct them to upload directly over HTTPS, and discontinue SFTP use.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place an AWS DataSync agent on premises to periodically synchronize the SFTP server's directories to S3, and have partners continue to connect to the existing SFTP server.

exam-sap-c02-4.explanation: The correct answer is the Transfer Family SFTP server. Because it is managed, there is no server operating burden, it stores directly in S3, it supports user name and public key authentication, it can import the existing host key to avoid host key warnings on the partner side, and a Route 53 record can point the existing domain to the new endpoint. EC2 with OpenSSH leaves server operations and patching in place and requires building the S3 copy separately. Presigned URLs change the protocol, which requires changes on the partner side. DataSync is a file synchronization tool, so it cannot replace the SFTP server, and operation of the on-premises server continues. Because partners cannot change their settings, keeping the host key and domain is mandatory, which a managed SFTP endpoint satisfies, whereas options that require a protocol change are eliminated. Because partners cannot change their settings, keeping the host key and domain is mandatory, and options that require a protocol change are eliminated.

exam-sap-c02-5.prompt: A financial company has firewall appliances deployed across two Availability Zones in a central inspection VPC, and spoke VPCs in 12 accounts are connected with a transit gateway so that all traffic between spoke VPCs goes through this VPC. Recently, some TCP connections are intermittently dropped when two spoke VPCs communicate with each other. Investigation shows that requests and responses pass through firewalls in different Availability Zones, so the stateful inspection firewalls do not recognize the session. The symptoms occur regardless of the time of day, the service impact is large, and the time window for changes is short. Security policy requires keeping the Availability Zone configuration for firewall redundancy, and the network team has 3 people, so a large-scale routing overhaul is difficult. The firewall appliances are vendor-provided AMIs, one per Availability Zone for a total of 2, and traffic from the spoke VPCs to the internet uses a separate path, so it is unrelated to this symptom. Incidents are reported 3 to 4 times a week. The problem reproduces only when the two spoke VPCs are in subnets in different Availability Zones, and the configuration of the transit gateway route tables itself has already been verified. The firewall vendor support contract covers only log analysis. Which method solves this problem with the FEWEST configuration changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduce the attachment subnets of the inspection VPC so that only one Availability Zone is used, and stop the firewall appliance in the other Availability Zone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enable appliance mode on the inspection VPC's transit gateway attachment so that both directions of a flow's traffic pass through the firewall interface in the same Availability Zone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add static routes toward the peer VPC CIDR to each spoke VPC's route table, turn off transit gateway route table propagation, and manually adjust the priority of the route toward the inspection VPC.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on the appliance vendor's state replication feature so that the firewall appliances synchronize session state across Availability Zones, and leave the transit gateway settings unchanged.

exam-sap-c02-5.explanation: When appliance mode is off on an attachment, a transit gateway keeps traffic in the Availability Zone it originated from, so a request and its response can pass through appliances in different Availability Zones. When appliance mode is turned on, both directions of a flow are delivered to the network interface in the same Availability Zone for the lifetime of the flow, which guarantees symmetric routing. The change is a single attachment option. Reducing to one Availability Zone makes the problem disappear but gives up Availability Zone fault tolerance, which violates the availability constraint. Adding static routes in the spokes is unrelated to the asymmetric cross-Availability Zone path problem. Vendor state replication must be supported by the appliance, requires much larger configuration changes, and does not resolve the cause on the transit gateway side. Because the change window is short and Availability Zone redundancy must be kept, appliance mode, which requires only a single attachment option, carries less risk and fewer changes than the other options. Because the change window is short and Availability Zone redundancy must be kept, appliance mode, which requires only a single attachment option, involves the fewest changes.

exam-sap-c02-6.prompt: A securities firm must retain trade confirmation PDFs in Amazon S3 for 7 years. Regulations require that no user, including the root user of the AWS account, can delete or overwrite objects during the retention period. In addition, some objects designated as under dispute must be preserved even after 7 years until the responsible person releases them, and the data must also be replicated to a separate bucket in another Region for disaster recovery. There are already hundreds of millions of objects, so per-object manual management is not feasible. The audit firm verifies that retention settings have not been arbitrarily weakened during the retention period, and the compliance team has 3 people. About 200,000 uploads occur per day, and the average object size is 300 KB. Versioning is currently off on the bucket, and the replication destination Region is Tokyo, with Seoul as the source. Each object is a PDF that is never modified once written, and the legal team estimates that a few dozen objects per year become subject to disputes. The operations team is comfortable with the AWS console but has no time to build separate tools. Which configuration meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on S3 Versioning and Object Lock on the bucket and set the default retention to Governance mode for 7 years, granting the bypass permission to a single security team role only. Set the default retention once at the bucket level to avoid per-object management.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add statements to the bucket policy that deny s3:DeleteObject and s3:PutObject for all principals, give only the security administrator permission to change the policy, and delete the objects with a lifecycle rule after 7 years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on S3 Versioning and Object Lock on the bucket, set the default retention to Compliance mode for 7 years, apply Legal Hold to disputed objects, and configure cross-Region replication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immediately transition the objects to the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class and expire them after 7 years with a lifecycle rule, and attach a tag that excludes disputed objects from the expiration rule.

exam-sap-c02-6.explanation: The correct answer is the combination of Object Lock in Compliance mode and Legal Hold. In Compliance mode, no one, including the root user, can delete or overwrite an object version during the retention period, and the retention period cannot be shortened. A Legal Hold protects an object until it is released, with no expiration date, so it meets the requirement for disputed objects. Governance mode allows users with bypass permission to delete objects, which conflicts with the requirement that no one, including root, can do so. A bucket policy is not WORM because an administrator can edit the policy to remove the restriction. Transitioning to Glacier Deep Archive only changes storage cost and does not prevent deletion. Because of the regulation that blocks even the root user and the scale of hundreds of millions of objects, an immutable mode applied in bulk through the bucket default retention is a mandatory condition. Because of the regulation that blocks even the root user and the scale of hundreds of millions of objects, Compliance mode applied in bulk through the bucket default retention is required, and Governance mode is eliminated because it has a bypass permission.

exam-sap-c02-7.prompt: A data platform team wants analytics roles in more than 200 accounts in AWS Organizations to be able to read an Amazon S3 data lake bucket in an analytics account. New accounts are added every week and some accounts are closed. Accounts outside the organization and external partner accounts must not be able to access this bucket. Currently, account IDs are listed one by one in the bucket policy, and the policy is approaching the size limit. The 2 administrators of the analytics account want to stop editing the bucket policy every time accounts are added or removed. The data grows by tens of TB per month, and the analytics role names in the consuming accounts all follow the same naming convention. The analytics roles in the consuming accounts read this bucket from Amazon Athena and Amazon EMR, and the consuming accounts are scattered across multiple organizational units (OUs). Access is read-only, and writes occur only in the analytics account. Development and production accounts are mixed, so every account can be given the same read scope, and because the data contains no personal information, object-level fine-grained permissions are not required. The current bucket policy is managed manually, so changes are often delayed. Which method has the LEAST operational overhead and applies automatically to new accounts without modifying the policy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Split the list of account IDs in the bucket policy into separate policy statements per account, and automate with a CI pipeline that adds the corresponding statement whenever a new account is created.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a cross-account IAM role per account in the analytics account, and have the analytics role in each consuming account assume the role with sts:AssumeRole to read the bucket.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the bucket policy, set Principal to * but allow read access only when the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition equals the organization ID, and attach to the analytics roles in the consuming accounts an identity-based policy that allows access to this bucket.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Share the S3 bucket with the entire organization by using AWS RAM so that all accounts see the bucket as a resource in their own account.

exam-sap-c02-7.explanation: The aws:PrincipalOrgID condition specifies all organization members in one line instead of listing account IDs, is applied automatically without editing the policy when accounts are added or removed, and denies principals outside the organization. Because this is cross-account access, an allow is also needed in the identity-based policy of the consuming account roles. Splitting statements per account still adds a statement for every account and does not fundamentally solve the policy size limit. Per-account cross-account roles require managing as many roles and trust relationships as there are accounts. S3 buckets are not resources that can be shared through RAM. The constraints that accounts change weekly and that the policy is already near its size limit eliminate listing per account or using per-account roles, and an organization-level condition solves it in one line. The constraints that accounts change weekly and that the policy is near its size limit eliminate the per-account listing and per-account role approaches.

exam-sap-c02-8.prompt: A telecommunications company connects 30 VPCs across 8 accounts in the Seoul Region with a single transit gateway and wants to connect them to its on-premises network over redundant connections at a single AWS Direct Connect location. The redundant connections are already installed, the Direct Connect gateway is owned by the network account, and the transit gateway is owned by a separate hub account. New VPCs are added at a rate of 3 to 5 per quarter, and the company wants to eliminate the process of creating a new virtual interface (VIF) each time a VPC is added or having each account team request a connection from the circuit owner. The network team has 4 people, and the on-premises routers have a limit on the number of BGP advertised prefixes. The VPCs have non-overlapping CIDRs, and the on-premises environment consists of one data center with two routers. In the earlier phase, communication between VPCs in different accounts must also go through the transit gateway. The hub account and the network account are managed by different teams and changes take several days to approve, so the structure must not require repeating this approval process even as VPCs grow after being configured once. The circuit bandwidth itself is sufficient. Which configuration MOST appropriately meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a private virtual interface for each VPC and attach it to each VPC's virtual private gateway, and add a VIF the same way whenever a new VPC is created.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Connect the 30 VPCs to each other with a full mesh of VPC peering, then attach a private VIF to the virtual private gateway of one representative VPC so that the remaining VPCs route through it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach a transit VIF to the Direct Connect gateway, have the hub account send an association proposal for the transit gateway, have the gateway owner account accept it, and specify the allowed prefixes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Order a separate Direct Connect hosted connection for each account and connect each account's VPCs directly with a private VIF on that connection.

exam-sap-c02-8.explanation: When a Direct Connect gateway is associated with a transit gateway and a transit VIF is used, multiple VPCs in the same Region share one connection, so no VIF is needed when a VPC is added. When the gateway and the transit gateway are owned by different accounts, the transit gateway owner account sends an association proposal, the gateway owner account accepts it, and the allowed prefixes can be adjusted. Creating a private VIF per VPC is the opposite of the requirement. VPC peering does not support transitive routing, so routing through a representative VPC does not work. Ordering a connection per account greatly increases circuit cost and operational burden. Given that VPCs grow every quarter, only a structure that connects to the transit gateway through a single transit VIF meets the scaling requirement of not adding VIFs. Given that VPCs grow every quarter, only a structure that connects to the transit gateway through a single transit VIF meets the scaling requirement of not adding VIFs.

exam-sap-c02-9.prompt: A manufacturing company is improving disaster recovery (DR) for 40 servers made up of Amazon EC2 and Amazon EBS. The servers are a mix of Linux and Windows, the EBS disks total 25 TB, and both on-premises and cloud servers can be targets. Currently, nightly AMI copies give an RPO of one day. The new requirements are an RPO of a few seconds and an RTO within 1 hour, while avoiding the cost of continuously running the same servers as production in the DR Region. The team has chosen Tokyo as the DR Region, and regular recovery drills must not affect production servers.
