exam-sap-c02-34.explanation: The correct answer is a warm standby that combines Aurora global database replication with a continuously running scaled-down web tier. Because a warm standby is already deployed and running, it can handle traffic immediately with reduced capacity and only needs to scale out with Auto Scaling, which meets the 10-minute RTO and the requirement for immediate handling, and scaling down keeps it within the 30% cost limit. An always-on active-active setup with 40 instances greatly exceeds the cost limit. Backup copies and redeployment have an RTO measured in hours and cannot meet 10 minutes. A configuration with web servers turned off, like pilot light, must first launch and configure them, which does not fit the immediate handling requirement and the RTO. To satisfy both an RTO of 10 minutes and a cost of 30% or less, a warm standby that always replicates the data and always runs a scaled-down web tier is right.

exam-sap-c02-35.prompt: A marketplace serves from the Seoul Region and uses the Osaka Region for DR. Management refuses failover based on automated health checks, to avoid unnecessary failovers caused by false positives when a Regional failure is suspected, and requires failover only after a person approves it. However, the console and control plane APIs may be unstable during an outage, so the failover action itself must run with data-plane-level high availability. The same application is deployed behind an ALB in both Seoul and Osaka, and the data is already being replicated. Failover authority belongs only to two operations leads, and every failover attempt must be recorded for audit. The two operations leads must be able to approve a failover from their mobile phones as well, and they also practice failing back after a failover every quarter. DNS is currently in Amazon Route 53, where an alias record points to the Seoul ALB with a TTL of 60 seconds. Data replication between the two Regions works in real time. Management must report the results of the failure drills to the audit team each quarter, and the report must include who failed over and at what time. When Seoul recovers after a failover, traffic is returned in the same way. What is the SAFEST failover method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prepare a script that changes the Seoul and Osaka weights of Route 53 weighted records through the API during a failure, and after approval lower the Seoul weight to 0. After approval, the script modifies the records through the Route 53 API, and the change is recorded in AWS CloudTrail.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use routing controls in Amazon Route 53 Application Recovery Controller as on/off switches, and after approval perform the failover with a script that calls the data plane API against the cluster endpoints.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Associate Route 53 health checks with the Seoul endpoint and configure a failover routing policy in which DNS automatically responds with the Osaka record on failure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Write an operating procedure to change the AWS Global Accelerator endpoint group traffic dials, after approval, to 0% for Seoul and 100% for Osaka.

exam-sap-c02-35.explanation: The correct answer is ARC routing controls. A routing control is a switch-type Route 53 health check that does not inspect actual health and can be turned on and off, and it lets a person fail over at the desired time through highly available data plane endpoints. Changing weights and changing traffic dials are control plane operations, so they are less resilient during an outage. Health-check-based failover routing is automatic failover, which conflicts with the requirement to fail over only after a person approves and still has the false positive concern. The conditions of failover after human approval and preparing for control plane instability point to routing controls, which operate on the data plane.

exam-sap-c02-36.prompt: A company is moving 100 Windows application servers to Amazon EC2. The servers are joined to an on-premises Active Directory domain and use Group Policy (GPO). The on-premises AD will be kept for the time being and user accounts are managed there. Even if AWS Direct Connect is temporarily interrupted, domain authentication between servers inside AWS must continue, and the company wants to reduce the burden of operating domain controller servers itself. The servers have many logons during business hours and apply security settings through GPO. Direct Connect has only one circuit, so there is a short maintenance interruption about once a month, and the staff to operate domain controllers is insufficient. The 100 servers run Windows Server 2019, and user logons mostly concentrate at 9 AM. The on-premises AD has 5,000 users, and the company wants to keep using the domain management tools and GPO that server administrators use. During the migration period, user authentication must continue to be based on the on-premises AD, and the long-term plan is to move it to AWS. AWS and on premises are currently connected with Direct Connect, and there is no redundant circuit yet. The server settings are already organized in GPO, and the company wants these settings to be applied in the same way on the AWS side as well. Which configuration is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an AD Connector that proxies authentication requests to the on-premises AD, and join the EC2 servers to the on-premises domain through the AD Connector. Store credentials only in the on-premises AD to reduce management to a single point.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a Simple AD, join the servers to it, and establish a trust relationship with the on-premises AD so that Group Policy is shared on both sides.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create AWS Managed Microsoft AD in AWS, join the EC2 servers to this directory, and set up a trust relationship with the on-premises AD so that on-premises users are also authenticated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Install Windows Server domain controllers on EC2 instances and join them to the on-premises AD as additional domain controllers, and operate patching and backups yourself.

exam-sap-c02-36.explanation: The correct answer is AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a trust relationship. The managed domain controllers run inside AWS, so authentication between AWS servers continues even during a Direct Connect interruption, GPO is also supported, and on-premises users are authenticated through the trust, with low operational burden. AD Connector proxies authentication to on premises, so authentication fails if the connection is cut. Simple AD does not support trust relationships and has limited functionality. EC2 domain controllers carry the burden of operating patching and backups yourself. Because authentication must continue inside AWS even during a Direct Connect interruption and DC operations must be avoided, Managed AD, which places an actual directory on the AWS side, is right.

exam-sap-c02-37.prompt: A SaaS company's audit log group (about 3 TB ingested per day) has accumulated for 3 years with a retention setting of never expire. After 30 days, the logs are only occasionally queried with CloudWatch Logs Insights during incident investigations, and this log group uses no metric filters or subscription filters. The class of a log group cannot be changed after creation. The current Amazon CloudWatch Logs cost is tens of thousands of dollars per month, most of which is ingestion cost. The legal team has confirmed that retention beyond 3 years is not required. The logs contain JSON events, and investigators run Logs Insights only about 10 times a year. The team does not need real-time alerts on data older than 30 days, and since the 3 years of raw data cannot be migrated at once, the team can accept a transition in which new logs are sent to a new group. The cost reduction target is about half of the ingestion cost. The event structure of the log group is consistent, and personal information is masked before storage. The security team wants to send only new logs to the lower-cost option without moving all 3 years at once, while the existing logs are cleaned up naturally through retention expiry. Which method improves costs MOST cost-effectively while keeping the investigation capability?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the console, change the class of the existing log group to the Essentials (formerly Infrequent Access) class and leave the retention period as is.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Switch ingestion to a new log group in the Essentials (formerly Infrequent Access) class, and set a retention policy on the existing group so that old events expire.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extract only the needed metrics with metric filters and store them, and then delete the raw events in the log group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use a subscription filter to store all logs in Amazon S3 through Firehose, reduce the log group retention to 1 day, and handle investigations from S3.

exam-sap-c02-37.explanation: The Essentials (formerly Infrequent Access) log class has a lower ingestion price than Standard (storage and Logs Insights charges are the same) and supports most Logs Insights commands, which suits occasional post-incident investigations. Essentials does not support metric filters, subscription filters, or Live Tail, but this log group uses none of those features, so the limitation is not a problem. Because the class cannot be changed after creation, switch to a new log group, and specify a retention period on the existing group to stop accumulating storage cost. Changing the class of the existing group is not possible. If you keep only the metrics and delete the raw data, the events needed for incident investigation are lost. Subscription filters and Firehose require building a new configuration and an S3 query system yourself and give up the Logs Insights investigation capability. The constraint that a log group class cannot be changed after creation eliminates the option of changing the existing group and requires switching to a new group.

exam-sap-c02-38.prompt: A company wants to modernize a 20-year-old Java monolith (on-premises Tomcat) incrementally, feature by feature. It cannot stop developing new features, and service interruption is not allowed. The team first wants to split the order lookup feature into an independent service and run it in containers. The monolith shares a single in-house Oracle database and has a low level of test automation. Management requires a phased plan that lets it check transition progress and risk every quarter, and new feature requests arrive every week, so a development freeze is not possible. If a problem occurs, the company must be able to revert to the previous state within minutes. Order lookup is a read-heavy feature that receives millions of requests a day, and the response data comes from three Oracle tables used by the monolith. The team wants to split out the second and third features in the same way within 6 months after moving to AWS. The monolith is currently connected to AWS with Direct Connect, and the URL path is distinguished as /orders. The team currently has 8 people and has little container operations experience. Splitting the database all at once is out of scope for this phase, and management requires visible results in the first quarter. Which modernization approach reduces risk the MOST?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a parallel project that redevelops the new architecture from scratch, develop it separately from the existing system until all features are complete, and then switch all traffic in one day once complete. Stop new feature development for 6 months before the switch and focus on the new system.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Build the entire monolith into a single container image and move it to AWS Fargate, splitting the order lookup feature into a separate process within the same container.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Place an ALB in front, use path-based rules to send only order lookup requests to a new service on Amazon ECS Fargate while keeping the rest on the existing monolith, migrate features one at a time in the same way, and separate the data per service gradually (strangler pattern).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Have the order lookup service read and write the monolith's database tables directly, let both systems modify the same tables concurrently, and reconcile conflicts later in application code.

exam-sap-c02-38.explanation: The correct answer is the strangler pattern. The routing layer gradually shifts requests to new services feature by feature while the existing system handles the rest, so new development can continue without interruption, and if a problem occurs, only the routing needs to be reverted. A full rewrite with an all-at-once cutover is high-risk and creates a burden similar to a development freeze. Putting the monolith in a single container is closer to rehosting and does not achieve the goal of splitting into independent services. If the two systems modify the same tables concurrently, conflicts and coupling increase and the risk of failure is high. The requirements of no downtime and rollback within minutes point to path-based gradual transition (strangler), and parallel redevelopment and concurrent table modification are risky.

exam-sap-c02-39.prompt: A company is assessing its cloud migration portfolio and classifying the migration strategy for each application according to the 7 Rs definitions in AWS Prescriptive Guidance. The classifications within the team have diverged on several cases, and before finalizing the large-scale migration plan, the team must first agree on classification criteria that match the definitions. The migration will proceed in 3 waves, the scope of the first wave is determined by the classification results, and cost and schedule are both hard to change once fixed. The 7 Rs are Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform, and Refactor. The portfolio has about 300 applications, and the assessment team is checking the cases one by one; because the post-migration cost model varies by classification, using a definition incorrectly causes errors in schedule and budget estimates. The assessment results are also used to assign teams to each strategy and to select migration tools, so a pairing of case and strategy must not conflict with the definition. This assessment covers only cases whose facts have already been verified. Which two of the following cases are MOST appropriately linked to the 7 Rs definitions? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: An internal tool consisting only of servers that have had no inbound connections for the last 90 days and have average CPU and memory utilization below 5% is classified as a Retire candidate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Replacing a self-installed CRM, for which the vendor provides a SaaS version, with a SaaS subscription and moving the data to the new system is a Repurchase strategy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Converting servers to AMIs without code changes and moving them to Amazon EC2 is a Refactor strategy that takes advantage of cloud-native features.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leaving a production equipment control app, which cannot be moved right now because of data residency regulations, in its current environment is a Retire strategy.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Installing an on-premises SQL Server on an EC2 instance with the same configuration and moving it is a Replatform strategy that uses some managed services.

exam-sap-c02-39.explanation: The correct answers are utilization-based retirement and Repurchase by replacing with SaaS. The 7 Rs guidance defines servers with no connections for a long period and very low utilization as retirement candidates, and replacing with a vendor SaaS as repurchase. Installing SQL Server on EC2 as is is Rehost, which moves without changes, and moving to a managed service such as Amazon RDS would be Replatform. An application that cannot be migrated because of regulations and is left in the current environment is not Retire but Retain. A migration without code changes is not Refactor but Rehost, and Refactor means changing the architecture to use cloud-native features. Because the question asks for pairs that match the definitions, options that confuse definitions, such as Rehost and Retain, are eliminated for not matching the definitions.

exam-sap-c02-40.prompt: An e-commerce company frequently creates public ALBs in 70 organization accounts. The security team wants every internet-exposed ALB to be automatically associated with a web ACL that contains common AWS WAF managed rules, to have the association restored if it is removed, and to prevent development accounts from removing it arbitrarily. AWS Config is already enabled in the target accounts. New ALBs are created directly by development teams, so the security team cannot set up a prior approval process, and a change to the rules made in one place must be reflected everywhere. The rule groups contain a mix of AWS managed rules and custom rules created by the security team, and when a new threat is confirmed, it must be reflected in all accounts within a day. Development accounts create ALBs directly with AWS CloudFormation or Terraform and must not have permission to modify the web ACL within their accounts. The security team has 3 people. Some of the 70 accounts already create and use their own web ACLs, so when the policy is introduced, the company wants the existing associations to be cleaned up as well. Rule change history must be kept for auditing. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From the AWS Firewall Manager administrator account, create an AWS WAF policy scoped to the entire organization or target OUs, specify ALB as the protected resource type, and turn on automatic remediation of noncompliant resources.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use an SCP to allow the ELB creation API only when a WAF association is present, so that creation of ALBs without a web ACL is denied.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deploy a common web ACL and managed rule groups to each account with a CloudFormation StackSet, have each application team perform the association with the ALB in its deployment pipeline, and check for missing associations in a monthly review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Subscribe all accounts to AWS Shield Advanced and register the ALBs as protected resources so that managed WAF rules are applied automatically.

exam-sap-c02-40.explanation: Firewall Manager is based on AWS Organizations and AWS Config; once you define a policy, it automatically associates a web ACL with existing and new resources (such as ALBs) in the target accounts, and with automatic remediation turned on it restores resources whose association was removed, so it meets the requirements. An SCP cannot check for WAF association as a condition on the ELB creation API, and the WAF association is a separate API, so it cannot implement the requirement. A StackSet only deploys the web ACL and leaves association and restoration of removals to the teams, which violates the requirements. Shield Advanced is a DDoS protection service and does not automatically associate managed WAF rules. Because the company needs automatic association and re-association without a prior approval process, and central rule revisions, a central policy with automatic remediation rather than prevention is required.

exam-sap-c02-41.prompt: A SaaS company's API connects from AWS Lambda to Amazon RDS for MySQL. When Lambda concurrency spikes because of an event, the database's maximum number of connections is exceeded and connection errors occur, and the DB password is stored in plaintext in the function environment variables, which was flagged in an audit. The company also wants to reduce the time connections are dropped during a failover. The database is already an RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ deployment, and Lambda runs in the same VPC. Traffic spikes occur briefly several times a day and most queries are short transactions. The function is written in Python, and concurrency is around 50 in normal times but rises to several hundred during events. The security team wants to rotate the DB password every 90 days but wants to avoid redeploying the function each time it is rotated. The team has 4 people, and changing the database engine or rewriting queries is difficult given the schedule. In the development environment the same function keeps its password separately, so this improvement targets only the production environment. The time from when connections drop during a failover until they recover currently takes more than 1 minute. Which method MOST appropriately meets these requirements while minimizing application changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Raise the DB instance class by one size to increase the maximum number of connections, and put the KMS-encrypted password in the Lambda environment variables for the function to decrypt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set a low reserved concurrency on the Lambda function so that the number of concurrent connections does not exceed the DB limit, and respond with 429 to requests over the limit. Also use a method of sending requests to Amazon SQS during spike periods to process them later.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Place Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Multi-AZ database to pool connections, manage credentials with an AWS Secrets Manager secret or IAM authentication, and have Lambda connect to the proxy endpoint.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a query result cache layer with Amazon ElastiCache to reduce the number of DB connections itself, and keep the cache connection information as constants in the function code instead of environment variables.

exam-sap-c02-41.explanation: The correct answer is RDS Proxy. Connection pooling and reuse keep spiking Lambda connections from exceeding the DB connection limit, during a failover it connects automatically to the standby instance and preserves application connections to shorten the disconnection time, and Secrets Manager or IAM authentication also eliminates the plaintext password. In most cases you only need to change the endpoint, with no code changes. Scaling up the instance only raises cost, is not a fundamental fix, and leaves the password exposure problem. Reserved concurrency gives up processing requests altogether. A cache layer does not solve the write and cache-miss connection problem, and hard-coding credentials in code is the opposite of the audit finding. The requirements of minimal application changes and password rotation point to a proxy that provides connection pooling and credential management at once.

exam-sap-c02-42.prompt: A company is moving its on-premises Oracle 12c database (8 TB) to Aurora PostgreSQL to reduce licensing costs. There are many PL/SQL packages and procedures, and cutover downtime must be within 30 minutes. The on-premises environment and AWS are connected with AWS Direct Connect. Oracle has about 400 PL/SQL packages, some of which use Oracle-specific functions. The application team wants to know in advance the list of objects that will not convert automatically, and the cutover will be performed once on a weekend night. The source has about 1,500 tables, and batches generate writes even on weeknights. The cutover will be performed only once on a weekend night, and a rollback plan is also required. There are 3 DBAs, there is no budget to purchase a new commercial conversion tool, and the migration period is 4 months. The application team can modify some queries. Management requires that not a single record of data be lost during cutover, and it will give cutover approval only after confirming in advance that replication lag is nearly zero. Which migration method MOST appropriately meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Convert the schema and PL/SQL code with AWS DMS Schema Conversion (or AWS SCT), keep CDC running after a full load with DMS, and at cutover stop writes and, once the lag is cleared, switch the application over.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create only a DMS full load and CDC task to replicate to the Aurora PostgreSQL target, use the default table structure created on the target as is, and expect the procedures to work naturally after the migration.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Export an 8 TB dump with Oracle Data Pump, upload it to Amazon S3, and import it directly into Aurora PostgreSQL, applying changes made after the dump with manual SQL. After migrating to the target, reproduce and apply the changes by looking at the application logs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Move Oracle to Amazon RDS for Oracle using the license-included model, and if needed carry out a separate project to move to Aurora PostgreSQL later.

exam-sap-c02-42.explanation: The correct answer is the combination of a schema and code conversion tool with a DMS full load and CDC. A heterogeneous migration must convert code objects such as PL/SQL, so DMS Schema Conversion or SCT is needed, and if CDC catches up with changes after the full load, the cutover downtime can be reduced to within 30 minutes. DMS alone focuses on moving data and does not convert code objects such as procedures. A Data Pump dump is in an Oracle-specific format that PostgreSQL cannot read, and manually applying the changes means a long outage. RDS for Oracle does not meet the goals of reducing licensing cost and moving to Aurora PostgreSQL. Because the list of objects that do not convert automatically must be known in advance and the downtime must be within 30 minutes, the approach that uses conversion assessment together with CDC is right.

exam-sap-c02-43.prompt: A company's web tier is an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB that uses simple scaling based on average CPU and a 300-second cooldown. When requests spike because of an event, it takes 8 minutes after boot for a new instance to enter service, because initialization downloads a large cache dataset to a local EBS volume, and 5xx errors occur during that time. The instances have EBS root volumes and the company uses only On-Demand Instances. On weekdays the service request volume varies by up to 3 times the average during the day, and even if an instance that has finished initialization is stopped and started again, the data downloaded to EBS remains. The team does not use Spot and wants to minimize On-Demand cost increases. Observation shows that the time periods when requests surge are hard to predict, and the 8 minutes it takes one instance to download the whole cache accounts for most of the scale-out delay. The group's minimum capacity is 10 instances, and the ALB health check grace period is already set as needed. The operations team wants a configuration that automatically follows the weekday daytime variation. The cost owner accepts a temporary capacity increase due to scale-out but wants to avoid more idle instances during normal times. All instances download the same cache content. Which actions should be taken to reduce the scale-out delay? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Remove the simple scaling policy and use only scheduled scaling actions to match capacity before the event time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the scaling cooldown to 3,600 seconds so that unnecessary scale-outs do not occur.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure a warm pool and use a lifecycle hook to keep instances that have finished downloading the cache data waiting in a stopped state so that they can be put into service quickly on scale-out.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use a target tracking scaling policy with the ALBRequestCountPerTarget metric as the target value so that capacity increases in proportion to request load.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Change the instance type to one size smaller to shorten boot time and increase the number of instances.

exam-sap-c02-43.explanation: The correct answer is a target tracking policy and a warm pool. A target tracking policy that uses ALBRequestCountPerTarget adjusts capacity in proportion to the increase in requests, so it reacts to load faster than simple scaling, which reacts only after CPU rises. A warm pool prepares instances that have already finished initialization, such as downloading cache data, in a stopped state in advance so that scale-out skips that time, and in the stopped state you pay only for the EBS volumes with no instance cost. Increasing the cooldown makes scale-out even slower. Switching to a smaller instance does not shorten initialization because the amount of data to download is the same, and only the number of instances grows. Scheduled scaling alone cannot respond to unpredictable surges. The condition that post-boot initialization takes 8 minutes calls for a warm pool, and the unpredictable surges call for request-count-based target tracking.

exam-sap-c02-44.prompt: A video processing company's Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group runs On-Demand m5.2xlarge instances that fluctuate between 20 and 40 instances depending on demand, with a daily average of about 28 instances. At least 20 instances are always needed stably for the baseline load, and the excess scales up and down with queue length and can be retried if a job is interrupted. Using Spot with a single instance type has often caused capacity shortages. Jobs finish within 15 minutes, and if interrupted they are returned to the queue and retried, and code that handles the 2-minute Spot interruption notice already exists. The operations team wants to reduce compute cost as much as possible without harming availability. Encoding jobs read from an Amazon SQS queue and delete the message after completion, and the jobs handled by the 20 baseline instances have an SLA and must not be interrupted. The current monthly compute cost is about 20,000 dollars. The m5, m5a, and m6i families can all be used, and instances can be deployed across 3 Availability Zones in the Seoul Region. The operations team wants capacity shortages to be automatically replaced with other instance types and Availability Zone pools so that queue processing delay does not exceed 30 minutes even if Spot interruptions cluster. Currently only a single type is specified, and there have been times when replacement capacity could not be found after an interruption notice. What is the MOST cost-effective way to improve this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the entire group to single-type Spot, and have an operator switch to On-Demand manually when interruptions occur.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Purchase all 40 On-Demand instances as 3-year commitment Reserved Instances to lower the hourly rate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have a separate Spot-only group handle the baseline load up to 20 instances and minimize the On-Demand group by shrinking it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use a mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base capacity of 20 instances and fill the excess with Spot, specifying multiple instance types and Availability Zones and allocating with price-capacity-optimized.

exam-sap-c02-44.explanation: A mixed instances policy guarantees the stability of the 20-instance baseline load with On-Demand base capacity and fills only the excess with Spot, and by specifying multiple instance types and Availability Zones, the capacity pools increase and Spot capacity shortages decrease, and the price-capacity-optimized strategy chooses pools with a low likelihood of interruption and low price. Single-type Spot with manual switching leaves the capacity shortages and reduced availability in place. Committing to all 40 instances for 3 years means committing to 40 instances even in hours when only the average of 28 are used, which wastes money in the fluctuating range. If Spot carries the baseline load, the always-needed 20 instances would be shaken on interruption, which violates the availability constraint. The condition that the 20 baseline instances must not be interrupted and the experience of Spot capacity shortages point to a mix of On-Demand base capacity and multi-type Spot.

exam-sap-c02-45.prompt: In a logistics company's order processing system, order events for the same customer must be processed in the order they occurred, and an event must not be processed twice. There are tens of thousands of customers, and events for different customers must be processed in parallel to achieve throughput. Producers can retry. Thousands of events per second arrive at peak, and consumers scale horizontally across 10 containers. Even when one customer's events surge, processing for other customers must not be blocked, and duplicate processing would lead to payment errors. Each customer has at most a few events per second, and one event takes 200 ms to process on average. A producer may resend the same event on a network error, and the consumer containers restart on every deployment. The team does not want to build a separate database or sharding code for ordering control. After a failure, the producer resends the event with the same unique ID as before, so the deduplication feature can make use of this ID. This system is new development, so the queue type can be chosen freely. Which messaging configuration MOST appropriately meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue, specify the customer ID as the message group ID and the event's unique ID as the deduplication ID, and run multiple consumers to process in parallel by group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use an SQS standard queue, add a timestamp to each message so that consumers sort by customer before processing, and check for duplicates against the application database to see whether processing is complete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use an SQS FIFO queue but specify the same message group ID for all messages to guarantee the order of all events, and increase the number of consumers to raise throughput. Use high throughput mode to avoid throughput limits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Publish events to an Amazon SNS standard topic, create a Lambda subscriber per customer, and have each subscriber receive only that customer's events and process them in order.

exam-sap-c02-45.explanation: The correct answer is a FIFO queue that uses the customer ID as the message group ID. FIFO guarantees strict ordering within the same group, prevents duplicates on producer retries with the deduplication ID, and allows consumers to process different groups concurrently. A standard queue does not guarantee ordering or single delivery, so you would have to implement sorting and duplicate checks on the consumer side yourself. Using a single group ID processes everything sequentially and eliminates parallelism. An SNS standard topic does not guarantee ordering, and a subscriber per tens of thousands of customers is not realistic. Per-customer ordering together with parallel processing across different customers points to a FIFO queue that uses the customer ID as the message group ID.

exam-sap-c02-46.prompt: A company's stateless web tier behind an ALB always needs 20 instances in normal times and up to 40 more at daytime peaks. The instance family must be changeable across future generations. The 20 base instances must not be interrupted, but the extra peak capacity can tolerate some interruptions as long as the ALB and Auto Scaling replenish it. Peaks occur on weekdays between 9 AM and 6 PM, the web servers store no state, and they can accept traffic within 2 minutes of launch. The team has already implemented graceful shutdown on receiving an instance termination notice. The base 20 instances run continuously all year, and the company wants the same commitment to remain valid even when instance generations are upgraded in the future. Outside weekday peak hours, no extra capacity is needed, and the peak extra capacity is used only 9 hours a day. The larger the cost savings the better, but the stability of the base capacity comes first. Partial upfront payment is acceptable. The base 20 instances currently run On-Demand, and using a commitment tool lowers the hourly rate but cannot be canceled during the commitment term, so the company must prepare for changes in instance family. Finance allows commitments of up to 1 year. What is the MOST cost-effective purchasing and placement strategy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Commit the base 20 instances with Compute Savings Plans, and in the Auto Scaling mixed instances policy set the On-Demand base capacity to 20 and fill the peak extra capacity with Spot across multiple instance types.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Commit the entire 60-instance scale with EC2 Instance Savings Plans on a single instance family, and stop unused instances outside peak hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure the entire Auto Scaling group with Spot Instances, using the lowest-price allocation strategy without distinguishing the base 20 from the peak extra capacity. Automatically replace with other Spot pools on interruption and do not distinguish base capacity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run both the base 20 instances and the peak extra capacity On-Demand, manage cost with AWS Budgets alerts, and consider reservations when needed.

exam-sap-c02-46.explanation: The correct answer is the combination of Compute Savings Plans for the base capacity and multi-type Spot for the peak extra capacity. Compute Savings Plans apply even when the instance family, generation, or Region changes, which fits the requirement to change generations. The On-Demand base capacity of 20 instances honors the requirement that they not be interrupted, and Spot across various types helps secure available capacity and greatly lowers the cost of the peak portion. EC2 Instance Savings Plans are tied to one family and are less flexible, and a 60-instance commitment is wasted outside the peak. All Spot violates the requirement that the base 20 instances must not be interrupted. All On-Demand is the most expensive. Because the company must prepare for instance generation changes and the base capacity must not be interrupted, the combination of Compute Savings Plans, On-Demand base capacity, and Spot extra capacity is right.

exam-sap-c02-47.prompt: A financial company's security team wants to use SCPs to prevent member account administrators from leaving the organization (LeaveOrganization) and disabling GuardDuty. However, some legacy workloads and their administrator roles are still running in the management account. The default FullAWSAccess SCP remains in place. In this month's audit, the security team must prove that not only member account administrators but also administrators who operate legacy workloads in the management account cannot disable GuardDuty, and organization management permissions are held only by a small, separate group of staff. All the target member accounts belong to the same OU. The fact that SCPs do not apply to users and roles in the organization's management account is the key issue in this audit. The security team wants to simplify change history by attaching the SCP to one place, either the root or an OU, and the legacy workloads can be migrated within two months. Under the requirement interpretation, SCPs do not apply to actions performed by service-linked roles, and the auditor will check at the account level in which accounts the deny policy has effect. Which actions must be taken to meet the requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: If the same Deny SCP is attached to the management account, it applies equally to the management account's users and roles, so there is no need to migrate the workloads.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attach to the organization root or the target OU an SCP that denies organizations:LeaveOrganization and the actions related to disabling GuardDuty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deny the actions performed by service-linked roles with the same SCP to also block disabling performed on behalf of AWS services.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Move the workloads and administrator permissions running in the management account to a member account so that the SCP applies to them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Remove the FullAWSAccess SCP and attach no Allow SCP so that the default is deny.

exam-sap-c02-47.explanation: The correct answers are attaching a Deny SCP to the root or OU and moving the management account's workloads to a member account. SCPs take effect only on IAM users and roles in member accounts and do not apply to users and roles in the management account, so to control them the workloads must be moved to a member account. Attaching an SCP to the management account has no effect even if it is attached. The actions of service-linked roles cannot be restricted by SCPs, so this approach does not work. Removing FullAWSAccess without a replacement policy would cause all actions in the member accounts to fail, resulting in a total outage rather than the selective blocking that was requested. Because the management account is not affected by SCPs, attaching an SCP to it has no effect and the workloads must be moved to member accounts.

exam-sap-c02-48.prompt: In a financial company's production account, security groups and IAM roles deployed with AWS CloudFormation were modified directly in the console during incident response and no longer match the template. Since then, stack updates fail and it is not known which resources changed or how. The stack has about 40 resources, and some are values that were intentionally changed during incident response and may need to be kept. Under the change management policy, evidence of which values changed must be kept. The change management policy requires that when drift is confirmed, the owner decide whether to carry over the manually changed values and then leave an approval record. The stack does not include a database, and the service runs 24 hours a day, so securing a maintenance window is difficult. The team has 2 people. Some changes are the opening of security group rules, made intentionally during incident response, so the template side may need to be fixed to keep them, while other changes must be reverted to their original values. The team wants to handle the two cases separately. Which method is MOST appropriate for identifying the changes and restoring consistency with the template without interrupting the running service?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delete the stack and deploy it anew from the template to return all resources to their initial state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Manually search AWS CloudTrail logs for modification events and revert all changes one by one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set a CloudFormation stack policy so that later updates overwrite all resources with the template values and manual changes are automatically reverted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run stack drift detection to see the drifted resources and property differences, and then align either the template or the resources to the intended values to restore consistency.

exam-sap-c02-48.explanation: Drift detection shows, resource by resource, the resources and property differences that were changed outside CloudFormation, so by deciding the intended values and either modifying the template or reverting the resources, you can restore consistency without service interruption. Deleting and redeploying the stack replaces production resources and carries a high risk of interruption. Manually searching CloudTrail takes a long time, risks omissions, and is inefficient for the purpose of checking differences against the template. A stack policy is a mechanism that prevents changes to specific resources during an update; it is not a feature that forces overwrites, and it does not tell you what has drifted. Because evidence of changes must be kept and some must be retained, checking the differences with drift detection rather than deleting or overwriting is right.

exam-sap-c02-49.prompt: A shopping mall's web tier uses sticky sessions on an ALB in front of an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group and keeps sessions in instance memory. Every scale-in or instance replacement logs users out and empties shopping carts, causing many complaints. The team wants to make the instances stateless so that it can scale in freely, and both session lookup and update latency must be under 1 millisecond. Session data is a few KB per user, peak concurrent users number 80,000, and the team wants to use a managed service without adding server operations staff. Session data consists of login information, the shopping cart, and coupon codes, and the TTL is 30 minutes. There are currently 20 instances on average, and the team has determined that a separate failover configuration is needed for the session store. Developers can make changes at the level of session library settings but cannot rewrite the entire application. Testing shows that session lookups must finish within an average of 0.4 ms to meet the current response time target. A new requirement has come in that users must stay logged in during blue/green deployments, and losing session data leads to cart abandonment. Which improvement is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the ALB sticky session duration to the maximum so that the same user stays on the same instance for longer, and also slow down the instance replacement cycle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store session files in an Amazon EFS shared directory so that all instances read the same sessions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Move the session store to Amazon ElastiCache and set the session TTL so that instances hold no session state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on scale-in protection for all instances so that instances in use are not terminated.

exam-sap-c02-49.explanation: ElastiCache, an in-memory store, stores sessions with sub-millisecond latency and manages expiration with TTL, so because the instances hold no state, scale-in and replacement do not affect logins. Extending the sticky session duration leaves the problem of sessions disappearing at scale-in or replacement and also harms load distribution. According to the documentation, EFS has read latency of about 1 millisecond and write latency of about 2.7 milliseconds, so it does not meet the requirement that both reads and updates be under 1 millisecond. Scale-in protection blocks scale-in itself, which conflicts with the goal of making instances stateless so that scale-in is free, and it does not solve session loss during replacement. The requirements of sub-millisecond latency and a managed service point to an in-memory store, and EFS does not meet the latency requirement.

exam-sap-c02-50.prompt: A security team has dozens of cases per month across 60 accounts where a security group opens SSH (22) to 0.0.0.0/0, and it closes each one manually every time. The team must handle this from detection to remediation without human intervention, and remediation records must be kept. It wants to minimize custom code. Remediation must happen within an average of 15 minutes of detection, and SSH rules restricted to approved office IPs are considered normal. AWS Config is turned on in all target accounts, and the security team lacks the staff to maintain custom code. Many of the dozens of cases per month are ones that developers opened directly for temporary access in the development environment. The security team has decided that a human approval step before remediation is not needed, and the permissions to run remediation in each account are prepared through a delegated administrator structure. For audit evidence, the team wants to look up remediation history in Config. A notification system is already configured to send an informational email to the developer who requested the work after a rule is remediated. Almost none of the dozens of cases are legitimate rules, but false positives must be minimized. Which method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Receive Amazon GuardDuty findings by email and have an operator delete the relevant security group rule in the console.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Write your own Lambda function that iterates through the security groups in all accounts every hour, deletes risky rules, and leaves logs in Amazon CloudWatch.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use an SCP to deny the entire security group modification API so that no account can open rules.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deploy the AWS Config managed rule restricted-ssh across the entire organization and attach an automatic remediation action that uses an AWS Systems Manager Automation document to noncompliant resources.

exam-sap-c02-50.explanation: The Config managed rule restricted-ssh evaluates security groups that open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 as noncompliant, and an automatic remediation action fixes noncompliant resources with a Systems Manager Automation document without a human, and evaluation and remediation records remain in Config, so almost no custom code is needed. Email notifications and manual deletion involve people, which conflicts with the requirement. A self-built Lambda iteration requires you to maintain per-account permissions, error handling, and the schedule yourself, which goes against the requirement to minimize custom code. Blocking the entire modification API with an SCP would make even legitimate security group changes impossible and paralyze operations. Because the company must handle everything from detection to remediation without human intervention and reduce custom code, the combination of a managed rule and automatic remediation is right.

exam-sap-c02-51.prompt: A media company stores 300 TB of photos and videos in Amazon S3. All objects are 1 MB or larger and the access pattern is unpredictable; many objects go unqueried for months and then suddenly become frequently used again. Reads must always have millisecond response, and there must be no restore wait or per-retrieval charges. The company also wants to reduce the operational burden of continually adjusting lifecycle rules. Data will keep growing, and there is no plan to delete because of legal retention periods. The storage team has no staff to review the storage class policy every month. Most objects are between 5 MB and several GB, and about 2 TB of new data accumulates per day. Editors often suddenly reopen videos that are months old to work on them, so access cannot be predicted. The budget owner wants lower storage cost but will not tolerate work stoppages caused by latency or restore delays. Objects are never modified once written, and versioning is turned off. The budget is approved monthly, and the finance team wants monthly cost fluctuations to be small. Which storage strategy is the MOST cost-effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Store the objects in the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class so that they move automatically between tiers according to access patterns, and do not enable the archive access tiers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store in S3 Standard and apply a lifecycle rule that transitions to Standard-IA after 30 days, with an owner returning frequently accessed objects to Standard. Review monthly and adjust the rules to match access statistics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apply a lifecycle rule that transitions to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and when access is needed, send a standard restore request to create a temporary copy in S3 and then read it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Store all objects in S3 One Zone-IA and run a weekly job that analyzes object access logs and a script that promotes frequently used objects to Standard.

exam-sap-c02-51.explanation: The correct answer is S3 Intelligent-Tiering. When the access pattern changes, it automatically moves between frequency tiers while keeping millisecond access, has no retrieval charges for reads, and has no additional charge for tier movement, so no rule tuning is needed. Because objects are 1 MB or larger, the small per-object monitoring charge is also efficient. Standard-IA adds per-GB retrieval charges on reads and requires manual promotion. Glacier Flexible Retrieval violates the millisecond response requirement because of restore waits. One Zone-IA has retrieval charges and single-AZ risk, and you must operate the promotion script yourself. The conditions of unpredictable access, immediate response, and no restore charges point to automatic tiering without archive tiers.

exam-sap-c02-52.prompt: Five consuming applications read a Kinesis data stream (20 shards, provisioned mode) at an advertising technology company with GetRecords over shared throughput. Since consumers were added, some consumers' iterator age has grown and delivery delay exceeds 1 second, violating the SLA. The company wants to eliminate read contention between consumers while avoiding adding shards, which would increase write costs. All of the consuming applications are KCL 2.x (or 3.x) based apps in the same account whose code cannot be changed significantly, and the record size averages 5 KB, so write throughput has headroom against the shard limit. The five consumers are each owned by a different team and handle billing, real-time bid analysis, fraud click detection, a dashboard, and archiving. Currently the five consumers share the per-shard read limit, and write cost is already close to the budget limit. Each consumer has a different SLA, so one consumer's delay must not affect the others. Enhanced fan-out can be used only with KCL 2.0 and above, and these apps are already on that version, so they can switch by changing only the library's retrieval setting without code changes. The stream is in a single AWS account and all five consumers run in the same Region. Which improvement is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double the number of shards to increase the total shared read throughput across shards.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have each consumer call GetRecords more often by shortening the polling interval and increase the number of calling threads to match the number of consumers to reduce delay.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Register the consumers as enhanced fan-out consumers so that each consumer receives dedicated read throughput per shard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Extend the stream retention period to 7 days so that data is not lost even if consumers fall behind.

exam-sap-c02-52.explanation: Shared throughput consumers split 2 MB/s of reads per shard, so propagation delay grows as consumers increase, and enhanced fan-out is supported with KCL 2.0 and above (if an app is KCL 1.x, the version must be upgraded first), and because these apps are already on that version, they can use it just by switching a setting. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer dedicated read throughput per shard and pushes records, so the contention disappears. Adding shards violates the constraint that write costs increase and also leaves the shared structure among consumers unchanged. Increasing polling runs into the per-shard read call limit and shared throughput even faster and does not resolve the contention. Extending retention only prevents data loss, does not reduce delay, and increases storage cost. Because the company must avoid adding shards that increase write cost and eliminate contention between consumers, an approach that gives each consumer dedicated throughput is right.

exam-sap-c02-53.prompt: A media company wants on-premises servers to access Amazon S3 over a private path through AWS Direct Connect without traversing the internet. Under security policy, on premises must access S3 only through private IP addresses inside a VPC, not S3 public IPs, and a public virtual interface and allowing the S3 public IP ranges are not permitted. Workloads inside the VPC in the same Region should access S3 at no additional cost. On-premises servers look up S3 names through the internal DNS, and the network team also wants to reduce NAT gateway usage cost. This configuration applies to one VPC in the Seoul Region. On premises already has a private virtual interface configured over Direct Connect and has internal DNS servers. S3 access targets only buckets in the Seoul Region, and the network team can set up DNS conditional forwarding. When EC2 workloads in the same VPC access S3, no additional hourly charge should be incurred. The security team must prove at audit time that traffic from on premises to S3 was never placed on an internet route table under any circumstances. There is only one S3 bucket Region, Seoul. DNS lookups from both on premises and the VPC must go to the correct endpoint. Which actions must be taken to configure this to meet both requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create only an S3 gateway endpoint, and route the on-premises routes advertised over Direct Connect toward the gateway endpoint.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an S3 interface VPC endpoint so that on premises can access S3 with private IP addresses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a static route toward the S3 public IP ranges on the on-premises servers and communicate through a public virtual interface.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apply the interface endpoint's private DNS only to the inbound Resolver endpoint, and have workloads inside the VPC use the gateway endpoint.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Send on-premises traffic out to the S3 public endpoint through the NAT gateway in a private subnet.

exam-sap-c02-53.explanation: A gateway endpoint cannot be used for traffic from on premises, from peered VPCs in other Regions, or through a transit gateway, so an interface endpoint is needed for on-premises private IP access. In that case, if private DNS is applied only to the inbound Resolver endpoint, on-premises lookups go to the interface endpoint's private IP and in-VPC lookups go to the gateway endpoint, so the interface endpoint charges are incurred only for on-premises traffic. A gateway endpoint alone cannot be reached from on premises. A NAT gateway is for workloads inside the VPC, is not a path for on-premises traffic, and also incurs data processing charges. A public VIF and a public IP path violate the security policy that access must be only through private IPs. Because on premises must use only private IPs and VPC workloads must incur no additional cost, the two kinds of endpoints are used separately by purpose.

exam-sap-c02-54.prompt: A security operations team wants to receive high-severity GuardDuty findings and Config noncompliance events from 80 organization accounts in a central security account and run an automated isolation Lambda function. Accounts are added frequently, and the central account's credentials or long-term access keys must not be stored in each account. The event forwarding rules and the forwarding IAM roles in each account are already set up to be deployed automatically to new accounts by the account baseline StackSet. The security team does not want to ask each account owner for separate configuration even as accounts grow, and the delay from when an event occurs until the isolation Lambda function runs must be within 1 minute. The isolation Lambda function runs in the central account, and the permission to isolate target accounts is already configured through role delegation. The event types are GuardDuty findings and Config compliance changes, and thousands occur per day. The central security account has 3 owners and does not want to manage separate queues or subscriptions for each account. The IAM role for event forwarding is already deployed in each account, and the central account's event bus name is the same in every account. The target events are small and do not hit forwarding limits. Which configuration meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Put a resource policy on the central account event bus that allows PutEvents from organization accounts with the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition, have each account's rule specify the central bus as its target, and have a central rule invoke the Lambda function.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Publish events from each account to an Amazon SNS topic, and have a Lambda function in the central account subscribe to all topics with IAM user access keys.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Send each account's events to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and have a Lambda function in the central account query the log groups of all accounts every 5 minutes to check the conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a separate event bus per account ID in the central account, and operate a procedure that adds the new account's ID to the bus policy whenever a new account is created.

exam-sap-c02-54.explanation: The resource-based policy of an EventBridge event bus can grant permission with an organization condition, so new accounts can send events without modifying the central policy, and because the rule deployed as part of the baseline specifies the central bus as its target, no long-term credentials are needed. The SNS subscription and access key approach violates the constraint of not storing long-term keys. Log polling has a 5-minute interval, so it cannot meet the 1-minute isolation requirement, and it requires giving query permissions to all accounts, which is a heavy operational burden. Per-account-ID buses and the policy modification procedure require human intervention for every new account, so they do not suit an environment where accounts are added frequently. The conditions of no long-term credentials and no configuration needed even as accounts grow point to a central event bus with an organization-level resource policy.

exam-sap-c02-55.prompt: A company must deploy an audit IAM role and a CloudWatch alarm baseline to 120 accounts in 3 organizational units (OUs) in its organization and to accounts created in the future. The baseline template is revised once or twice a month, and revisions must be applied consistently to all accounts. The company does not want to create a pre-provisioned administrator role in each account. Deployment results must be viewable in one place, and when a new account is created, the baseline must be in place within a day. The security team wants to minimize the principals that have permission to deploy IAM roles. The baseline contains one IAM role that auditors use read-only and 12 CloudWatch alarms, and the names must be identical in all accounts. New accounts are created by Control Tower, and the target OUs do not change. The security team wants to see on one screen which account failed and why when a deployment fails. Currently, every time an account is created, the owner manually copies the baseline in the console, which often causes omissions lasting weeks, and an audit finding noted that some accounts remain on an older version after revisions. The baseline targets only the Seoul Region, not all Regions. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a self-managed StackSet, manually create a StackSet execution role in each account, and directly specify and update the list of target accounts for deployment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Share an AWS Service Catalog portfolio with the organization and ask each account administrator to launch the baseline product themselves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a service-managed AWS CloudFormation StackSet for the target OUs with trusted access enabled with AWS Organizations, and enable automatic deployment so that template revisions and deployment to new accounts are handled automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Have a script in the management account assume the OrganizationAccountAccessRole and deploy the stack to each account in a loop, detect new accounts with a weekly cron job and deploy to them, and have an owner retry failed accounts manually.

exam-sap-c02-55.explanation: A service-managed StackSet automatically configures the required roles through Organizations trusted access, so no per-account pre-provisioned role is needed. With automatic deployment on, the stack is deployed automatically to accounts added to the target OUs, and updating the template applies the same change to all target accounts. The self-managed method conflicts with the constraint of having to create an execution role in each account. Service Catalog requires account administrators to launch it themselves, so it does not result in consistent enforced deployment. A looping script and cron are self-built automation, so you are responsible for error handling and revision consistency yourself, and reflecting new accounts is delayed by up to a week. Because the baseline must be deployed automatically, even to new accounts, without a pre-provisioned administrator role, a service-managed StackSet is right.

exam-sap-c02-56.prompt: A financial group operates 140 member accounts in AWS Organizations across multiple OUs, and new accounts are created every week. Because of data residency regulations, it must preventively block resource creation in Regions other than Seoul (ap-northeast-2) and N. Virginia (us-east-1), and the actions of the account root user are also in scope. However, calls to global services such as IAM, Amazon CloudFront, and Amazon Route 53 must continue to work. The security team manages policy change history in a code repository, and this control must be deployed before the external audit next quarter. Besides the approved Regions, some services provide global endpoints only in us-east-1. The team wants a staged rollout in which the policy is applied first to a test OU to check the impact and then broadened to the root. Policy documents go through code review in Git, the security team has 3 people, and no exception accounts are allowed. The service-linked roles and the management account are outside the effect of SCPs, so it has already been decided to put a separate control on the management account side. This question targets all principals in member accounts, including the root user. Which method that applies automatically to new accounts without per-account manual work has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leave the default FullAWSAccess SCP as is, and additionally attach to the root an SCP with an Allow statement that permits only the approved Regions so that actions in other Regions are blocked, opening the global services with a separate Allow statement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deploy AWS Config rules to all accounts to detect resources created in nonapproved Regions, and configure a Lambda function to delete those resources immediately upon detection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach to the IAM users and roles in each member account a permissions boundary that denies actions in nonapproved Regions, and have the account creation pipeline apply the same permissions boundary automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Attach to the organization root an SCP that denies when aws:RequestedRegion is not an approved Region, and exclude global service actions from the deny with NotAction.

exam-sap-c02-56.explanation: A Deny SCP attached to the organization root is inherited by all child OUs and new accounts and also applies to the account root user, so using the aws:RequestedRegion condition together with a NotAction exception for global services implements the preventive control in one step. An SCP that adds an Allow statement while FullAWSAccess is kept blocks nothing, because a policy allowing all actions remains. The AWS Config and Lambda deletion approach reacts after the resource is created, so it is after-the-fact detection and does not meet the preventive requirement. A permissions boundary applies only to IAM users and roles, so it cannot block the root user and needs application work in every account. Note, however, that SCPs do not apply to the management account. Because the control must also block the root user and make global services exceptions, an aws:RequestedRegion deny SCP with a NotAction exception is right.

exam-sap-c02-57.prompt: A SaaS company connects production (prod) VPCs in 6 accounts, development (dev) VPCs in 9 accounts, and a shared services VPC that hosts common tools to a single transit gateway. Communication between production and development VPCs must be blocked at the network level, both environments must be able to reach the shared services VPC, and adding a new VPC must not require modifying the existing routing configuration. The network team has only 3 people and cannot handle routing change requests manually, and during compliance reviews the isolation between environments must be demonstrated through the routing configuration. Isolation between environments is verified through routing, and 2 to 3 new VPCs are created each month. The shared services VPC hosts DNS, CI tools, and an artifact repository, which both environments must reach. The CIDRs of all VPCs do not overlap, and the transit gateway is in a single Region, Seoul. The servers in the shared services VPC must respond to requests from both environments, so the return path must also work in both directions. Isolating with network ACLs or security groups alone is not accepted by auditors. Which design meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create separate transit gateway route tables for production, development, and shared services, associate each attachment with its corresponding table, propagate only the shared services route to the production and development tables, and propagate the routes of both environments to the shared services table.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Propagate the routes of all attachments to a single default route table, and set deny rules for the other environment's CIDR in the security groups and network ACLs of the production and development VPCs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enter blackhole static routes in the default route table that point production and development CIDRs at each other, and update the blackhole routes with the new CIDR every time a VPC is added.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create separate transit gateways per environment and connect each to the shared services VPC with VPC peering, create no peering between production and development, allocate separate CIDR ranges to each environment, and have each environment's team approve routing changes.

exam-sap-c02-57.explanation: If you associate attachments with per-environment transit gateway route tables and propagate only the required routes, production and development do not have each other's routes, so they are separated at the network level, and a new VPC only needs to be associated with the corresponding table and propagated to the shared services table. Blocking with security groups and ACLs on a single default table leaves routing open, so it is not network-level separation, and the rules grow with every account. Blackhole static routes require editing CIDRs every time a VPC is added, which violates the requirement not to modify the existing configuration. Mixing per-environment transit gateways with peering increases the number of gateways and peering connections and adds more operational burden. Because routing changes must not be needed when VPCs are added and isolation must be demonstrated through routing, separating TGW route tables and using propagation is right.

exam-sap-c02-58.prompt: A retailer's network team controls VPCs, subnets, route tables, and NAT gateways in a central network account, and wants the 30 application team accounts in the same organization to deploy Amazon EC2 and Amazon RDS directly into that network. Teams must not be able to see each other's resources and must not be able to change routing or subnet configuration, and the goal is to reduce the number of VPCs to manage and the cost of connections between accounts (peering and transit gateway attachments). The security team must demonstrate at audit time that team accounts cannot arbitrarily change subnets and routing, and the network team wants to consolidate NAT gateway costs in one place. Application teams must be able to launch their own EC2 and RDS directly in the subnets, but security groups are managed by the team accounts themselves. The central network account operates the NAT gateways and VPC flow logs in one place, and all 30 accounts are in the same organization and the same Region. RDS is owned by the team accounts, and the central account is not involved in subnet group configuration. Isolation between teams has already been agreed upon through security groups and IAM. The network team has 3 people. Which approach MOST appropriately meets the requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a VPC in each team account and connect them all to a transit gateway, control traffic with the central route table, and give teams no permission to modify attachments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a VPC in each team account, establish VPC peering with the network VPC, and restrict permission to edit route tables with IAM policies so that teams cannot change routes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have the network account share the subnets with the team accounts in the organization by using AWS RAM, and have the team accounts deploy their own resources directly into the shared subnets.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Publish the service in the network VPC as a PrivateLink endpoint service, and have each team account VPC create an interface endpoint to access it.

exam-sap-c02-58.explanation: With VPC subnet sharing, the VPC owner (the network account) shares subnets with participant accounts in the same organization, and the participant accounts create their own resources such as EC2 and RDS in those subnets, cannot see other participants' resources, and the number of VPCs and cross-account connections also decreases. Routing and subnets are controlled by the owner. Creating a VPC per team and joining them with a transit gateway increases VPCs and attachments in proportion to the number of accounts, which is the opposite of the reduction goal. VPC peering also increases VPCs and connections per account and weakens control because teams own their own VPCs. PrivateLink is a service-level access mechanism and not a way to deploy team resources into a central network. Because teams must not be able to change subnet configuration and the number of VPCs and NAT cost must be reduced, RAM subnet sharing is right.

exam-sap-c02-59.prompt: A fintech's payment lookup API runs hundreds of AWS Lambda functions concurrently and connects to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. During every marketing event, the number of connections reaches max_connections, causing connection errors and CPU spikes. Requests should be queued and processed rather than rejected whenever possible, and application changes must be limited to replacing the connection endpoint. The database is already a Multi-AZ configuration, the write load is not high, and a secondary goal is to reduce the time application connections are dropped during a failover. The Lambda functions are written in Node.js, and concurrency rises to 10 times normal during events. The connection information is specified by a host name in an environment variable, so only the endpoint string needs to be changed, and with a team of 3, there is no capacity to write and maintain connection pooling logic ourselves. Events are held two or three times per quarter. A recent incident report recorded that when payment lookup requests are rejected during connection errors, retries from merchant apps flood in and make the situation worse. Which improvement is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lower the Lambda function reserved concurrency to at or below the database max_connections to throttle excess requests, and modify the client code so that callers retry with exponential backoff.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scale the Aurora instance to a larger class to raise the max_connections value and leave function concurrency as it is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the Lambda code to open a new connection on each invocation and close it immediately after processing so that idle connections do not accumulate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora cluster and have the Lambda functions connect to the proxy endpoint so that database connections are pooled and reused.

exam-sap-c02-59.explanation: RDS Proxy maintains and reuses a connection pool and queues or throttles connections that cannot be handled immediately, so spiking Lambda connections do not overwhelm the database, and it can be introduced just by replacing the endpoint. Lowering with reserved concurrency throttles excess requests, which conflicts with the requirement not to reject requests. Scaling up the instance raises the limit but leaves the connection surge pattern unchanged, so it only adds cost and does not solve the root cause. Opening and closing a connection on each invocation increases connection creation load and actually worsens the problem. Application changes must be limited to replacing the endpoint and requests should be queued whenever possible, so a connection pooling proxy is right, while throttling rejects requests.

exam-sap-c02-60.prompt: A company that is migrating from Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL using a DMS full load and CDC is preparing for cutover. It wants to switch over with no data loss or inconsistency at cutover. The source database operates until just before the switch, and downtime must be short. The source Oracle receives writes until just before the switch, and the migration team performed one rehearsal before cutover. Some of the target tables have LOB columns, so it is hard to be confident of consistency from row counts alone. The Oracle source retains archive logs for the last 3 days, and the DMS replication instance has ample CPU headroom. Cutover approval is given by two owners only after they review evidence of data consistency, and the evidence must include validation results provided by DMS. The cutover window is 2 hours starting at 2 AM. Some tables in the source Oracle have no primary key, which made change tracking tricky, and in the rehearsal the row counts of two tables temporarily diverged and were resolved as CDC caught up. After the switch, the source is kept read-only for a week. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the cutover window, stop application writes, confirm that the DMS source and target CDC latency metrics are close to 0 and that validation has passed, and then switch the connections to the target database.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before cutover, reduce the source database's change log retention period to the minimum so that DMS has less log to read and CDC runs faster. Record the rehearsal results on the team wiki and check the change log retention period again.

choices.label: C
choices.text: While the source is still receiving writes, stop the DMS task immediately and switch connections to the target database, and clean up changes after the stop with a later batch.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Just before starting the cutover, restart the DMS task with the reload-target option to reload the tables from scratch, which automatically guarantees consistency.

choices.label: E
